A diagonal entry is one with y = y, where the prediction agrees with the label, so the diagonal counts the correctly classified data points, and the off-diagonal entries count each kind of misclassification separately. The standard classification metrics are ratios of entries of the confusion matrix. The accuracy is the sum of the diagonal divided by m. Normalizing a row by its sum yields the fraction of data points of that class that are detected (for the positive class, the recall), while normalizing a column yields the fraction of predictions of that class that are right, the precision. For the learned classifier of Fig.~2, with frost as the positive class, the recall is 1/6 and the precision is 1/2. The baseline has a recall of 0, and its precision is not defined at all, since it never predicts frost (pythondemos/cm.py). On imbalanced data, the confusion matrix exposes what a large accuracy can hide. A classifier that never predicts the rare class fills the row of that class with misclassifications while keeping most predictions correct. The always-above-zero baseline in Fig.~2 does exactly that (see baseline). All numbers above are computed on the training set D(train), the 40 days the classifier was learned from. A frost warning is judged on days that did not belong to D(train), so the confusion matrix, and every ratio taken from it, must be computed again on a validation set before one classifier is preferred over the other.

terms.name: convex
terms.abstract: A subset of the Euclidean space is convex if it contains the line segment between any two of its points. A function is convex if its epigraph is a convex set. A convex optimization problem is the minimization of a convex function over a convex set. Empirical risk minimization is a convex optimization problem whenever the hypothesis space is parameterized by a convex set of model parameters and the loss function is convex in those model parameters. Any local minimizer of a convex objective function is necessarily also a global minimizer, so a method that reaches a local minimum has solved the optimization problem.
terms.description: Many machine learning methods learn model parameters by an iterative optimization method: each iteration updates the current model parameters to reduce an objective function within a neighborhood of these model parameters. Widely used examples are gradient descent and its variants. These optimization methods work particularly well when the objective function is a convex function of the model parameters. Indeed, for a convex function every local minimum is necessarily a global minimum: any choice of model parameters at which no small change reduces the objective function already attains the smallest value that the objective function takes anywhere. The average squared error loss of linear regression is a convex function of the model parameters, and so is the objective function of the support vector machine. Empirical risk minimization over a hypothesis space parameterized by a convex set of model parameters, with a loss function that is convex in them, is a convex optimization problem: the minimization of a convex function over a convex set. For differentiable convex objective functions and suitable step size choices, gradient descent converges to such a minimum. Convexity is defined both for sets and for functions. For sets, the definition is geometric. A subset C ⊆ Rd of the Euclidean space Rd is referred to as convex if it contains the line segment between any two of its points. For w, w' ∈ C, that is \beta {\mathbf w} + (1-\beta) {\mathbf w}' \in \mathcal{C} \quad \text{for all } \beta \in [0,1] \text{.} Similarly, a function f: Rd → R is convex if its epigraph ( wᵀ,t )ᵀ ∈ Rd+1: t ≥ f(w) is a convex set. Examples of a convex set and of a convex function are illustrated in Fig. 1. Two families of convex sets appear throughout machine learning. The first is the halfspace w ∈ Rd: aᵀ w ≤ b. It is determined by a nonzero normal vector a ∈ Rd 0, which fixes the direction of the bounding hyperplane, and an offset b ∈ R, which fixes its position. If two points satisfy the inequality, so does every point of the segment between them. The second is the convex hull of finitely many vectors x(1), …, x(m). It is defined as the set of all their convex combinations, \[ \operatorname{conv}\big\{ {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf x}^{(m)} \big\} := \Big\{ \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta_{r} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} : \beta_{r} \geq 0 \text{ for } r = 1, \ldots, m, \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta_{r} = 1 \Big\} \text{.} \] It is the smallest convex set that contains these vectors. Halfspaces are not merely one example among others. Every closed convex set is given by the intersection of all halfspaces that contain it \begin{equation} \mathcal{C} = \bigcap \big\{ H \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d} : H \text{ is a halfspace}, \mathcal{C} \subseteq H \big\} \text{.} \end{equation} In general, intersecting a subset of the halfspaces containing a convex set yields a convex set that contains the original one, i.e., an outer approximation (see Fig.~2). Approximate inference in probabilistic models defined over a graph uses this construction. The set of achievable marginal distributions is a convex set described by a large number of linear inequalities. Message-passing methods optimize over an outer approximation of it obtained from a subset of those inequalities. Returning to the halfspace intersection \eqref{equ_halfspace_intersection_dict}, that intersection can be narrowed: it needs to consider only those halfspaces that are bounded by a supporting hyperplane. Every boundary point of a non-empty convex set carries such a hyperplane, and each point outside the set is already excluded by one of the halfspaces that these supporting hyperplanes bound: for a point x ∉ C and C closed, there is a unique nearest point p ∈ C to x. That nearest point is a boundary point of C, and therefore one of the points that carry a supporting hyperplane: a point of the interior could be moved a little toward x and would still lie in C, so it would not be the nearest one. The hyperplane through p with normal vector x - p supports C at p, and the halfspace it bounds contains C but not x (see Fig.~3). Fig.~4 shows eight supporting hyperplanes of an ellipse. For the epigraph of a differentiable convex function f, the supporting hyperplane is determined by the gradient. At the boundary point (wᵀ, f(w))ᵀ, its normal vector is (∇ f(w)ᵀ, -1)ᵀ, since \[ \big(\nabla f({\mathbf w})^{\top}, -1\big) \left[ \begin{pmatrix} {\mathbf w}' t \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} {\mathbf w} f({\mathbf w}) \end{pmatrix} \right] \leq 0 \quad \text{for every } \big({\mathbf w}'^{\top}, t\big)^{\top} \in \operatorname{epi} f \text{.} \] This is the first-order condition f(w') ≥ f(w) + ∇ f(w)ᵀ (w' - w) written as a statement about the epigraph. Of the two families of convex sets introduced above, the convex hull is the one that characterizes the linear separability of data points with binary label values. Consider m data points with feature vectors x(r) ∈ Rd and labels y(r) ∈ -1,+1, for r = 1, …, m. These data points are linearly separable if some linear classifier predicts every label correctly, i.e., there are w ∈ Rd 0 and b ∈ R with y(r) ( wᵀ x(r) + b ) > 0 for r = 1, …, m. This holds precisely when the convex hull of the feature vectors labeled +1 and the convex hull of those labeled -1 do not intersect. Separability is therefore a property of two convex sets built from the data points. Convexity also appears in the study of probabilistic models, where it singles out a widely used family. In particular, an exponential family is constituted by the probability distributions whose probability density function has the form \[ p({\mathbf x}; {\mathbf w}) = h({\mathbf x}) \exp\big({\mathbf w}^{\top} \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x}) - A({\mathbf w})\big) \text{.} \] This probability density function is parameterized by the vector w and the sufficient statistics t(·). The log-partition function A is fully determined by requiring p(x; w) to integrate to one. Its Hessian is the covariance matrix of the sufficient statistics t(x) under p(x; w), \[ \nabla^{2} A({\mathbf w}) = {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x}) \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x})^{\top} \big\} - {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x}) \big\} {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x}) \big\}^{\top} \text{,} \] which is positive semi-definite. A twice-differentiable function whose Hessian is positive semi-definite is convex, so A is a convex function on its domain. The convexity of A implies that the negative log-likelihood function of a training set, up to an additive constant that does not depend on w, \[ - \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf w}^{\top} \mathbf{t}\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) + m A({\mathbf w}) \text{,} \] is a convex function of w. Thus, for an exponential family, maximum likelihood estimation is a convex optimization problem.

terms.name: covariance matrix
terms.abstract: The covariance matrix of a random vector consists of the covariances between its entries. In particular, the diagonal entries are the variances of the individual entries. Together with the mean vector, the covariance matrix collects the second-order statistics of a random vector. For a Gaussian random vector, the mean vector and the covariance matrix determine the linear hypothesis with the smallest risk and that risk: the model parameters of this hypothesis and its risk are computed from the entries of the covariance matrix. For a Gaussian random vector, the smallest risk of predicting one entry from the others under the squared error loss is the reciprocal of a diagonal entry of the inverse matrix of the covariance matrix, the precision matrix.
terms.description: A patient's record holds d biomarker measurements, such as blood pressure, cholesterol, and glucose, and across patients some pairs of them rise and fall together while others do not. The covariance matrix of the measurement vector records, for every pair, how strongly the two vary together, and on its diagonal how much each varies on its own. Formally, the covariance matrix of a random vector x ∈ Rd is defined as the expectation of the outer product of the centered vector x - Ex with itself (if it exists): \mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})} := \mathbb{E} \bigg \{ \big( {\mathbf x} - \mathbb{E} \big\{ {\mathbf x} \big\} \big) \big({\mathbf x} - \mathbb{E} \big\{ {\mathbf x} \big\} \big)^{\top} \bigg\} \text{.} The entry in row j and column j' is the covariance of the entries xj and xj', with the diagonal entries ( C(x) )j,j, the entries in row j and column j, being the variances of the individual entries. The mean vector Ex is the center of the cloud of realizations in Fig.~1 and of the ellipse drawn there. Two properties follow directly from the definition. A covariance matrix is always positive semi-definite, i.e., vᵀ C(x) v ≥ 0 for every v ∈ Rd, since this quadratic form is the variance of vᵀ x. It is invertible, and then positive definite, exactly when no entry of x is, with probability one, an affine function of the other entries, since the variance of vᵀ x vanishes for some v ≠ 0 exactly when vᵀ x is constant with probability one. Invertibility is assumed wherever the inverse matrix ( C(x) )-1 appears below. The empirical counterpart computed from a dataset is the sample covariance matrix. Fig.~1 shows how the entries of the matrix are visible in a cloud of realizations: the variances set the spread of the cloud along the two axes, and a nonzero covariance tilts it. Beyond describing a cloud of realizations, the covariance matrix determines the best predictions within it. Fig.~2 shows this for a regression task with one feature. The data points of a training set, a validation set, and a test set are modeled as realizations of independent and identically distributed Gaussian random vectors z(r) = ( x(r), y(r) )ᵀ ~ N(μ,C) (see multivariate normal distribution). The ellipse in Fig.~2 is the constant-density contour z: (z - μ)ᵀ C-1 (z - μ) = 4 of this probability distribution. Its principal axes point along the eigenvectors v(1), v(2) of the covariance matrix C, with lengths proportional to the square roots 1, 2 of the corresponding eigenvalues (see eigenvalue decomposition). The long axis of the ellipse is the direction of largest variance of z. The same ellipse fixes the best prediction of the label from the feature. The hypothesis with the smallest risk under the squared error loss is linear for this probabilistic model, with slope given by the ratio of the covariance between x and y to the variance of x (see linear regression). Its risk is the variance of y minus the squared covariance between x and y divided by the variance of x, so both the slope, a model parameter of the linear model, and the smallest risk are computed from the entries of C. With more than two entries, the inverse matrix of the covariance matrix takes over the role of the ellipse. The biomarker example of the opening paragraph shows how. Predicting one feature of a data point from its other features is a common task in health records. Each data point is a patient, and the entries x1, …, xd of x are biomarker measurements. The biomarker xj of a new patient, being expensive to measure, is to be predicted from the remaining ones. The smallest risk achievable by such a prediction is 1 / ( ( C(x) )-1 )j,j, the reciprocal of the diagonal entry ( ( C(x) )-1 )j,j of the inverse matrix of an invertible covariance matrix, as shown below. This inverse matrix is referred to as the precision matrix. The remaining features form the vector x-j := ( x1, …, xj-1, xj+1, …, xd )ᵀ ∈ Rd-1. For a Gaussian random vector x ~ N(μ,C(x)) (see multivariate normal distribution), the conditional probability distribution of xj, given x-j, is Gaussian with a variance that does not depend on the value of x-j. This conditional variance is 1 / ( ( C(x) )-1 )j,j. This conditional variance becomes a bound on every machine learning method once the data points follow the same Gaussian probabilistic model. Let the data points be realizations of independent and identically distributed random vectors x(r) ~ N(μ,C(x)). The conditional variance is also the smallest risk that any hypothesis can achieve under the squared error loss, \[ \min_{h: \mathbb{R}^{d-1} \to \mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E} \Big\{ \big( x_{j} - h\big({\mathbf x}_{-j}\big) \big)^{2} \Big\} = 1 \big/ \big( \big( \mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})} \big)^{-1} \big)_{j,j} \text{.} \] This smallest risk is the Bayes risk of this regression problem. It is attained by the Bayes estimator E xj | x-j, which depends linearly on x-j in the Gaussian case. Since the smallest risk of predicting xj from the other features is 1 / ( ( C(x) )-1 )j,j, the diagonal of ( C(x) )-1 yields a baseline, one entry per feature. A large diagonal entry marks a biomarker that the remaining biomarkers predict with a small squared error, and under this probabilistic model no machine learning method can push the risk of predicting that biomarker below 1 / ( ( C(x) )-1 )j,j, the reciprocal of its diagonal entry.

terms.name: data
terms.abstract: Data are representations of information, recorded in a form suitable for storage, communication and processing, and the word carries three technical senses in machine learning. In its general sense, it denotes recorded information in a form suitable for processing by machine learning methods. As a data point, it is an elementary information-carrying unit; as a dataset, it is an indexed collection of data points. A related regulatory term, personal data, is defined in the general data protection regulation and adopted by the EU AI Act.
terms.description: A weather station measures the temperature at its location and stores the value 23.4 ∘C together with a timestamp (see Fig.~1(a)). Such recorded values are data: representations of information, recorded in a form suitable for storage, communication, and processing by ML systems. Every machine learning method trains a model on data, and the usefulness of the hypothesis the method learns is limited by the quality and quantity of the available data. The word data is used in three technical senses, summarized in Fig.~1, and additionally in a legal sense. In its broadest use, data refer to recorded information. This sense applies when the distinction between unit and collection is irrelevant. Examples are raw sensor measurements such as the temperature reading in Fig.~1(a) and compound terms such as data parallelism, networked data, and data augmentation. As a formal unit, a data point is the fundamental information-carrying unit (Fig.~1(b)). Its information is contained in two types of properties: features, which are easy to measure or compute, and labels, which are difficult to measure or compute or need human annotation. The formal model of a domain set, a label set and a labeling function that assigns each domain point its label is given by Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014, Sect. 2.1). As a formal collection, a dataset D = z(1), …, z(m) is the indexed collection of data points on which model training and validation are performed (Fig.~1(c)). The word data also carries a regulatory meaning. The general data protection regulation defines personal data as any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. The EU AI Act adopts that definition and defines biometric data as personal data resulting from specific technical processing. Several regulatory obligations on ML systems, including the data minimization principle, the right to erasure, and the right to explanation, refer to data in this legal sense.

terms.name: data augmentation
terms.abstract: Data augmentation enlarges a training set with synthetic data points obtained from transformations or perturbations of existing ones. Typical examples are rotating or cropping an image and adding small perturbations to the features and labels of a measured data point. If the label does not change under a transformation, training on transformed copies makes the learned hypothesis vary little under it. Sensing devices measure with limited precision, so perturbed copies reflect the uncertainty interval around each recorded value. Data augmentation is a form of regularization, beside model pruning and adding a penalty term to the training error. For linear regression, perturbing the features with zero-mean noise is equivalent to adding the ridge regression penalty term.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows three data points that represent daily weather conditions at Krems an der Donau. Each data point is characterized by the maximum daytime temperature as its feature x, and the maximum daytime temperature of the next day as its label y. The figure also shows a learned hypothesis map h, obtained by empirical risk minimization using the polynomials of degree two as hypothesis space. The learned hypothesis achieves zero training error but delivers poor predictions outside the training set, which is overfitting. On a held-out set of 125 data points obtained from other days of 2024, whose feature lies inside the measured range, its average squared error loss is 256.2 squared degrees. One reason for the failure of h is that the training set is too small. For almost every training set of sample size m = 3 there is one polynomial of degree two passing through its data points. Data augmentation enlarges a dataset with synthetic data points, obtained by carefully chosen perturbations of the features and labels of the measured ones. Sensing devices have imperfections such as thermal noise, so a reading x is one representative of an uncertainty interval U(x). Any other value from that interval could have been observed instead. Considering the weather data from Fig.~1, a temperature reading x carries U(x) = [x - 1, x + 1]. Each measured day ( x,y ) is replaced by 400 copies ( x + ε,y + ε' ), whose perturbations ε and ε' are realizations of RVs distributed uniformly on [-1, 1]. The augmented training set D holds 1200 data points, none of which required a new temperature measurement. Fig.~1 also shows the polynomial of degree two h' that empirical risk minimization learns using D as training set. The hypothesis h' no longer passes through the three measured days, but it behaves much better outside the training set. Its training error on them is 2.8 squared degrees, but its average squared error loss on the held-out data points falls to 24.7. The coefficient of x2 drops from w2 = 0.71 for h to w2' = 0.06 for h'. The choice of the uncertainty interval used for the perturbation of the features and labels is a hyperparameter. One basic way to determine it is to try a few choices and compare the validation error of the resulting learned hypotheses. Enlarging D with perturbed copies is one basic form of regularization, beside model pruning, which shrinks the hypothesis space, and adding a penalty term to the training error. These different forms of regularization are sometimes equivalent in their effect on the learned hypothesis (Fig.~2). For linear regression, adding zero-mean perturbations with covariance matrix σ2 I to each feature vector yields the ridge regression solution, asymptotically in the number of copies. Its penalty term is σ2 ‖ w ‖22 for the weight vector w. Instead of adding noise to the features and labels, perturbations can also come from a transformation T of the feature space. A transformation known to leave the label alone is a symmetry of the learning task. A rotated or cropped image of a cat still shows a cat, while its feature vector, obtained by stacking the pixel color intensities, changes. The transformation must preserve the label, and a rotation does so only up to a point. Fig.~3 reduces images of the handwritten digits 6 and 9 to their first two principal directions (see principal component analysis) as features x1, x2. A small rotation T keeps an image of a 6 among the other 6s. However, rotating an image by 180 degrees carries it into the 9s, where the label has changed.

terms.name: data imputation
terms.abstract: Data imputation replaces missing attribute values of data points by estimates computed from the attribute values that were recorded. In tabular data a missing value is an empty cell of the table, and imputation fills the cell. It is one response to missing data, alongside discarding the incomplete data points. The filling is a machine learning problem: the missing value is the label of a data point, the recorded values beside it are its features, and the complete data points form a training set on which a hypothesis map (an imputer) is learned.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau records, for each day, the minimum temperature, the precipitation, and the maximum temperature. The year 2024 is therefore a table with one row per day and one column per quantity. This table is tabular data. A day on which the thermometer failed leaves the maximum-temperature cell of its row empty, while the table keeps its shape (Fig.~1). Data imputation fills such a cell: it replaces missing attribute values of data points, features or labels, by estimates computed from the attribute values that were recorded. It is one response to missing data, alongside discarding the incomplete data points or using a method that tolerates the gaps. The filling is a machine learning problem. The empty cell is the label of its row, and the recorded cells of the same row are its features. The complete rows form a training set, since each one supplies both a feature vector and the label that belongs with it. A hypothesis map, an imputer, is learned from them by empirical risk minimization. Applying that hypothesis to an incomplete row yields the estimate that fills its cell. The simplest imputation fills every empty cell of a column with the sample mean of the recorded cells of that column, which is the hypothesis that ignores the feature vector. A numerical experiment takes 15 days spread over the year and empties the maximum-temperature cells of 3 of them. From the 12 complete rows, it learns a linear regression hypothesis that maps the minimum temperature of a day to its maximum temperature. The emptied cells are then filled with its predictions, shown as a scatterplot in Fig.~2. The removed values are known, so the filling can be evaluated. The average squared error loss on the 3 cells, in squared degrees Celsius, is 17.6 for the learned hypothesis and 150.2 for the column average. A missing value can sit among other missing values, so that the feature vector of its row is itself incomplete. The filling then proceeds in sweeps: the missing values start at the sample mean of the recorded ones, and each sweep re-estimates them from the values that their neighbors currently hold, until the values no longer change. Rectangular patches lost from an aerial photograph are such a case. Each pixel is a data point, its features are the colors of the eight pixels around it, and its label is its own color. A numerical experiment fills the lost pixels with a linear regression hypothesis learned from the intact ones. The average squared error loss on the lost pixels is half that of the baseline that fills every one of them with the average color, and the boundaries where the colors change sharply come out blurred. An imputed value is an estimate and not a measurement, and a method trained on imputed data points cannot tell the two apart. Part of the training set was produced by a hypothesis rather than observed, so the training error it reports is smaller than the loss on measured values. A single filled value also carries no information about the uncertainty of the estimate. Recording which values were imputed, and keeping them out of the test set, keeps the estimate of the risk free of values that a hypothesis produced.

terms.name: data leakage
terms.abstract: Data leakage arises when a machine learning method uses features that are available during training but not at prediction time. For example, in weather forecasting each data point covers a time interval, and one feature is the temperature one hour ahead of the forecast time. On historic data this later measurement is available, but when a forecast is actually computed it is not, so the feature leaks information. A leaked feature makes the loss on the training set and test set look near zero, yet the learned hypothesis fails after deployment, because the feature cannot be reproduced at prediction time. The term is also used, in a security sense, for the unintentional release of sensitive information.
terms.description: Consider a machine learning method trained on an hourly temperature sequence, where each data point is a sliding window of three consecutive hours (Fig.~1). The label is the temperature of the middle hour, and one of the features is the measurement one hour later. On historic data this later measurement is available, so the loss on the training set and test set looks near zero; but in real time the middle hour must be predicted before the next hour is measured, so the learned hypothesis is useless. This is data leakage: a feature used during training or evaluation is unavailable when a prediction must be delivered. More generally, a leaked feature is one whose value cannot be reproduced at prediction time, whether it is measured only later (as above) or computed from the label. Data leakage is formalized by Kaufman et al. (2012), who also give methods to detect and avoid it. Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) survey it as a cause of the reproducibility crisis in machine learning-based science. Test set contamination, the presence of test set data points in the training set, is a related form of data leakage. The term data leakage is also used, in an unrelated security sense, for the unintentional release of sensitive information (data exfiltration from a trained system), a meaning distinct from the methodological one defined above.

terms.name: data point
terms.abstract: A data point is the elementary information-carrying unit on which machine learning methods operate. The properties of a data point fall into two categories: features, which are easily measurable or computable, and labels, which are higher-level facts that typically can only be determined using human expertise. Whether a given property is treated as a feature or a label is a design choice that depends on the machine learning application.
terms.description: A data point is an object that conveys information~; such objects are the elementary units on which machine learning methods operate. Examples include students, radio signals, trees, images, RVs, real numbers, or proteins. Data points of the same type are described by two categories of properties. The first category includes features that are measurable or computable properties of a data point. They can be automatically extracted or computed using sensors, computers, or other data collection systems. The second category includes labels that are higher-level facts, or quantities of interest, that typically require human expertise or domain knowledge to determine rather than being directly measurable. Whether a given property serves as a feature or a label is ultimately a design choice that depends on the resources available in a given machine learning application. Fig. 1 shows an image as an example of a data point. Several properties of the image can serve as features: the color intensities x1, …, xd of all image pixels, the timestamp xd+1 of the image capture, and the spatial location xd+2 of the image capture. Higher-level facts can serve as labels: the number of cows y1, the number of wolves y2, and the condition of the pasture y3 (e.g., healthy or overgrazed). For a data point that represents a patient, a feature could be the body weight, while the label could be the presence of cancer, the ground-truth fact of interest. Determining this label requires a medical expert (or even a committee of experts) to examine the patient. A property treated as a label in one setting (e.g., a cancer diagnosis) may serve as a feature in another, where reliable automation (e.g., image analysis) allows the property to be computed without human intervention. Machine learning aims to predict the label of a data point from its features. Both kinds of properties are error-prone. For many machine learning applications, it is rarely possible to access the true labels. For example, a medical expert's diagnosis can be wrong, rendering it a noisy proxy for the patient's true condition. Errors of this kind, called label noise, arise whenever a label is only a proxy for the true quantity of interest, whether that proxy is produced by human judgment or by an automated system. Features are also a source of error within a machine learning method. A feature is obtained by measuring or computing a property of a data point. Physical and chemical sensing devices have a finite measurement uncertainty, and computing a feature on a finite computer introduces rounding errors. These imperfections make the recorded value deviate from the true feature value. This discrepancy is feature noise. Machine learning methods should be robust to both feature and label noise. Their predictions on new data points should not degrade sharply when some features or labels in the training set are corrupted. The EU AI Act reflects this concern: training data must, to the best extent possible, be ``free of errors'', and high-risk AI systems must attain an appropriate level of robustness. Robustness to feature and label noise can be improved by data augmentation, which deliberately perturbs the features or the label of a training data point (see Fig.~2). Training on such perturbed data points acts as regularization and reduces the influence of corrupted feature or label values on the learned hypothesis.

terms.name: dataset
terms.abstract: A dataset is a finite collection of data points on which model training and validation are performed. Strictly speaking, a dataset is a set of distinct data points. With slight abuse of terminology, the term is also used interchangeably with sample, a finite sequence that may contain repetitions. In practice, machine learning methods do not access the data points themselves but a representation of them, such as a table of the relational model, which records their attributes and nothing about the dataset's fitness for a purpose.
terms.description: A dataset is a collection D = z(1), …, z(m) of data points. Machine learning methods use a dataset for model training and validation. Strictly speaking, a dataset is an unordered collection of distinct data points, i.e., a set with no repetitions. In machine learning literature, however, the term is often used for a sample: a sequence of m data points, indexed by r = 1, …, m, that may contain repetitions (see Fig.~1). The notion of a dataset is broad: data points may represent concrete physical entities (such as humans or animals) or abstract objects (such as numbers). For illustration, Fig.~2 depicts a dataset whose data points are cows. In machine learning applications, it is often not possible to directly access the underlying dataset. For instance, accessing the dataset in Fig.~2 would require visiting the cow herd. What a machine learning method processes instead is a representation of the dataset within some data model, a rigorous formalism for representing and processing data. For example, the relational model organizes data as a collection of tables, or relations. A single table consists of rows and columns, where each row corresponds to a single data point and each column represents a specific attribute of a data point. The order of rows is immaterial, and each attribute is associated with a domain that specifies its set of admissible values. Machine learning methods use these attributes as the features or the label of a data point, so the attribute domains correspond to the feature space and the label space. Table~1 shows an example obtained from the dataset in Fig.~2. \begin{table}[H] \refstepcounter{table} a̧ption*{ ȩntering \scshape TABLE \thetable [0.5ex] \scshape Relation (or Table) Representing a Dataset of Cows } ȩntering \begin{tabular}{lcccc} \hline Name & Weight & Age & Height & Stomach temperature \hline Zenzi & 100 & 4 & 100 & 25 Berta & 140 & 3 & 130 & 23 Resi & 120 & 4 & 120 & 31 \hline \end{tabular} \end{table} A table captures the content of a dataset, but not whether that content is appropriate for a given purpose. A dataset used in ethical and lawful ML systems is required to satisfy further properties. For example, the EU AI Act requires that datasets on which high-risk ML systems are trained be ``sufficiently representative'' of the intended use cases. Trustworthy artificial intelligence also requires documenting how a dataset was assembled, for example through a datasheet that records the dataset's motivation, composition, and collection process. When the data points are personal data, this becomes a legal duty: under the purpose limitation principle, the general data protection regulation requires that such data be collected for ``specified, explicit and legitimate purposes'' that are fixed at the time of collection.

terms.name: decision tree
terms.abstract: A decision tree is a flowchart-like representation of a hypothesis map: a root node reads in the feature vector of a data point and evaluates a basic test on it. The test result selects a child node, which applies a further test, and the forwarding continues until the feature vector reaches a leaf node. A leaf node has no children and represents one specific function value, i.e., a prediction. The tree partitions the feature space into decision regions, one per leaf node, on which the represented hypothesis is constant. A maximum depth and a family of node tests define the model, the hypothesis space of all such trees, which has no vector of model parameters of fixed length and is therefore searched greedily rather than by gradient methods. Decision trees serve as base models of the random forest and of gradient-boosted decision tree methods. Small decision trees yield interpretable machine learning if the user can comprehend the tests executed at their nodes.
terms.description: A bank's loan approval can be written as a chain of simple tests on the applicant's features that ends in an ``approve'' or ``reject'' prediction. For example, is the income above a threshold? Is the credit score large enough? A decision tree is such a chain in general form: a flowchart-like representation of a hypothesis map h. More formally, a decision tree is a directed acyclic graph containing a root node that reads in the feature vector x of a data point. The root node then forwards the data point to one of its child nodes based on some elementary test on the features x. If the receiving child node is not a leaf node, i.e., it has child nodes itself, it represents another test. Based on the test result, the data point is forwarded to one of its descendants. This testing and forwarding of the data point is continued until the data point ends up in a leaf node without any children, which carries the prediction y = h(x) returned by the tree for this data point (Fig.~1). The leaf nodes partition the feature space into decision regions; in Fig.~1, each test compares an entry of x with a threshold, so the decision regions are rectangles. Next to each node, Fig.~1 highlights the part of the feature space that contains the feature vectors reaching that node. Fixing a maximum depth D and a family of allowed tests defines the model: the hypothesis space H of all decision trees of depth at most D whose node tests belong to the family, for instance all threshold tests xj ≤ ε with j ∈ 1, …, d and ε ∈ R. A tree in H is specified by its shape, by the index j of the feature and the threshold ε that each test node compares, and by the value of each leaf node. This hypothesis space has no natural parametrization. The shape of the tree and the index j of the feature tested at each node are discrete choices, and how many of them a tree has depends on its shape, so H is not the image of a vector of model parameters of fixed length: there is no parameter space Rn on which the training error is a function. The thresholds form a vector once the shape and the tested features are fixed, but the training error is piecewise constant in each of them, since a data point changes child only when the threshold crosses its feature value, so the gradient is zero wherever it exists. Empirical risk minimization over H can therefore not use gradient descent, and a fixed point view of the training iteration does not apply: an iteration adds a node, it does not update a vector. Minimizing a bound that adds a size penalty to the training error is computationally hard, and the methods below search H greedily. Training a decision tree amounts to extending a leaf node by attaching another decision tree. In the simplest case, a leaf node is replaced with a test node whose children are new leaf nodes (Fig.~2). Widely used training methods for decision trees include classification and regression trees (CART), iterative dichotomiser 3 (ID3), and C4.5. Starting from a single leaf node, CART repeatedly replaces a leaf node with a test node. An impurity measure assigns a nonnegative number to a set of labels: it is zero when the labels agree, and it grows as they spread out. Among candidate tests that compare a single feature with a threshold, CART scores each test by the impurity of the two children, weighted by the fraction of data points routed to each of them, and greedily selects the test with the smallest score, i.e., with the largest reduction against the impurity of the parent node. Common impurity measures are the Gini index and the entropy for classification, and the squared error around the mean label for regression. This selection is a combinatorial search over candidate tests rather than a gradient-based update of continuous model parameters. The growth stops only when a leaf node contains too few data points, not when no candidate test reduces the impurity much, since a test that reduces the impurity little can enable a strong test below it. The large tree is then pruned back by cost-complexity pruning, which removes the subtrees whose impurity reduction does not pay for the leaf nodes they add. The depth of a decision tree is the number of tests on the longest path from the root node to a leaf node; the tree in Fig.~1 has depth two. Fig.~3 shows, as a scatterplot, the result of this training on real data. Each day of 2024 at the Finnish Meteorological Institute weather station Helsinki Kaisaniemi is a data point, with the minimum temperature of the day as its feature and the maximum temperature as its label. The learned depth-2 tree is a piecewise constant hypothesis with four pieces, one per leaf node, each equal to the mean label of the days routed there. The tree was grown to depth two rather than until the stopping rule above fired, so that each of its four pieces is visible in the picture. Decision trees serve as base models of the random forest and of gradient-boosted decision tree methods. A decision tree with a small number of nodes is often considered interpretable: its computation can be traced by following the data point from the root node to a leaf node. This makes small decision trees a common choice in interpretable machine learning.

terms.name: dimensionality reduction
terms.abstract: Dimensionality reduction uses a map h: Rd → Rd' to replace a raw feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ by a shorter feature vector z = (z1, …, zd')ᵀ, with d' < d. Using fewer features lowers the effective dimension of a model, which reduces the chance of overfitting. Moreover, it lowers the amount of computation needed for model training and for inference. It also enables visualization: two features can be used as the coordinates in a scatterplot. Principal component analysis learns a linear map by minimizing the reconstruction error, while a random projection uses a linear map drawn at random, without any training. An autoencoder learns a nonlinear map represented by an artificial neural network.
terms.description: Dimensionality reduction uses a map (or transformation) h: Rd → Rd' to replace the raw feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ of a data point by a shorter feature vector z = (z1, …, zd')ᵀ, with d' < d (Fig.~1). Using a shorter feature vector is beneficial in several ways: \begin{itemize} \item Statistical benefit: It typically reduces the chance of overfitting, as reducing the number of features often reduces the effective dimension of a model. \item Computational benefit: Using fewer features lowers the amount of computation needed for model training and for inference. As a case in point, linear regression methods need to invert a matrix whose size is determined by the number of features. \item Visualization: A map can be learned that delivers two features z1,z2, which can then be used as the coordinates in a scatterplot. Fig.~2 places each square patch of a photograph at the two features that principal component analysis learns for it, which keep most of the variance of the raw feature vectors. Each patch is first averaged down to a 4 × 4 grid of colors, so its raw feature vector holds 48 numbers, still too many to plot. \end{itemize} Dimensionality reduction methods differ in the hypothesis space used for the map, in the criterion they learn it by, and in whether the map is learned from data at all. Principal component analysis learns a linear map: the map is a matrix chosen so that the reconstruction error, the squared distance between x and the feature vector reconstructed from z by a second linear map, is minimal on average over the training set. An autoencoder learns a nonlinear map represented by an artificial neural network, under the same criterion. A random projection uses a random matrix without any training: by the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma, the distances between the feature vectors of the data points are approximately preserved. Nonlinear methods beyond the autoencoder include the manifold-learning family, among them t-SNE and UMAP, which are used mainly for visualization.

terms.name: distribution shift
terms.abstract: Distribution shift is a mismatch between the probability distribution underlying the training set and test set of a machine learning method and the probability distribution of the data points that the learned hypothesis faces after deployment. The average loss on the test set estimates the risk under the training probability distribution only, so a small test error is no evidence for a small loss on data points outside the test set. Factoring the joint probability distribution of features and labels separates the named special cases of covariate shift and label shift.
terms.description: The Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI) station Helsinki Kaisaniemi records the minimum and the maximum air temperature of each day. Every summer day is a data point: its feature is the day's minimum temperature, its label the day's maximum. A linear hypothesis h(x) = 0.481 x + 14.5, learned from 62 days of June--August 2026 by minimizing the average squared error loss, reaches a training error of 5.0 and a test error of 6.5 on a test set of the 30 remaining summer days. Deployed at the northernmost FMI station, Utsjoki Nuorgam (70.1∘ N), on the 90 days of December 2025--February 2026, the same hypothesis incurs an average error of 242.1, which is 37 times its test error (Fig.~1). Every winter morning at Nuorgam is colder than each summer morning in the training set, and the extrapolation overshoots: the mean winter day at Nuorgam has a minimum of -19.8 ∘C and a maximum of -9.6 ∘C, while h assigns such a morning a maximum of +5.0 ∘C. Distribution shift is a mismatch between the probability distribution p underlying the training set and test set of a machine learning method and the probability distribution p' of the data points the learned hypothesis faces after deployment. The average loss on the test set estimates the risk under p, since the independent and identically distributed assumption covers draws from p, not from p'. A small test error is therefore no evidence for a small loss under p' ≠ p: the densities in Fig.~2 show how a threshold placed for p fails under p', and the two stations of Fig.~1 realize the failure with measured temperatures. The named special cases of distribution shift correspond to the two factorizations of the joint probability distribution of a data point (x, y). Under the factorization p(x, y) = p(y | x) p(x), covariate shift changes only the marginal p(x) of the covariates (the features) and leaves the conditional p(y | x) untouched. An example is a second weather station in a colder climate at which cold mornings precede rain in the same way. Concept drift changes that conditional itself over time, as when a warming climate alters which morning temperatures precede rain. Under the reverse factorization p(x, y) = p(x | y) p(y), label shift changes only the frequency p(y) of the label values and leaves the class-conditional p(x | y) untouched. The two-station example is a pure case of none of the three: the marginal of the feature moves, since winter mornings are colder, and the conditional moves as well, since a linear hypothesis learned from the winter days has slope 0.77 against the summer slope 0.48. Distribution shift is detected by comparing summary statistics of the features between the training set and the data points arriving after deployment, or by monitoring the incurred loss whenever labels become available. One response is sample weighting: each data point of the training set is weighted by the ratio p'(x)/p(x). This weighting corrects covariate shift under two conditions: the conditional p(y | x) is unchanged, and every feature vector occurring under p' also occurs under p, so that the ratio is defined. Both conditions fail in the two-station example: no reweighting of summer days produces a winter morning at -20 ∘C. Responses that remain applicable are transfer learning and fine-tuning on data points from p', domain adaptation, which uses unlabeled data points from p' while the hypothesis is still being learned, and online learning, which updates the hypothesis as data points from the drifting probability distribution arrive.

terms.name: eigenvalue
terms.abstract: An eigenvalue of a square matrix A is a number λ for which some nonzero vector x satisfies Ax = λx. Such a vector is an eigenvector of A. Multiplying an eigenvector by the matrix rescales it without moving it off the line it spans. The eigenvalues of a diagonalizable matrix form the diagonal factor of its eigenvalue decomposition. An iterative method that applies an affine update, such as gradient descent for linear regression, converges to the unique fixed point of the update, for every initialization, exactly when each eigenvalue of the update matrix has magnitude less than one. The second-smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian matrix of an undirected graph measures how well the graph is connected and underlies spectral clustering.
terms.description: A square matrix A represents a linear map from Rd to Rd; the image of a vector x under this map is the product Ax. Multiplying a vector by a square matrix normally moves it off the line it spans. Some nonzero vectors are exceptions: each stays on the line it spans and is only rescaled. The factor by which such a vector is rescaled is an eigenvalue. Formally, a number λ ∈ R is an eigenvalue of a square matrix A ∈ Rd × d, one with d rows and d columns, if A x = λ x for some nonzero vector x ∈ Rd; such a vector is an eigenvector of A. For an eigenvector, the image Ax stays on the line x spans, pointing the same way when λ > 0 and the opposite way when λ < 0 (see Fig.~1). Arranging d linearly independent eigenvectors of a diagonalizable matrix as the columns of V, and the corresponding eigenvalues in a diagonal matrix Λ, yields the eigenvalue decomposition A = V Λ V-1. Eigenvalues can be used to study iterative machine learning methods with an update of the form \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf M} {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + {\mathbf b} \text{.} \] An example is gradient descent for linear regression, whose update operator F(η): w ↦ M w + b is affine with iteration matrix M = I - (2η/m) XᵀX. Here, I is the identity matrix, η the learning rate, m the number of data points, and X the feature matrix of the training set (see linear regression). Such an iteration converges to the unique fixed point w of F(η), for every initialization, if and only if the spectral radius ρ of M, the largest magnitude of an eigenvalue of M, satisfies ρ < 1. Beyond the convergence of iterative methods, eigenvalues are also used to measure the connectivity of an undirected graph G with n nodes. The Laplacian matrix L(G) of G is positive semi-definite, with eigenvalues 0 = λ1 ≤ λ2 ≤ … ≤ λn. The second-smallest eigenvalue λ2, the algebraic connectivity of G, quantifies connectivity: λ2 > 0 if and only if G is connected, and λ2 close to zero indicates two clusters of nodes with few edges between them. Fig.~2 shows three edge sets on the same six nodes: adding edges increases λ2 from 0, for two clusters without a connecting edge, to 6, for the complete graph. The eigenvector corresponding to λ2, referred to as the Fiedler vector, can be used to partition G into two clusters: each node is assigned according to the sign of its own component of the Fiedler vector.

terms.name: expectation–maximization (EM)
terms.abstract: The expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm is an iterative optimization method for a particular class of maximum likelihood problems. In particular, EM is useful for probabilistic models that involve observed and unobserved (or latent) attributes of a data point. Each iteration of the EM algorithm alternates an E-step with an M-step. The E-step computes the posterior distribution of the unobserved attributes under the current model parameters. The M-step minimizes the negative log-likelihood of the complete data points averaged under this posterior distribution, which for many probabilistic models has a closed form. Mathematically, the EM algorithm is an instance of a majorize–minimize method. A canonical soft clustering method uses the EM algorithm to learn the model parameters of a Gaussian mixture model.
terms.description: The nightly minimum temperatures recorded over one year at the weather station of Krems an der Donau (Austria) scatter around two regimes, cold-season and warm-season nights. A probabilistic model for such data points has, besides the observed temperature, an unobserved attribute: the regime a night belongs to. Fig.~1 shows the histogram of the temperatures together with a Gaussian mixture model consisting of a separate normal distribution for each regime. The EM algorithm is an iterative optimization method for approximately solving maximum likelihood optimization problems for probabilistic models with an unobserved attribute. Consider a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) whose data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. The underlying probability distribution is a probabilistic model p(x',y')(x,y;w) for the observed feature vector x and an unobserved attribute y with values in a finite set Y. This probabilistic model is a family of probability distributions parameterized by model parameters w in a parameter space W. Maximum likelihood is an instance of empirical risk minimization: it minimizes the empirical risk \begin{equation} \widehat{L}\big({\mathbf w}|\mathcal{D}\big) := - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \ln \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} p^{({\mathbf x}',y')}\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},y;{\mathbf w}\right)\text{,} \end{equation} the average negative log-likelihood of the observed feature vectors. The sum inside the logarithm is what makes \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict} hard to minimize directly: if the attributes y(r) were observed, the empirical risk would be an average of -ln p(x',y')(x(r),y(r);w), which for many probabilistic models has a closed-form minimizer. The EM algorithm solves the maximum likelihood problem \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict} by alternating two steps. The E-step computes, for every data point, the posterior distribution of the unobserved attribute under the current model parameters w, \begin{equation} p^{(y'|{\mathbf x}')}\left(y;\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right) = \frac{p^{({\mathbf x}',y')}\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},y;\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right)} {\sum_{y'' \in \mathcal{Y}} p^{({\mathbf x}',y')}\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},y'';\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right)} \quad \text{for } y \in \mathcal{Y} \text{ and } r = 1, \ldots, m\text{.} \end{equation} The M-step minimizes over w ∈ W the empirical risk of the complete data points, averaged under these posterior distributions, \begin{equation} Q({\mathbf w} \mid \widehat{{\mathbf w}}) := - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} p^{(y'|{\mathbf x}')}\left(y;\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right) \ln \frac{p^{({\mathbf x}',y')}\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},y;{\mathbf w}\right)} {p^{(y'|{\mathbf x}')}\left(y;\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right)}\text{.} \end{equation} Algorithm~1 states the method in full. \begin{algorithm}[H] a̧ption{Expectation-maximization } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Require dataset D, probabilistic model with parameters w ∈ W, initialization w(0), iteration count T \For{t = 0, 1, …, T-1} \State E-step: form Q(w | w(t)), the expectation of the complete-data empirical risk under the current parameters \State M-step: w(t+1) argminw ∈ W Q(w | w(t)) \EndFor \Ensure w(T) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} One E-step followed by one M-step constitutes one iteration of the EM algorithm. The EM algorithm is a majorize–minimize method: each iteration minimizes a surrogate Q(w | w) of the empirical risk \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict}. The surrogate \eqref{equ_em_mstep_dict} has three properties (whose lower bound on the log-likelihood is this surrogate written for the negative log-likelihood;). First, it majorizes the empirical risk, Q(w | w) ≥ L(w|D) for all w ∈ W, by Jensen's inequality applied to the concave logarithm. Second, it is tight at the current iterate, Q(w | w) = L(w|D). Third, it is minimized exactly by the M-step. Any model parameters w(t+1) that minimize the surrogate built at w(t) therefore satisfy L(w(t+1)|D) ≤ Q(w(t+1) | w(t)) ≤ Q(w(t) | w(t)) = L(w(t)|D): no iteration increases the empirical risk. The monotone decrease of the empirical risk \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict} along the EM iterates yields a stopping criterion: the iteration stops as soon as the decrease of the empirical risk achieved by the last iteration falls below a given threshold. The empirical risk \eqref{equ_em_emprisk_dict} is in general a non-convex function of the model parameters, and EM might converge to a local minimum. It is therefore typically run several times with different initializations, keeping the run with the smallest empirical risk. The EM algorithm is a fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(w(t)). The operator F maps the current model parameters w to the result of one E-step followed by one M-step. The E-step \eqref{equ_em_estep_dict} at w builds the surrogate Q(· | w), and the M-step \eqref{equ_em_mstep_dict} minimizes it, \mathcal{F}(\widehat{{\mathbf w}}) := \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathcal{W}} Q({\mathbf w} \mid \widehat{{\mathbf w}})\text{.} The fixed points of F are model parameters that minimize their own surrogate: there, the surrogate touches the empirical risk from above, so no further descent step is available, and the gradient of the empirical risk vanishes. EM is used to learn the model parameters of a Gaussian mixture model, where the unobserved attribute of a data point is its cluster index I(r) ∈ 1, …, k and the model parameters are the cluster probabilities pc, means μ(c), and covariance matrices C(c). The E-step \eqref{equ_em_estep_dict} becomes the degree of belonging \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} := \mathbb{P}\left(I^{(r)} = c \mid {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\right) = \frac{p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})} {\sum_{c'=1}^{k} p_{c'} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c')},\mathbf{C}^{(c')}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})}\text{,} \end{equation} and minimizing the surrogate \eqref{equ_em_mstep_dict} yields the M-step in closed form. The cluster probability pc is the average of uc(r) over the data points, while μ(c) and C(c) are the mean and covariance matrix of the feature vectors weighted by uc(r). The learned degrees of belonging \eqref{equ_em_gmm_estep_dict} constitute a soft clustering. Fixing every cluster probability at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix I with a common σ2 that shrinks towards 0 turns the degrees of belonging into 0 or 1, and EM reduces to Lloyd's algorithm for k-means. Consider next, as an illustration of the EM algorithm, the Gaussian mixture model of Fig.~1 for the temperature dataset. The feature of a data point is the nightly minimum temperature x ∈ R, and its unobserved attribute is the regime y ∈ cold, warm. The model parameters are the probabilities pcold, pwarm = 1 - pcold of the two regimes, the means μcold, μwarm and the variances σ2cold, σ2warm of the two normal distributions, so w = (pcold, pwarm, μcold, μwarm, σ2cold, σ2warm)ᵀ ∈ R6. The E-step \eqref{equ_em_estep_dict} computes for every night the probability of the cold regime, and the M-step \eqref{equ_em_mstep_dict} re-fits w as averages weighted by these probabilities. On the 366 nights of 2024, EM learns pcold = 0.83, μcold = 5.1, μwarm = 17.2, σ2cold = 39.7, and σ2warm = 3.3. Fig.~2 shows the majorize–minimize view for this Gaussian mixture model as the cold-season mean μcold varies, while pcold, μwarm and σ2warm are fixed at their learned values and σ2cold is fixed at 16. The empirical risk is then a function of μcold alone, and so is each surrogate. Each surrogate lies above the empirical risk, touches it at its iterate, and its minimizer is the next iterate. Fig.~3 shows how the empirical risk decreases monotonically as the EM iterations proceed.

terms.name: ensemble
terms.abstract: An ensemble method combines several machine learning methods, each referred to as a base learner. Ensemble methods differ in how they construct the base learners and in how they combine their results. Bagging trains each base learner on a resampled copy of the training set. Boosting runs them sequentially, each one fitted to the errors of the previous ones. Stacking uses base learners to train different models on the same training set and learns an aggregation rule. For the squared error loss the gain is exact: the error of the average prediction is the average error of the base learners minus their average disagreement, so base learners that disagree are what makes an ensemble worth forming.
terms.description: Predicting the maximum temperature of a day at the weather station Krems an der Donau from the minimum temperature of the same day can be done with a linear model, with a decision tree, or with an artificial neural network. Fig.~1 shows all three learned from the 366 days of 2020. None of them is the best everywhere: the linear hypothesis is too stiff at the cold end, the decision tree answers with a staircase, and the artificial neural network bends where the other two cannot. Model selection would keep one of them and discard the rest. Is there a better way to combine these base learners instead of choosing one of them? Combining several machine learning methods into one predictor is an ensemble method: each combined method is a base learner. The base learners can be empirical risk minimization-based, using different choices for the loss, model, and training set. Of M base learners, base learner ℓ learns a hypothesis h(ℓ) from its hypothesis space H(ℓ) and its, possibly perturbed, training set D(ℓ), and an aggregation rule φagg combines the outputs of these hypotheses into the final prediction. The aggregation can amount to averaging (in regression), as in Fig.~1, or to a majority vote (in classification); Fig.~2 shows the general shape. What the combination buys is exactly the disagreement among the base learners. For the squared error loss, the error of the average prediction is the average error of the base learners minus their average disagreement, where the disagreement of a base learner is the squared difference between its own prediction and the average one. This is an identity, not an approximation: on the held-back days of Fig.~1 the average member error 26.47 minus the average disagreement 0.52 is the 25.95 that the average prediction actually incurs. Two consequences follow. The average is never worse than its base learners are on average, since a disagreement cannot be negative. And base learners that agree everywhere buy nothing, which is why they are trained on different models or on different data points. Beating the best single base learner is a different and weaker claim: over 50 repetitions on random halves of the training set, the average did so 22 times. The same point in terms of variance: consider M base learners whose predictions are identically distributed, each with variance σ2 and pairwise correlation ρ. The average of these predictions has variance \rho \sigma^{2} + \frac{1-\rho}{M} \sigma^{2}\text{.} The second of these two summands vanishes as M grows, while the first, set by the correlation between the base learners, limits what averaging can achieve. Ensemble methods differ in how they construct the base learners and in how they combine their results. Bagging trains each base learner on a random resample of the training set and averages them; it reduces the variance of an unstable base learner such as a deep decision tree, while the systematic part of its error, the bias, is left unchanged. A random forest is bagging of decision trees with, in addition, a random choice of the features considered at each split, which lowers the correlation between the trees. Boosting runs the base learners sequentially, each one fitted to the errors of the previous ones. The number of rounds is a hyperparameter: the training error keeps decreasing while the validation error eventually rises, so boosting overfits when run for too long. Stacking trains the base learners on the same training set with different models and learns the aggregation rule itself by a second machine learning method. The second method is trained on predictions for data points the base learners did not see. Otherwise the base learners that fit the training set best are favored regardless of how they generalize.

terms.name: empirical risk minimization (ERM)
terms.abstract: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) selects a hypothesis by minimizing the average loss on a given training set D(train), the empirical risk. Machine learning methods aim at a hypothesis that incurs a small loss on any data point, and ERM replaces this unknown quantity by its average over the training set. Different machine learning methods arise from different choices of the model H and the loss function L, both of which depend on the feature space X and the label space Y of a given method.
terms.description: A weather forecaster predicting tomorrow's maximum daytime temperature is useful only if its predictions are accurate on the large majority of days, not only on the days it was tuned on. This forecaster is a hypothesis: it maps a day's features to a prediction of tomorrow's temperature, and its loss quantifies how far that prediction lies from the measured value. More generally, machine learning methods aim to find a hypothesis that incurs a small loss for any data point. The phrase any data point is made precise by a probabilistic model for the generation of data points, as follows. If data points are assumed to be drawn from a probability distribution, then the risk of a hypothesis is defined as the expectation of its loss under that probability distribution. The ideal choice is then the hypothesis with minimal risk. However, in most machine learning applications, the underlying probability distribution is not known. Instead, only a finite training set D(train) of data points is available. ERM replaces the intractable risk with its sample-average surrogate, the empirical risk on D(train), and picks the hypothesis that minimizes this surrogate. For a fixed choice of loss function and hypothesis space, ERM is a map A that reads in a training set D(train) = z(r)r=1m of data points z(r) = ( x(r),y(r) ). The map returns a learned hypothesis h = A(D(train)) ∈ H that minimizes the empirical risk on D(train), \[ \widehat{h} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},h \right) \text{.} \] The hypothesis h is chosen from the underlying hypothesis space (or model) H. For an ERM-based method, model training is to compute A. In practice, the map A is computed by an iterative optimization method. Many of these optimization methods can be represented as a fixed-point iteration that starts with an initial hypothesis h(0) and then repeatedly applies an update operator F, h^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{F}\big( h^{(t)} \big) \text{, for } t=0,1,\ldots \text{.} The update operator F depends on the training set, the loss function, and the hypothesis space. It is chosen such that its fixed points are minimizers of the empirical risk. For ERM using a parametric model H, the fixed-point iteration can be formulated directly in terms of the model parameters w instead of the hypothesis h. In particular, starting with initial model parameters w(0), the update operator F is applied repeatedly to the model parameters, {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{F}\big( {\mathbf w}^{(t)} \big) \text{, for } t=0,1,\ldots \text{.} One important example of such a fixed-point iteration is gradient descent, which updates the model parameters in the direction of the negative gradient of the empirical risk (which needs to be differentiable). ERM presupposes that the loss L(z(r),h ) can be evaluated for every hypothesis h ∈ H and every training data point z(r). This full-feedback requirement is what distinguishes ERM from reinforcement learning algorithms, which use partial feedback. In particular, at each time instant t = 1, 2, …, a reinforcement learning algorithm chooses an action, the prediction of its current hypothesis h(t), and observes only the loss incurred by that action. It has no information about the loss that would have been incurred by any other hypothesis h ∈ H h(t). ERM can also be implemented as an online algorithm, which is useful when the data points in D(train) can only be accessed sequentially. Such sequential access arises, for instance, when memory limits prevent loading the entire training set at once. The canonical online form of ERM is the Follow-The-Leader algorithm, which, at every round, solves a partial ERM problem on all data points seen so far. Assuming that the data point z(t) arrives at time instant t=1,2,…, Follow-The-Leader updates the learned hypothesis h(t) by \widehat{h}^{(t)} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{t} \sum_{r=1}^{t} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},h \right) \text{.} Implementing this partial ERM separately for each time instant can become computationally expensive (and wasteful), as it does not exploit the similarity between consecutive partial ERM problems. This similarity can be exploited by online gradient descent, which performs a single gradient descent step on the new data point z(t) at every time instant t. Different machine learning methods arise from different design choices for the two ingredients of the map A: the model H and the loss function L. Both depend on the nature of the data points, i.e., on the feature space X and the label space Y. For example, image data points with a high-dimensional feature space and a finite label space typically call for an artificial neural network together with the logistic loss. Conversely, data points with few real-valued features and a real-valued label often allow for a linear model together with the squared error loss. Fig.~1 illustrates ERM for a linear model on data points with a single feature x and label y. Each hypothesis is a linear map h(x) = w1 x + w0 with model parameters w0, w1. ERM picks the model parameters that minimize the empirical risk on D(train).

terms.name: eigenvalue decomposition (EVD)
terms.abstract: An eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) of a square matrix breaks the linear map it represents into elementary operations: expanding a vector in the eigenvectors of the matrix, multiplying each expansion coefficient by the corresponding eigenvalue, and summing the scaled terms up again. A matrix that has an EVD is called diagonalizable; symmetric matrices and matrices with distinct eigenvalues are diagonalizable. A dataset with numeric feature vectors can be characterized by the EVD of its sample covariance matrix. The EVD can be used to speed up computations such as the gradient step of gradient descent methods. For linear regression, each gradient descent iteration then reduces to element-wise operations. The EVD of the Laplacian matrix of an undirected graph is instrumental for spectral clustering.
terms.description: Each day of 2024 at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria) is recorded with its lowest and its highest temperature, stacked into a feature vector x = ( x1, x2 )ᵀ ∈ R2. Fig.~1 shows the m = 366 days x(1), …, x(m) as a scatterplot together with an ellipse that is computed from their sample mean and sample covariance matrix. The sample mean of the days is \[ \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \text{,} \] and their sample covariance matrix is \[ \widehat{{\mathbf C}} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big) \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} \text{.} \] The shape of the ellipse, which outlines the dataset, is determined by an EVD of the sample covariance matrix C. An EVD for a square matrix A ∈ Rd × d is a factorization of the form \[ {\mathbf A} = \mathbf{V} {\boldsymbol \Lambda} \mathbf{V}^{-1} \text{.} \] The columns of the matrix V = ( v(1), …, v(d) ) are eigenvectors of the matrix A. The diagonal matrix Λ = diag λ1, …, λd contains the eigenvalues λj corresponding to the eigenvectors v(j). Multiplying the factorization by v(j) gives A v(j) = λj v(j): each eigenvector is a direction that A only scales, by the factor λj; a single such pair satisfies A x = λ x, and the EVD collects d of them, indexed by j. Unlike the singular value decomposition, which exists for every matrix, square or not, the EVD is defined for square matrices only, and it need not exist. Moreover, the same matrix might allow for different EVDs: any nonzero linear combination of eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue is again an eigenvector with this eigenvalue. The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue is the maximum number of linearly independent eigenvectors with this eigenvalue. The EVD breaks the linear map u ↦ A u into three elementary operations. A vector u is expanded in the eigenvectors, u = Σj=1d βj v(j) with the expansion coefficients β = V-1 u; each coefficient is multiplied by its eigenvalue; and the scaled terms are summed up again, A u = Σj=1d λj βj v(j). Matrices that allow for an EVD are called diagonalizable. One example of a diagonalizable matrix is \[ {\mathbf A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.3 & 0.8 0.4 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \text{.} \] Fig.~2 illustrates its EVD. Two sufficient conditions for a real-valued square matrix to be diagonalizable are that it is a symmetric matrix or that its d eigenvalues are distinct. For a real-valued symmetric matrix, the EVD has additional structure: the eigenvectors can be chosen to form an orthonormal basis, i.e., the matrix V in the factorization can be chosen to be orthogonal. For a complex-valued matrix, the first condition is that it is Hermitian; a complex symmetric matrix need not be diagonalizable. The condition that is both necessary and sufficient is that every root of the minimal polynomial of the matrix is simple. The matrix A of Fig.~2 is not symmetric, since its off-diagonal entries 0.8 and 0.4 differ, but its two eigenvalues 1.7 and 0.5 are distinct, so it has an EVD. When neither condition holds, an EVD may not exist: the matrix \[ {\mathbf N} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \] is not symmetric and has the eigenvalue 0 twice, since the eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal entries. The eigenvectors of N are all located on the line (a, 0)ᵀ: a ∈ R, so there is no invertible matrix V whose columns are eigenvectors of N. The ellipse in Fig.~1 is the set of feature vectors x for which the quadratic form (x - μ)ᵀ C-1 (x - μ) equals 4. This set can be characterized more conveniently using an EVD of the sample covariance matrix C. The matrix C is symmetric, so it has an EVD C = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V that contains the eigenvectors in its columns. Transforming the feature vector x of a day according to x := Vᵀ (x - μ) turns the quadratic form into \[ ({\mathbf x} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu})^{\top} \widehat{{\mathbf C}}^{-1} ({\mathbf x} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu}) = \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{\top} {\boldsymbol \Lambda}^{-1} \widetilde{{\mathbf x}} = \frac{\widetilde{x}_{1}^{2}}{\lambda_{1}} + \frac{\widetilde{x}_{2}^{2}}{\lambda_{2}} \text{,} \] since C-1 = V Λ-1 Vᵀ. The ellipse is therefore the set where x12/λ1 + x22/λ2 = 4, with half-axes 21 and 22 along the coordinate axes of x, that is, along the eigenvectors. The transformed days have the sample covariance matrix Vᵀ C V = Λ: the two new coordinates have sample covariance zero, and the eigenvalues are their sample variances. Replacing each day by its first coordinate x1 alone keeps the direction of largest variance, which is the idea of principal component analysis. Besides describing the shape of a dataset, the EVD can be used to speed up the implementation of a machine learning method. Consider gradient descent for linear regression, with the update w(t+1) = w(t) - (2η/m) Xᵀ ( X w(t) - y ) for the feature matrix X and label vector y of the training set (see linear regression). The matrix XᵀX is symmetric, so it has an EVD XᵀX = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V. In the transformed coordinates w(t) := Vᵀ w(t), the update decouples into \[ \widetilde{w}_{j}^{(t+1)} = \big( 1 - (2\eta/m) \lambda_{j} \big) \widetilde{w}_{j}^{(t)} + (2\eta/m) \big( \mathbf{V}^{\top} {\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf y} \big)_{j} \text{.} \] After the one-time computation of the EVD, each iteration is an element-wise multiplication and addition of vectors of length d (pythondemos/evd.py). Another application of the EVD in machine learning is the clustering of graph-structured data. Consider data points represented as the nodes i = 1, …, n of an undirected graph G, e.g., the users of a social network with edges given by friendships. The Laplacian matrix L(G) of the graph G is symmetric and positive semi-definite. It has an EVD L(G) = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V and nonnegative eigenvalues. If the graph G is connected, the EVD has additional structure: the eigenvalue 0 has multiplicity one, with the all-ones vector as its eigenvector. Moreover, there is then a distinguished eigenvector, called the Fiedler vector: an eigenvector of the smallest nonzero eigenvalue, the algebraic connectivity of G. The Fiedler vector can be used for clustering the nodes of the graph, which is the idea of spectral clustering. Fig.~3 shows the Fiedler vector of a connected graph with six nodes: two clusters of three nodes and a single edge joining the two clusters.

terms.name: explainability
terms.abstract: Explainability is the property of a machine learning method whose explanations let a human user anticipate the predictions it delivers. The method delivers an explanation along with every prediction, and that explanation is effective if it lets the user anticipate the prediction made for a data point; comprehending the explanation is not required for this test. Explainability is always relative to a specific user or group of users: an explanation can be effective for one and useless for another. Explainability can be measured by comparing the predictions of a learned hypothesis to the anticipations of a user before and after they are provided with an explanation.
terms.description: A machine learning method is explainable for a human user if the explanations it provides let the user anticipate the predictions it delivers. Explainability thus includes the notion of an explanation: each prediction is delivered with an explanation for this specific prediction (see Fig.~1), such as the feature values that drove it or, for image data, the relevant pixels. The definition asks for the existence of an explanation, not for a particular one: explainability is certified by exhibiting one explanation that works, and one explanation the user cannot follow does not show that the method is unexplainable. Explainability is relative to a specific user or group of users: the same learned hypothesis can be explainable for one user and inscrutable for another. The usefulness of an explanation can be measured by how much it enables the user to anticipate the predictions on a curated test set: the user states an anticipation for each data point in the test set. If the user comprehends the explanations, these anticipations should be close to the predictions of the learned hypothesis. A measure of this form is referred to as predictability.
