As with interpretability, predictability is weaker than comprehension of the explanations: anticipating the predictions does not require comprehending the provided explanations. The conditional differential entropy is defined for RVs. If the data point is modeled as the realization of a random variable, the prediction and the anticipation of the user are RVs too, and their joint probability distribution yields a second measure of this predictability: the conditional differential entropy of the predictions given the anticipations. A related measure, the mutual information between a selected subset of the features and the prediction, is maximized by the explainer of Chen et al. (2018, Sect. 2.1). The conditional differential entropy quantifies the uncertainty that remains about the predictions once the anticipations are known, so a smaller value means that the anticipations determine the predictions more tightly. In practice, this conditional differential entropy is unknown and must be replaced by an estimator. One such estimator bins the predictions and the anticipations on a test set, and takes the fraction of test data points that fall into each pair of bins as the joint probability distribution. An explanation raises explainability when the user can reason with it. Fig.~2 illustrates this for a user who reasons in terms of linear maps and anticipates the predictions of an opaque hypothesis (Gaussian kernel ridge regression, a kernel method). Without explanations, the user anticipates by a single linear map fitted to a few predictions, and the anticipations deviate strongly from the predictions. The explanation for a test data point with feature value x0 is a local linear approximation of the hypothesis around it (cf. local interpretable model-agnostic explanations), a slope and an intercept that the user evaluates at x0. With this explanation, the anticipations match the predictions almost exactly. The example presupposes that the user knows how to apply a linear approximation: the anticipations improve only because the user can evaluate the explanation for a data point. A user who cannot is left where they started. An explanation can also mislead. A computed explanation can be unfaithful to the learned hypothesis, so that anticipations based on it are confidently wrong. Saliency maps, intensity maps over the pixels of an input image (see explainable artificial intelligence), barely change for some methods when the trained deep net is replaced by one with random weights. The predictability test detects such an explanation: anticipations drawn from it deviate from the predictions. The international terminology standard for artificial intelligence defines explainability as the property of an artificial intelligence system to express important factors influencing its results in a way that humans can understand. An explanation is intended to answer the question of why the artificial intelligence system produced a result, without arguing that the result was optimal. The AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) ties explainability to a representation of the mechanisms underlying the operation of an artificial intelligence system. NIST reserves interpretability for the meaning of the output in the context of the designed purpose. The two frameworks thus divide the terms differently. The expressed factors influencing a result, which the terminology standard places under explainability, are close to the NIST notion of interpretability; the NIST notion of explainability is instead close to interpretability as comprehension of the computation of the method. Regulation treats explainability as an ingredient of transparency. The EU AI Act requires that high-risk AI systems are sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately. For individual automated decisions, the right to explanation entitles an affected person to a clear and meaningful account of the role that an artificial intelligence system played in the decision. The Colorado Automated Decision-Making Technology Act of 2026 requires that the deployer give the affected consumer a plain-language description of the decision and of the role the technology played in it, together with the means to request further information. What counts as an automated decision is drawn widely: the Court of Justice of the European Union held that a credit information agency computing a person's ability to meet future payments already makes one, when a third party draws strongly on that value.

terms.name: explanation
terms.abstract: An explanation accompanies a prediction delivered by a machine learning method and states which properties of the data point led to that prediction. Explanations can be text, a score per feature, a simple hypothesis that approximates the learned one near the data point, or a heat map drawn over an image. Two requirements can be contradictory. On the one hand, an explanation must be faithful: it must reflect the computation by which the learned hypothesis arrives at the prediction. On the other hand, it must be understandable: its user must be able to anticipate the predictions it accompanies. An explanation that agreed with the learned hypothesis everywhere would be that hypothesis again, so a simpler one may have to give up faithfulness somewhere.
terms.description: One approach to enhance the transparency of a machine learning method for its human user is to provide an explanation alongside each prediction delivered by the method. Explanations can take different forms. For instance, they may consist of human-readable text or quantitative indicators, such as feature importance scores for the individual features of a given data point~, obtained, e.g., via the weights of a local linear approximation. Fig. 1 illustrates two types of explanations for a learned hypothesis h(x) of a single feature x. The first is a local linear approximation g(x) of the nonlinear h(x) around a specific feature value x'. The second form of explanation depicted in the figure is a sparse set of predictions h(x(1)), h(x(2)), h(x(3)) at selected feature values, possibly chosen by the user. Another form of explanation is a heat map: an intensity map that scores each region of an image by how much it drove the prediction, drawn over the image itself. For a convolutional neural network, those scores are computed from the network's own activations, which is what a class activation map does. Explanations differ in scope. The local linear approximation of local interpretable model-agnostic explanations concerns a single prediction; a global explanation, such as a decision tree fitted to the predictions of the learned hypothesis, describes its behavior across the whole feature space. A counterfactual answers a different question: not which features drove the prediction, but what change of the feature vector would have changed it. Whatever form it takes, an explanation carries two requirements: it must be (i) understandable and (ii) faithful. Understandable means that the user can work with the explanation on their own. Faithful means that the explanation reflects the computation the learned hypothesis carries out, rather than one that is easier to present. An intensity map over the pixels of an image is faithful when manipulating a few of the pixels it highlights changes the prediction while changing dark ones does not (see explainable artificial intelligence). These two requirements can be contradictory. An unfaithful explanation can even be understandable and let the user anticipate well, whenever it tracks the prediction without carrying anything about the computation. For some saliency methods, the map computed from a network with random weights is nearly the same as the map computed from the trained network. Such a map traces the edges of the input image and carries nothing about the prediction, yet it looks like a plausible explanation. An explanation that agreed with the learned hypothesis everywhere would be that hypothesis again, so a simpler explanation may have to give up faithfulness somewhere. Fig.~2 shows both requirements at work on a prediction made from weather radar. The features are the hourly precipitation over a 120 km box around Krems an der Donau, and the prediction answers whether it will rain at Krems two hours later. A convolutional neural network fitted to these images is explained by a class activation map, which scores each cell of the image by how much it contributed to the prediction. For the hour drawn, the network is certain of rain, and the CAM puts its weight on the bands of precipitation south and south-east of the town rather than on the rain already overhead. Setting the precipitation to zero in the 360 cells with the highest CAM scores lowers the predicted score by 1.57, against 0.26 for the 360 cells with the lowest scores, and the same holds on 63 of the 72 held-out hours. The same content can be delivered as text. The sentence under the panels is generated from the CAM by computing the radius that holds the cells it scores highest and the direction of their center of mass. It is therefore faithful by construction and can be checked against the radar image on the left.

terms.name: fairness (machine learning)
terms.abstract: Fairness (machine learning) is the property of a learned hypothesis, or of the decision rule built on it, to treat data points with different values of a sensitive attribute, such as gender or age, in a comparable way. A counterfactual criterion requires the prediction to be unchanged if the sensitive attribute had taken another value. An individual criterion requires similar predictions for data points that are similar under a task-specific metric. Group criteria equate a measure across the groups: the approval rates (demographic parity), the true-positive and false-positive rates (equalized odds), or the probability of the label given the score (calibration). The criteria are incompatible in general: calibration and equalized odds cannot both hold when the groups differ in their share of positive labels. A chosen criterion is met by a design choice for a component of empirical risk minimization: excluding the sensitive attribute and the features correlated with it from the model, adding a penalty term or a constraint to the loss function, or resampling the training set.
terms.description: Consider a bank that approves a loan when the creditworthiness predicted by a learned hypothesis h exceeds a threshold τ. The feature vector x of an applicant collects the income, the gender, and further attributes, and h was learned from the training set D(train) of completed loans. An applicant with feature vector x' obtains h(x') = 2.94, below τ = 3.8, and is rejected. The same applicant with only the gender flipped, x⋆, obtains h(x⋆) = 3.93 and is approved. Whether this system is fair has several precise answers, and they cannot all hold at once. Fairness in machine learning is the property of a learned hypothesis, or of the decision rule built on it, to treat data points with different values of a sensitive attribute s, such as gender, race, or age, in a comparable way, on top of making accurate predictions. It is one of the key requirements for trustworthy artificial intelligence. Three families of fairness criteria are distinguished. A counterfactual criterion requires that the prediction for a data point would not change if its sensitive attribute had taken another value, under a causal model of how s affects the other features (see causality). An individual criterion requires that data points that are similar under a task-specific metric, such as one that ignores s, receive similar predictions. A group criterion requires equality of some measure across the groups defined by s. Demographic parity equates the approval rates, \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{h}({\mathbf x}) \geq \tau \mid s = 0\right) = \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{h}({\mathbf x}) \geq \tau \mid s = 1\right) \text{,} \end{equation} where the data point is modeled as the realization of a random variable. For a binary label y ∈ 0,1, such as whether a loan was repaid, equalized odds equates the true-positive rate and the false-positive rate across the groups, and calibration equates P(y = 1 | h(x) = c, s) across the groups for every score c. Fig.~1 shows the credit-scoring example. The horizontal axis is a one-dimensional sketch of the feature vector; the gender flip moves the applicant from x' (open square) to x⋆ (open triangle). The gap h(x⋆) - h(x') = 0.99 (double arrow) is caused by the gender alone, so h fails the counterfactual criterion. It fails the individual criterion under a metric that ignores s as well: x' and x⋆ are then the same data point, yet they receive predictions on opposite sides of τ. The group criteria cannot be checked from five loans. They compare the predictions of h over the population of applicants, which the probability distribution of the demographic-parity condition \eqref{eq_fairness_dempar} describes. The criteria are mutually incompatible in general. Kleinberg et al. (2017) and Chouldechova (2017) show that calibration and equalized odds cannot both hold when the fraction of data points with y = 1 differs between the groups and h is not perfect. Fairness in machine learning is therefore not a single property to be optimized but a choice among criteria. The choice depends on the application: on the harm caused by a wrong prediction, and on the applicable law. Two examples are Art.~22 of the general data protection regulation on automated decisions and the duty under the EU AI Act to examine the training set of a high-risk artificial intelligence system for biases that lead to discrimination (see data governance). Once a criterion is chosen, it is met by a design choice for one of the components of empirical risk minimization. The model can exclude the sensitive attribute; x' and x⋆ then coincide and the gap in Fig.~1 vanishes. Excluding s alone does not suffice, since features correlated with it, such as the postal code, carry the same information. The loss function can carry a penalty term for the gap, or the gap can be a constraint of the constrained optimization problem that replaces empirical risk minimization. The training set can be resampled so that the groups are represented equally (see imbalanced data). Each choice lowers the gap of the chosen criterion and raises the average loss on D(train) or the gap of another criterion.

terms.name: feature learning
terms.abstract: Feature learning is the task of learning, from a dataset, a feature transformation that turns the raw features of a data point into new features that make a subsequent learning task easier. A feature learning method is specified by the two feature spaces, by a hypothesis space of candidate feature transformations, and by a quantitative measure of how useful a feature transformation is, computed from a dataset that need not carry labels. Principal component analysis learns a linear feature transformation to fewer features, judged by the linear reconstruction error, and an autoencoder obtains a nonlinear one by the same criterion. The hidden layers of a deep net form a chain of feature transformations learned jointly with the output layer, so that each layer builds its features from those of the previous one. Pretraining an encoder on unlabeled data points learns features that are reused across learning tasks. In weather forecasting, forty measurements from the five days before are turned into two learned features from which linear regression predicts the maximum temperature of the next day.
terms.description: Consider the task of forecasting the weather of tomorrow at a weather station from the measurements of the previous five days. Each day is a data point, and its label is the maximum temperature of that day. Its raw features are eight daily measurements: the lowest, highest and mean air temperature, the precipitation, the sunshine duration, the humidity, the air pressure and the wind speed. Taken over each of the five previous days, that is a list of forty numbers. A point with forty coordinates cannot be drawn in a scatterplot. A feature transformation that delivers two new features from the forty raw ones places every day in a scatterplot (see Fig.~1), and a linear model of the two new features may already predict the label. Feature learning is the task of learning such a feature transformation from a dataset instead of designing it by hand. Feature learning is the task of learning a feature transformation {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}', \qquad {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf z} := {\mathbf \Phi}({\mathbf x}) \text{.} The transformation reads in the raw feature vector x ∈ X of a data point and delivers a new feature vector z from a new feature space X'. A feature learning method is specified by three design choices: the two feature spaces X and X', a hypothesis space H of candidate feature transformations, and a quantitative measure of how useful a specific Φ ∈ H is. The measure is computed from a dataset, which need not carry labels, and it need not be the dataset of the learning task at hand. A useful feature transformation is one that makes a subsequent learning task easier: the data points become separable by a linear model, fewer features suffice, or the features learned once serve several learning tasks. In the weather example, usefulness is measured by the validation error of linear regression on the learned features. Alternative constructions of a feature transformation do not learn Φ. A kernel method fixes Φ through the choice of a kernel, with X' the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk and z = k(x,·), the kernel with its first argument fixed, never evaluated explicitly, and learns only a linear hypothesis on X'. A hand-designed Φ encodes domain knowledge instead of a dataset. A measure of usefulness can be built from a second map. The feature transformation is then read as an encoder, and a decoder Φ*: X' → X rebuilds the raw feature vector from the new one. What the encoder kept is then measured by how well the decoder rebuilds the data point from it, the reconstruction error \[ \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\Big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)}, {\mathbf \Phi}^{*}\big( {\mathbf \Phi}\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) \big) \Big) \text{.} \] The loss function L penalizes a rebuilt feature vector for differing from the original. A common choice is the squared error loss. The dataset it is computed on needs no labels: what the decoder has to reproduce is the data point itself. The decoder may be learned alongside the encoder. The measure is then the minimum of the reconstruction error over a second hypothesis space of decoders. It may instead be fixed, and the encoder alone must then supply what the decoder cannot. Restricting the decoder therefore decides what the new features have to carry. Principal component analysis is this construction with X := Rd, X' := Rd' for some d' < d, and the hypothesis space of linear maps, \mathcal{H} := \big\{ {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d'}: {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x} \text{ with some } {\mathbf W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times d} \big\} \text{.} The decoder is linear too and is learned alongside the encoder W. The usefulness of a specific Φ(x) = W x is therefore the minimum of the reconstruction error over the reconstruction matrices R. On the dataset D = x(1), …, x(m), that minimum is \min_{{\mathbf R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d'}} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf R} {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} The rows of the best W are the d' eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalues. An autoencoder keeps the same criterion and replaces both linear maps by ANNs, so that the new features come from a nonlinear feature transformation. With a linear decoder and the squared error loss, it spans the subspace principal component analysis finds. Applied to the weather example, principal component analysis delivers the two learned features of Fig.~1. The forty raw features of the 361 days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau are turned into two learned features. Each raw feature is first scaled to zero sample mean and unit sample variance, because temperatures, precipitation and pressure carry different units. Warm and cold days separate along the first learned feature: 89 percent of the warm days have a positive z1 and 92 percent of the cold days a nonpositive one. Linear regression on the two learned features is trained on the days from January to August. It then predicts the maximum temperature of the days from September to December with a validation error of 13.5 squared degrees Celsius. Linear regression on all forty raw features reaches 10.2, and predicting the sample mean of the training labels reaches 110.9. A deep net learns a chain of feature transformations. Each hidden layer ℓ = 1, …, L is a feature transformation Φ(ℓ) that reads in the activations z(ℓ-1) of the previous layer, with z(0) := x. The features delivered to the output layer are the composition z(L) = Φ(L) ∘ ∘ Φ(1) (x) (see Fig.~2). The feature transformations are learned jointly with the output layer by empirical risk minimization with the loss of the final prediction, so the usefulness of the learned features is measured by how well the output layer, typically a linear model, predicts the label from z(L). The chain is useful because each layer builds its features from those of the previous one, so the feature transformations Φ(ℓ) ∘ ∘ Φ(1) grow deeper with ℓ. In image classification, early layers deliver edges, later ones corners and object parts, and the features at the last hidden layer separate the classes by a linear surface. Pretraining an encoder on a large dataset of unlabeled data points, with a loss constructed from the data points themselves (see self-supervised learning), learns features that are reused across learning tasks. A new learning task appends a task-specific hypothesis with few model parameters to the learned Φ and adapts it by fine-tuning on its own dataset. The dataset used to learn Φ can then be much larger than any labeled dataset, because unlabeled data points are cheap to collect.

terms.name: feature
terms.abstract: A feature of a data point is one of its attributes that can be measured or computed easily, without human supervision. The features of a data point are collected into a feature vector, which a hypothesis map reads to predict the label of the data point. The red-green-blue (RGB) pixel intensities of a digital image or the signal values of an audio recording are typical features. Which attributes of a data point serve as features, rather than as labels, is a design choice within a machine learning application.
terms.description: A digital photo of a cow is a grid of pixels, and the red, green and blue intensity of each pixel is a number that a computer obtains without any human looking at the photo. Such a number is a feature of the data point: an attribute of the data point z that is measured, or computed, without human supervision. The features of a data point are assembled into a feature vector x = Φ(z) by a feature transformation, a function Φ: Z → X, viewing the data point itself as its raw features from which the computed features are obtained. A hypothesis map reads the feature vector and delivers a prediction of the label of the data point. The red-green-blue (RGB) intensities of the pixels of a digital image are one example of features. Another example is shown in Fig.~1, where the d signal values of a finite-duration audio signal are used as its features x1, …, xd. New features can be constructed by transforming existing features. Such a transformation can be an arithmetic computation applied to the existing features. For example, if a data point has a numeric feature x ∈ R, the quantities x2, exp(-x), and 3x can also be used as features of the data point. Instead of its raw signal values, the audio signal in Fig.~1 can be described by the magnitudes of its discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT). These features capture the frequency content of the signal and are unchanged by time shifts, which is useful for a stationary signal, one whose statistical properties do not change over time. Another example is the activation of a neuron within an artificial neural network: it is a new feature derived from the input features by a sequence of basic computations encoded by the artificial neural network. Using activations as features underlies a second, narrower use of the word feature in mechanistic interpretability: a feature is a human-interpretable concept encoded inside a trained artificial neural network, such as a curve detector or the presence of a wheel. The activations of a subset of d neurons (for example, a whole layer, or the neurons that an analyst selects for study) form a vector in a Euclidean space Rd. Whereas the broader sense above treats a single neuron activation as one feature, here a feature is obtained as a function of this whole activation vector a. One such function is the projection of the activation vector a onto a one-dimensional subspace spanned by a unit vector (or direction) u. This unit vector can be obtained from a hyperplane separating data points that express the concept from those that do not (see Fig.~2). Another construction of an activation-based feature is based on regions instead of directions in the activation space. In either case, constructing the function that maps the activation vector to the feature requires a set of data points labeled as representing the concept or not. Whether a given attribute is treated as a feature or a label is not inherent to the data point. It is more a design choice that depends on the machine learning application and the resources available for determining each attribute. An attribute should be used as a feature only if its value can be determined for every data point at the time the prediction is needed; an attribute that becomes known only afterwards is a candidate for the label instead. The accuracy of features also matters for regulation. The EU AI Act requires the training data of high-risk ML systems to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete. When features are personal data, the general data protection regulation adds the data minimization principle and the accuracy principle. Conversely, deliberately perturbing the features can be useful: adding small perturbations to the features of data points during training is a form of data augmentation that acts as regularization. For example, the ridge regression penalty equals the average loss under Gaussian feature perturbations: for a linear model with model parameters w, adding zero-mean Gaussian noise of variance α to each feature raises the expected squared error loss by α ‖ w ‖22, the ridge penalty.

terms.name: feature importance
terms.abstract: An importance score assigns a number to each feature of a learned hypothesis. With standardized features, a linear model's coefficient magnitude equals prediction change per standard deviation. Permutation importance is the average-loss increase when a feature is permuted across data points. Scores are computed for the hypothesis and scoring dataset.
terms.description: An importance score assigns a number to each feature of a learned hypothesis h. Predict tomorrow's daytime peak at a weather station from twelve features: today's and the previous day's high and low temperature, air pressure, humidity, sunshine duration and precipitation. A hypothesis learned by linear regression from one year predicts the next day's high with average squared error loss 8.8, versus label variance 84.6 (in squared degrees Celsius; Fig.~1). For a linear model with standardized features, h(x) = wᵀ x = Σj=112 wj xj and |wj| is the prediction change per standard deviation of feature j. Current-day high coefficient: 8.6; low coefficient: 0.02 (Fig.~2). Variable-importance scores appear in random forests. Permutation importance uses predictions from a fitted hypothesis. On the scoring dataset, the j-th feature's score is the average-loss increase after shuffling its column. Denote it Ij. With standardized features and squared error loss, replacing xj by an independent draw xj changes the prediction by δj=wj (xj-xj). The squared error loss increase is δj2 -2(y-h(x)) δj, where y is the label. Standardization gives unit variance, and zero covariance between xj and xj implies E(xj -xj)2=2. If the prediction error is uncorrelated with δj, the cross-term averages out: Ij ≈ Eδj2 = 2wj2. Fig.~2 plots Ij/2 next to |wj|; the two scores rank the features almost identically. The score measures the reliance of the learned hypothesis h on a feature, not the relevance of the feature itself: a feature that is predictive of the label obtains the score zero whenever h ignores it. For jointly Gaussian features and label, the score of a feature combines its covariance with the label and its covariances with the other features.

terms.name: feature matrix
terms.abstract: The feature matrix of a dataset collects the feature vectors of its data points as its rows, one row per data point and one column per feature. Its two most basic properties are the number of rows, which is the number of data points in the dataset, and the number of columns, which is the number of features of each data point. More properties of a dataset follow from the singular values of its feature matrix. The number of nonzero singular values is the rank, and a rank below the number of features leaves linear regression with infinitely many solutions. The ratio of the largest to the smallest nonzero singular value is the condition number of the feature matrix. The condition number determines the number of gradient descent steps required by linear regression and its robustness against perturbations of the features and labels in the training set.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau records eight measurements on each of the 366 days of the leap year 2024: the lowest, highest, and mean air temperature, the humidity, the wind speed, the precipitation, the sunshine duration, and the air pressure. Writing the eight measurements of one day as a row, and placing the rows of the 366 days under one another, gives a two-dimensional numeric array with 366 rows and eight columns. That array is a matrix, the feature matrix of the dataset whose data points are the 366 days, and each of its rows is the feature vector of one day. The feature matrix is the form in which machine learning software expects a dataset, and properties of the machine learning methods applied to the dataset, such as whether linear regression has a unique solution or how fast gradient descent converges, are determined by it. In general, consider a dataset D of m data points with feature vectors x(1), …, x(m), each in Rd. Stacking the feature vectors row-wise yields the feature matrix: {\mathbf X} := \big({\mathbf x}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf x}^{(m)}\big)^{\top} = \begin{pmatrix} x^{(1)}_{1} & x^{(1)}_{2} & ḑots & x^{(1)}_{d} x^{(2)}_{1} & x^{(2)}_{2} & ḑots & x^{(2)}_{d} \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots x^{(m)}_{1} & x^{(m)}_{2} & ḑots & x^{(m)}_{d} \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d} \text{.} The feature matrix is of size m × d, i.e., it has m rows and d columns. Each row is the transposed feature vector of one data point, and each column holds the values of one feature for all data points (see Fig.~1). Many properties of a dataset, and of the learning tasks built from it, are computed from X. The most basic ones are the numbers of rows and columns, m and d. The feature matrix also defines a linear map. A linear model with model parameters w from the parameter space Rd predicts wᵀ x(r) for the r-th data point, so the m predictions are the entries of X w. The feature matrix therefore maps each w ∈ Rd to the vector X w ∈ Rm, which is compared with the label vector y = (y(1), …, y(m))ᵀ ∈ Rm. Linear regression on a training set with feature matrix X and label vector y is the search for a vector w whose image X w is close to y in Euclidean norm. Linear regression has a unique solution only when X has full column rank, which requires m ≥ d (see normal equations). A rank below d leaves infinitely many parameter vectors w with the same training error, and the one a method returns can have a large loss outside the training set. Using more features than data points (i.e., d > m) forces this case, since then X has fewer rows than columns, which rules out full column rank. More properties of a dataset follow from the singular values of its feature matrix X. The singular value decomposition can be written as {\mathbf X} = \sum_{j=1}^{\min\{m, d\}} \lambda_{j} {\mathbf v}^{(j)} \big({\mathbf u}^{(j)}\big)^{\top} \text{,} where the vectors v(1), …, v(minm, d) ∈ Rm are orthonormal among themselves, the vectors u(1), …, u(minm, d) ∈ Rd are orthonormal among themselves. The singular values are ordered as λ1 ≥ … ≥ λminm, d ≥ 0. The number of nonzero singular values is the rank of X. A rank below d means that some feature is a linear combination of the others and adds no information beyond them. A small but nonzero singular value is the approximate form of such a dependence. The smallest singular value is the smallest Euclidean norm of a linear combination of the feature columns with unit-norm coefficients, \[ \lambda_{\min\{m, d\}} = \min_{{\mathbf u} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, \Vert {{\mathbf u}} \Vert = 1} \Vert {{\mathbf X} {\mathbf u}} \Vert \text{,} \] attained at the right singular vector u(minm, d). This holds since a unit-norm u = Σj cj u(j) gives X u 2 = Σj cj2 λj2, a weighted average of the squared singular values. A small singular value therefore says that some combination of the feature columns with unit-norm coefficients is nearly the zero vector: the features are nearly collinear, and the right singular vector names the combination. For the weather year of Fig.~1, with every measurement scaled to zero sample mean and unit sample variance, the smallest singular value is 0.05 against a largest of 36.4. Its right singular vector places all of its weight, to three decimals, on the lowest, the highest, and the mean temperature, with coefficients -0.37, -0.46, and 0.81, because the mean temperature of a day is the midpoint of its lowest and its highest up to a residual with standard deviation 0.03 degrees. Dropping the mean temperature raises the smallest singular value to 4.19 (pythondemos/featuremtx.py). The size of a singular value depends on the units of the columns, which is why the scaling to unit sample variance comes first. The squares of the singular values are the eigenvalues of Xᵀ X, which for features with zero sample mean is m times their sample covariance matrix. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Xᵀ X also determine principal component analysis. Its dimensionality reduction keeps the eigenvectors of the largest eigenvalues as the new features, and the sum over the data points of the squared errors of reconstructing the feature vectors from them is the sum of the eigenvalues dropped. Another important property of a feature matrix is the condition number κ (X) = λ1 / λrank(X), the ratio of the largest singular value to the smallest nonzero one. For full column rank, it is the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value. The condition number enters linear regression twice: through the number of gradient descent steps, and through the robustness of the learned model parameters against perturbations of the training set. The number that matters in both is its square κ (X)2. The objective function f(w) = (1/m) X w - y 2 has the constant Hessian (2/m) Xᵀ X, whose eigenvalues are the squared singular values of X scaled by 2/m. The condition number of Xᵀ X is therefore κ (X)2. The square κ (X)2 determines the convergence speed of gradient descent on the empirical risk minimization problem of linear regression. One step with an exact line search multiplies the gap between f(w(t)) and the minimum f(w) by at most 1 - 1/κ (X)2. The number of steps that reaches a given gap therefore grows in proportion to κ (X)2. Fig.~2 shows this for two feature matrices built from the weather measurements of Fig.~1. The features are the relative humidity and the wind speed, the label is the highest temperature, and each has its sample mean removed. In the recorded units the condition number is 14.5. After scaling each feature to unit sample variance, it is 1.45. Gradient descent starts at the point at distance w from w for which it is slowest, where the gap shrinks by exactly ((κ (X)2 - 1) / (κ (X)2 + 1))2 per step. A gap of 10-6 of the initial one then takes 731 steps in the recorded units and 7 after the scaling. The condition number κ (X) also governs the robustness of the model parameters w delivered by linear regression against perturbations of the training set. Let X have full column rank. Linear regression delivers the model parameters w = X+ y with the pseudoinverse X+ = (Xᵀ X)-1 Xᵀ. They are the unique solution of the normal equations Xᵀ X w = Xᵀ y, which state that the gradient of f vanishes at w. Consider perturbations of the training set that change X to X + δ X and y to y + δ y, with X + δ X still of full column rank, and let w + δ w be the model parameters learned by linear regression on the perturbed training set. They solve the normal equations of the perturbed training set, ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X})^{\top} ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X}) \big(\widehat{{\mathbf w}} + \delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}}\big) = ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X})^{\top} ({\mathbf y} + \delta {\mathbf y}) \text{.} Moving the terms with w to the right side and using Xᵀ r = 0 for the least squares residual r = y - X w, which is the normal equations of the unperturbed training set, gives the exact equation ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X})^{\top} ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X}) \delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X})^{\top} \big(\delta {\mathbf y} - \delta {\mathbf X} \widehat{{\mathbf w}}\big) + \delta {\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf r} \text{.} Solving for δ w applies the pseudoinverse of X + δ X to the noise in the labels and to the noise in the features acting on w, and the inverse matrix of (X + δ X)ᵀ (X + δ X) to the noise in the features acting on the residual. The largest singular value of X+ is 1 / λd, and that of (Xᵀ X)-1 is 1 / λd2. The same holds for X + δ X with its own smallest singular value. Let the largest singular value of δ X be at most ε λ1 and the Euclidean norm of δ y at most ε y, with ε κ (X) < 1. The smallest singular value of X + δ X is then at least λd - ε λ1, and taking Euclidean norms in the exact equation gives the perturbation bound \begin{equation} \Vert {\delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert \leq \frac{\varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)} {1 - \varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)} \Big( \frac{\Vert {{\mathbf y}} \Vert}{\lambda_{1}} + \Vert {\widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert \Big) + \frac{\varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)^{2}} {\big(1 - \varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)\big)^{2}} \frac{\Vert {{\mathbf r}} \Vert}{\lambda_{1}} \text{.} \end{equation} The bound \eqref{eq_featuremtx_bound} holds for every perturbation with ε κ (X) < 1. The bound \eqref{eq_featuremtx_bound} carries over to the prediction for any given feature vector x, such as that of a test data point. The learned linear model predicts xᵀ w before and xᵀ (w + δ w) after the perturbation. The prediction therefore changes by xᵀ δ w, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds this change by \begin{equation} \big| {\mathbf x}^{\top} \delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}} \big| \leq \Vert {{\mathbf x}} \Vert \Vert {\delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert \leq \Vert {{\mathbf x}} \Vert \Bigg( \frac{\varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)} {1 - \varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)} \Big( \frac{\Vert {{\mathbf y}} \Vert}{\lambda_{1}} + \Vert {\widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert \Big) + \frac{\varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)^{2}} {\big(1 - \varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)\big)^{2}} \frac{\Vert {{\mathbf r}} \Vert}{\lambda_{1}} \Bigg) \text{.} \end{equation} The change of the prediction is therefore at most x times the right-hand side of the bound \eqref{eq_featuremtx_bound}, and grows with the norm of the feature vector. Fig.~3 shows the robustness of w against perturbations on a related but different and smaller dataset, the first days of the twelve months of 2024, twelve of the rows of Fig.~1. Each day has the feature vector x = (1, x)ᵀ with x its lowest temperature, and its highest temperature as the label. A hypothesis of the linear model then has intercept w1 and slope w2, and the feature matrix has a column of ones and the column of the lowest temperatures. Its condition number is 14.9, and linear regression delivers the intercept 10.89 and the slope 1.05, with a residual of 0.20 times the norm of y. Two constructions of a perturbation of relative size ε = 0.01 are compared. The first is chosen adversarially, to make the change of the model parameters learned by linear regression as large as possible: δ X = -ε λ1 v(2) (u(2))ᵀ and δ y = ± ε y v(2), with the sign for which w moves more. It moves the intercept to 13.11 and the slope to 0.90, a change of norm 2.23, which is 64 percent of the right-hand side of the bound \eqref{eq_featuremtx_bound}, 3.46. The second construction uses 100 realizations of random δ X and δ y. They are generated with independent and identically distributed Gaussian RVs as their entries and then normalized so that the largest singular value of δ X is ε λ1 and the Euclidean norm of δ y is ε y. The largest change among the 100 realizations is 1.17, which is 34 percent of the right-hand side of the bound \eqref{eq_featuremtx_bound}. For a day with lowest temperature x the feature vector (1, x)ᵀ has norm 1 + x2. By the prediction bound \eqref{eq_featuremtx_predbound} the prediction therefore changes by at most 1 + x2 times the right-hand side of the bound \eqref{eq_featuremtx_bound}: 3.5 degrees at x = 0 and 69 degrees at x = 20. These are the two dotted curves in Fig.~3(a), which leave the plotted range. The hypotheses learned from the random perturbations stay within 1.6 degrees of the learned hypothesis over the plotted range, and the hypothesis after the adversarial construction within 3.1 degrees. Panel (b) repeats the comparison for ε from 5 · 10-4 to 5 · 10-2. The adversarial construction reaches more than half of the right-hand side of the bound \eqref{eq_featuremtx_bound} up to ε = 0.02, the random construction less than half at every ε.

terms.name: feature vector
terms.abstract: A feature vector is a list of numbers describing a data point, with one entry for each of its features. A feature is an attribute of the data point that is measured or computed without human supervision, so the length of the vector is the number of such attributes. A feature transformation computes the feature vector from the data point and delivers a point of the feature space, which a hypothesis map then reads to predict the label. Non-numeric features enter as numbers: a binary attribute as 0 or 1, a categorical one through one-hot encoding. Most machine learning methods use feature vectors in a Euclidean space whose dimension is the number of features. A feature vector can more generally be an element of a Hilbert space, which is how a kernel method uses one without ever forming it, reaching it only through inner products.
terms.description: A house offered for sale can be described to a machine learning method by three numbers: 85 square meters of living area, 3 rooms, and 1974 as the year of construction. That list (85, 3, 1974) is the feature vector of the house. In general, a feature vector gathers into one vector the features of a data point, those attributes of the data point that are measured or computed without human supervision. A list of d real numbers, for a natural number d, is an element of the Euclidean space Rd. The feature vector of a data point z is written x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ, and its entry xj is one feature of that data point. It is obtained from the data point by a feature transformation Φ: Z → X, x = Φ(z), which views the data point itself as its raw features and delivers a point of the feature space X (Fig.~1). A hypothesis map reads the feature vector and delivers a prediction of the label of the data point. Non-numeric features can also sit in the entries of a feature vector, once their values are encoded as real numbers. A binary feature, such as whether the house has a balcony, becomes 0 or 1. A categorical feature with K possible values, such as the heating type (gas, oil, or electric), is one-hot encoded: K entries of the feature vector carry the value 0 except for a single entry equal to 1, whose position names the value. A feature transformation also reaches data points that are not records of numbers. A text becomes a feature vector by counting how often each entry of a fixed word list appears in it, which gives one entry per listed word. A digital image is an array of pixels, and the red, green and blue intensities of those pixels become one entry each. Reading a 2 × 2 patch of such an image this way gives 2 · 2 · 3 = 12 features (Fig.~2). The order of the entries is arbitrary but fixed: every data point must be read in the same order, since a hypothesis map weights the entry at a given position, not the feature that happened to land there. An audio recording becomes a feature vector through the values its signal takes at successive instants, one entry per instant. The feature transformation differs in each case, and so does the dimension d of the resulting feature space: the house above needs seven entries once its balcony and heating type are encoded, while an audio recording read at 256 instants needs 256 (Fig.~3). Most machine learning methods use feature vectors in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space Rd, whose dimension d is the number of features. More generally, a feature vector can be an element of an abstract Hilbert space H. One way to build a feature vector of that kind starts from a kernel k: X × X → R on a given feature space X. The kernel assigns to each x ∈ X the function k(x,·): X → R, whose value at x' ∈ X is k(x,x'). That function is itself a vector in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space H, a Hilbert space whose elements are functions on X. A kernel method uses these feature vectors without ever forming them explicitly: it reaches them only through their inner products, which the reproducing property reduces to kernel evaluations, x·x'·H = k(x,x').

terms.name: fine-tuning
terms.abstract: Fine-tuning continues the training of a model on a task-specific dataset, starting from model parameters obtained by pretraining on a larger dataset. It solves an empirical risk minimization problem over a small training set under the constraint that the model parameters stay close to the pretrained ones. One form of fine-tuning runs a few gradient descent steps on the small training set, started at the pretrained model parameters. Forcing the model parameters to stay close to the pretrained ones is a form of regularization, since it limits the effective hypothesis space that is searched during fine-tuning. For a linear model, the generalization gap grows in proportion to how far the model parameters may move from the pretrained ones, which is why a small training set suffices.
terms.description: Consider daily weather at Krems an der Donau. A linear model that predicts the maximum daytime temperature from the morning minimum is trained on 360 days of one year. The task-specific datasets are the temperature measurements of a single month, and one task is to learn a forecaster tailored to that month. For a single month, thirty gradient descent steps on that month's 30 days adjust the model parameters, starting from those learned on the whole year (Fig.~1). Fine-tuning is this second step: it continues the training of a model on a task-specific dataset, starting from model parameters obtained by pretraining on a larger dataset. Formally, let f(w) denote the average loss on the task-specific training set D(train) = z(r)r=1m, \[ f({\mathbf w}) := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},{\mathbf w} \right) \text{.} \] Fine-tuning solves the empirical risk minimization problem for f under the constraint that the model parameters stay within a radius B of the pretrained ones w(pre), \[ \widehat{{\mathbf w}} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \overline{\mathcal{B}}_{B}(\widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{(\mathrm{pre})})} f({\mathbf w}) \text{.} \] Here, w(pre)B := w: w - w(pre) ≤ B is the closed ball of radius B around w(pre) (see Fig.~3). The radius B is what makes a small training set enough. Consider a linear model, whose hypotheses are h(w)(x) = wᵀ x. Let the feature vectors have norm at most R, and let the loss be ρ-Lipschitz in the prediction and bounded by c on the ball, as the hinge loss is. Let the data points be realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. Then, with probability at least 1 - δ, every w ∈ w(pre)B satisfies \[ \bar{L} \big( h^{({\mathbf w})} \big) \leq f({\mathbf w}) + \frac{2 \rho B R}{\sqrt{m}} + c \sqrt{\frac{2 \ln(2/\delta)}{m}} \text{.} \] This is the bound of Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014, Thm. 26.12) for model parameters of norm at most B, applied to the shifted model parameters w - w(pre). The shift adds the fixed number (w(pre))ᵀ x to the prediction for each data point, which the contraction step of the proof allows, as it admits a separate ρ-Lipschitz function per data point. The second term follows from the Rademacher complexity of the ball, which is at most B R / √(m). The generalization gap between risk and training error f(w) therefore grows in proportion to the radius B and not with the number d of model parameters. A gap of at most ε is guaranteed by m = (2 ρ B R + c √(2 ln(2/δ)))2 / ε2 data points, a number that falls with B. The constraint restricts the model the method searches, which is what regularization achieves by pruning a hypothesis space. The difference is that the pruned set is centered at the pretrained model parameters instead of at an arbitrary initialization. Gradient descent with few steps and a small step size, started at the pretrained model parameters, implements this constraint without enforcing it explicitly. Each step moves the model parameters by η times the norm of the gradient. After T steps with step size η, started at w(0) = w(pre), \[ \Vert {{\mathbf w}^{(T)} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{(\mathrm{pre})}} \Vert \leq \eta \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \Vert {\nabla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)})} \Vert \leq \eta T G \text{,} \] where G bounds the norm of the gradient along the iterates. The iterate therefore lies in the ball of radius B = η T G around w(pre). Limiting the number of iterations is thus a form of regularization: it limits the effective hypothesis space that is searched during fine-tuning, with the step size and the iteration count in the role of the radius. Fine-tuning is useful when the task-specific dataset is small. A hospital has a few hundred annotated scans and needs a tumor detector. Training a deep net from an arbitrary initialization on that many labeled data points usually ends in overfitting; starting from model parameters already learned from millions of unrelated photographs works markedly better. LLMs are adapted the same way: one pretrained on unlabeled text is fine-tuned on each task it is wanted for. The experiment pythondemos/finetuning.py measures the effect for linear regression with m = 15 data points and d = 30 model parameters. Gradient descent started at the pretrained model parameters with step size η = 0.02 dips to a validation error below twice the noise level after T = 16 steps. It has then moved the model parameters a distance 0.32, inside the ball of radius η T G = 0.72. The same iteration from an arbitrary initialization drives the training error to zero yet ends with a validation error more than four times larger, having moved a distance 2.6. A common variant freezes some layers and adapts only the remainder; parameter-efficient fine-tuning restricts the update to a low-dimensional set of new model parameters while leaving w(pre) untouched. Fig.~2 shows the effect on a small task-specific dataset that consists of four data points.

terms.name: Gaussian random variable (Gaussian RV)
terms.abstract: A Gaussian random variable (Gaussian RV) is a real-valued random variable whose probability density function is proportional to the exponential of a negative quadratic. The probability density function is determined by two numbers, the mean μ and the variance σ2 of the random variable; the probability distribution with these two parameters is denoted by N(μ,σ2). The standard Gaussian random variable is the special case μ = 0 and σ2 = 1; a general Gaussian random variable is obtained from it by scaling and shifting. A Gaussian random vector is an affine transformation of independent standard Gaussian RVs. Gaussian RVs arise naturally as limits of averages of many independent RVs through the central limit theorem. Among all random vectors with a given covariance matrix, the Gaussian random vector maximizes the differential entropy.
terms.description: A real-valued random variable z is a standard Gaussian random variable if its probability density function is \[ p^{(z)}\left(\eta\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp (-\eta^2/2) \text{.} \] Given a standard Gaussian random variable z, a general Gaussian random variable x with mean μ and variance σ2 can be constructed via x := σ z + μ, so that the probability distribution of x is the normal distribution N(μ,σ2), denoted by x ~ N(μ,σ2). The probability density function of x is, for every η ∈ R, \[ p^{(x)}\left(\eta\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}} \exp\Big( -\frac{(\eta-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} \Big) \text{.} \] The standard Gaussian random variable is the special case μ = 0 and σ2 = 1. The two parameters of N(μ,σ2) act separately on the probability density function, as shown in Fig.~1: the parameter μ is the mean of x, and the parameter σ is its standard deviation, the square root of the variance σ2. Adding μ to the scaled random variable σ z shifts the probability density function along the horizontal axis by μ, without changing its shape. For σ>0, multiplying z by σ stretches the probability density function horizontally by a factor of σ and lowers its peak by the same factor, so the area under it remains 1. There are two widely used constructions of Gaussian RVs. For exact generation, let U be a random variable uniformly distributed on the open interval (0,1) ⊂ R and let Φ be the cumulative distribution function of a standard Gaussian random variable. Then μ + σΦ-1(U) ~ N(μ,σ2), the same probability distribution as x but obtained from a different source of randomness. For approximate generation, let m be a positive integer and let v(1), …, v(m) be independent and identically distributed RVs, not necessarily Gaussian, with mean 0 and finite, nonzero variance τ2. Then the normalized sum \[ \frac{1}{\tau\sqrt{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}v^{(i)} \] converges in distribution to a standard Gaussian random variable as m increases. Thus, the central limit theorem makes a Gaussian approximation appropriate for averages of many independent contributions, which is why the measurement error of a sensor is usually modeled as Gaussian, although a finite sum need not be Gaussian. Fig.~2 shows both halves of that statement for coin flips, each taking the values +1 and -1 with probability 1/2. The probability mass function of the normalized sum of m = 8 of them already follows the shape of the standard Gaussian probability density function, and the sum still takes only 9 values. Convergence in distribution is convergence of the cdfs, so the largest gap between the cumulative distribution function of the normalized sum and that of a standard Gaussian random variable measures how far the approximation still is. It is 0.137 for m = 8 and 0.050 for m = 64. A Gaussian random vector x ∈ Rd with covariance matrix C and mean μ can be constructed as \[ {\mathbf x} := {\mathbf A} {\mathbf z} + {\boldsymbol \mu} \text{.} \] Here, z := ( z1, …, zd )ᵀ is a vector of independent and identically distributed standard Gaussian RVs. The matrix A ∈ Rd × d is a matrix square root of C, i.e., any matrix with A Aᵀ = C (a Cholesky factor, for instance). The probability distribution of a Gaussian random vector is referred to as the multivariate normal distribution, denoted by N(μ,C). A Gaussian random vector need not have independent components; its components are independent exactly when its covariance matrix is diagonal. A Gaussian random vector x=(x1, …, xd)ᵀ can be interpreted as a stochastic process indexed by the finite set 1, …, d. More generally, a Gaussian process is a stochastic process over an index set I whose restriction to every finite subset of I is a Gaussian random vector. A standard Gaussian random variable z obeys the Gaussian tail bound P(|z| ≥ t) ≤ 2 exp(-t2/2) for every positive number t. That bound also controls functions of independent and identically distributed RVs. Consider a standard Gaussian random vector z ∈ Rd and a function f: Rd → R that is Lipschitz with constant L, i.e., | f(z) - f(z') | ≤ L z - z' for every pair of vectors z, z' ∈ Rd. The deviation of f(z) from its expectation is then a sub-Gaussian random variable with parameter at most L. For every positive number t, \[ \mathbb{P}\left(\big| f({\mathbf z}) - \mathbb{E}\big\{ f({\mathbf z}) \big\} \big| \geq t\right) \leq 2 \exp\Big( \frac{-t^{2}}{2L^{2}} \Big) \text{.} \] The number d of arguments does not appear in this concentration inequality: the bound is the same for two arguments and for a thousand. It constrains the tails of f(z) and does not state that f(z) has a normal distribution. The Euclidean norm is an example with L = 1: the length z has expectation at most √(d) and deviates from it by more than t with probability at most 2exp(-t2/2), however large d is. Among all random vectors with a given covariance matrix C, the Gaussian random vector x ~ N(μ,C) maximizes the differential entropy. This property is one reason why additive Gaussian measurement noise is a widely used probabilistic model in the statistical analysis of machine learning methods: when only the variance of the noise is known, a Gaussian is the least restrictive assumption.

terms.name: gradient descent (GD)
terms.abstract: Gradient descent (GD) is an iterative algorithm for minimizing a differentiable function f: Rd → R. Each iteration updates the current estimate by a step along the negative gradient, scaled by a step size η. Such a gradient step can be interpreted as the application of an operator that is parameterized by the step size and the underlying function. GD and its variants are widely used to train parametric models in deep learning.
terms.description:
When training a deep net for image recognition, the average loss incurred by the network on a training set of labeled images is a function f(w) of the vector w ∈ Rd of its model parameters, and training means driving that function down. Many machine learning applications amount to such an optimization problem: an objective function f: Rd → R measures the quality of the model parameters w, which are the optimization variable. Minimizing f on the training set is a proxy: the goal is a small loss on data points outside it (see generalization), which is why the number of iterations and the step size are chosen by validation. In many important cases, the objective function is differentiable: at every point w there exists a gradient ∇ f(w) ∈ Rd, the vector of partial derivatives of f at w, which determines a local linear approximation of f (see differentiable). GD uses this local linear approximation to iteratively improve the current choice of the model parameters: starting from an initialization w(0), GD generates a sequence of estimates w(0), w(1), w(2), … that ideally converge to a minimum of f. GD and its variants are the standard solvers for model training in deep learning. At each iteration t, GD refines the current estimate w(t) by stepping in the direction of steepest descent of the local linear approximation to f at w(t). This direction is the negative gradient ∇ f(w(t)), giving the update  egin{equation} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} - \eta 
abla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) 	ext{,} \end{equation} where η > 0 is a step size; the update is a gradient step with step size η. For a sufficiently small η, each step decreases the function value, f(w(t+1)) ≤ f(w(t)), with strict decrease whenever ∇ f(w(t)) ≠ 0. Fig.~1 illustrates a single GD step. Algorithm~1 states the method in full.  egin{algorithm}[H] a̧ption{Gradient descent }  egin{algorithmic}[1] \Require objective function f, step size η > 0, initialization w(0), iteration count T \For{t = 0, 1, …, T-1} \State compute the gradient ∇ f(w(t)) \State w(t+1) w(t) - η ∇ f(w(t)) \EndFor \Ensure w(T) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} With a constant step size η, held fixed across iterations, a single step is described by the GD step operator F(η)(w) = w - η ∇ f(w), so GD is the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(η)(w(t)). Its fixed points, where F(η)(w) = w, are exactly the stationary points ∇ f(w) = 0. For convex f, these are the minima according to the zero-gradient condition. Consider shrinking the step size η in the GD step \eqref{equ_def_GD_step_dict} toward zero. For η → 0, the iterate w(t) converges to w(t η), the value at time t η of the continuous-time trajectory w(τ) that satisfies the ordinary differential equation w(τ) = -∇ f(w(τ)), known as gradient flow. In particular, GD is the explicit Euler discretization of this gradient flow with step η. Indeed, replacing the time derivative w(τ) by the difference quotient (w(t+1) - w(t))/η recovers the update \eqref{equ_def_GD_step_dict}. Fig.~2 illustrates how, for a small step size, the GD iterates closely follow the gradient flow trajectory. Returning to the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(η)(w(t)), its convergence is governed by the properties of the GD step operator F(η). Assume f is convex and its gradient is L-Lipschitz continuous, i.e., \Vert {
abla f({\mathbf w}) - 
abla f({\mathbf w}')} \Vert \le L \Vert {{\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}'} \Vert \quad 	ext{for all } {\mathbf w}, {\mathbf w}' \in \mathbb{R}^{d} 	ext{.} For 0 < η ≤ 1/L, the operator F(η) is then a non-expansive operator with respect to the Euclidean norm ·: it does not increase distances between any two points w, w', \Vert {\mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) - \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}')} \Vert \le \Vert {{\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}'} \Vert 	ext{.} Non-expansiveness alone does not guarantee a unique fixed point. Assume, moreover, that f is μ-strongly convex, i.e., the function f(w) - (μ/2) w 2 is still convex, so the curvature of f is at least μ > 0 in every direction. Then F(η) is a contractive operator with respect to the same norm, \Vert {\mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) - \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}')} \Vert \le (1 - \mu\eta) \Vert {{\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}'} \Vert 	ext{.} In this case, Banach's fixed-point theorem gives a unique fixed point w (the minimizer of f) to which GD converges at a geometric rate. For linear regression, these properties are explicit: the gradient of the average squared error loss is an affine function of w, and the contraction factor of F(η) is governed by the eigenvalues of the matrix XᵀX. Here, X denotes the feature matrix, whose rows are the feature vectors of the data points in the training set (see linear regression). How fast GD converges depends on the curvature of f, as quantified by the constants L and μ above. Let w be a minimizer and f⋆ = f(w). For convex f with L-Lipschitz gradient and the constant step size η = 1/L, f ig({\mathbf w}^{(T)} ig) - f^{\star} \le  rac{L \Vert {{\mathbf w}^{(0)} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert^{2}}{2 T} 	ext{,} so the suboptimality after T steps falls in proportion to 1/T: halving the suboptimality requires doubling the number of iterations. If f is in addition μ-strongly convex, the bound improves to the geometric rate f ig({\mathbf w}^{(T)} ig) - f^{\star} \le \left(1 - 	frac{\mu}{L}ight)^{T}  ig(f({\mathbf w}^{(0)}) - f^{\star} ig) 	ext{,} consistent with the contractive operator factor 1 - μη above. A geometric rate means that the suboptimality shrinks by at least the constant factor 1 - μ/L in every single iteration. Thus, halving the suboptimality now costs a fixed number of iterations, however small the current suboptimality already is. Momentum methods, discussed below, sharpen both bounds. In two common settings that motivate variants of GD, the assumptions behind these guarantees fail or the gradient becomes too costly. First, when f is non-smooth, its gradient may fail to exist and GD is replaced by subgradient descent, which steps along a subgradient in place of the gradient. A concrete case is the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator objective, whose penalty term α ‖ w ‖1 is non-smooth. Second, in empirical risk minimization-based methods, f is an average of m loss functions, one for each data point, so evaluating the full gradient sums m gradients and its cost grows in proportion to the training set size m. GD is thus replaced by stochastic gradient descent, which uses a cheap gradient estimate from a random subset of the training set at each step. Momentum methods provide another generalization of plain GD: each update combines gradients from several past steps rather than the current one alone. The name stems from a physical analogy: the iterates trace a particle whose momentum accumulates the force exerted by the negative gradient of the objective function. One prototypical example of a momentum method is Polyak's heavy-ball method. It adds a fraction β ∈ [0, 1) of the previous increment, {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} - \eta 
abla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) +  eta ig({\mathbf w}^{(t)} - {\mathbf w}^{(t-1)} ig) 	ext{, for } t=1,\ldots. For a strongly convex quadratic f, this iteration converges faster than plain GD. Fig.~3 compares plain GD with the heavy-ball method on a strongly convex quadratic function. A related momentum algorithm is Nesterov's accelerated variant of GD, which improves the 1/T bound above for convex f with L-Lipschitz gradient to f ig({\mathbf w}^{(T)} ig) - f^{\star} \le  rac{2 L \Vert {{\mathbf w}^{(0)} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert^{2}} {(T+1)^{2}} 	ext{.} In contrast to the bound for plain gradient descent, which falls in proportion to 1/T, this bound falls in proportion to 1/T2. For μ-strongly convex f, acceleration improves the contraction factor from 1 - μ/L to 1 - √(μ/L).

terms.name: generalization
terms.abstract: Generalization is the ability of a machine learning method to make accurate predictions on data points that have not been used during training. Many machine learning methods implement training via empirical risk minimization, i.e., learning a hypothesis h that minimizes the empirical risk on the training set D(train). The learned h is then used to compute predictions on new data points outside D(train). A probabilistic model for data generation quantifies the prediction errors beyond D(train) via the risk of h, i.e., the expected loss incurred on a new randomly chosen data point. The difference between the risk and the empirical risk is the generalization gap. The stability of the machine learning method bounds the expected generalization gap without reference to the size of the hypothesis space. A complementary deterministic view characterizes generalization via the robustness of h: its prediction changes by at most a bounded multiple of a perturbation of the features of a data point.
terms.description: A weather forecaster trained on past data is useful only if its predictions are accurate on future unseen data points. Generalization refers to the ability of a learned hypothesis h to make similarly accurate predictions on data points that have not been used during training. It is the central goal of machine learning: learning patterns in the features and labels of data points that extend beyond the training set. The canonical learning technique is empirical risk minimization: the machine learning system obtains h ∈ H by minimizing the empirical risk on the training set D(train). A low empirical risk on D(train) does not guarantee accurate predictions on data points outside D(train). Online learning and Bayesian inference face the same generalization challenge. Studying generalization mathematically requires formalizing the notion of unseen data points. A widely used approach is to assume a probabilistic model for the generation of data points, such as the independent and identically distributed assumption. Here, data points are interpreted as independent RVs with an identical, fixed but unknown, probability distribution P. Fig.~1 sketches this setup: the shaded ellipse depicts the region of typical data points under P, and the two large filled circles are the data points of the training set that empirical risk minimization fits with the learned hypothesis h. The risk of h is the expected loss: \[ \bar{L} \big( \widehat{h} \big) = \mathbb{E} \left\{ L\left({\mathbf z},\widehat{h} \right) \right\}. \] The difference L ( h ) - L(h|D(train)) is the generalization gap. For any fixed hypothesis h ∈ H, L ( h ) is a deterministic number that depends only on h and P. In contrast, the empirical risk L(h|D(train)) is a random variable that depends on D(train), which, in turn, is a realization of an independent and identically distributed sequence of RVs z(1), …, z(m) ~ P. Bounding the generalization gap therefore means controlling the probability of the (undesirable) event \mathcal{A}^{(h)} := \left\{ \mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}: \big| \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}\big) - \bar{L} \big( h \big) \big| > \varepsilon \right\}, where ε > 0 is a user-specified tolerance for the generalization gap. Each h ∈ H defines a different event A(h) (see Fig.~2), and generalization requires low probability of A(h) uniformly over H. Controlling every event A(h) uniformly over H is not the only probabilistic route. If the machine learning method is stable, i.e., replacing a single data point of the training set changes the loss of the learned hypothesis only slightly on average, then the expected generalization gap equals that average change, regardless of the size of the hypothesis space (see stability;). Probability theory is not the only route to generalization. A complementary deterministic approach uses robustness: a good hypothesis h should change its prediction h(x) by at most a bounded multiple of the perturbation of the feature vector x of a data point z, i.e., it should be Lipschitz. For example, an object detection system trained on smartphone photos should still detect the object if a single pixel is changed. Trained deep nets have been shown to lack this property. The system should also deliver the same result if the object in the image is slightly translated or deformed. The arrows in Fig.~1 indicate small perturbations of each data point in the training set of a machine learning method.

terms.name: Gaussian mixture model (GMM)
terms.abstract: A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) is a probabilistic model for the generation of data points with numeric feature vectors. Each data point is generated by first drawing a latent cluster index and then drawing the feature vector from the multivariate normal distribution of that cluster. The resulting marginal distribution is a weighted sum of multivariate normal distributions. The model parameters are chosen to maximize the likelihood function of a dataset. The resulting maximum likelihood optimization problem is an instance of empirical risk minimization using a specific choice for the loss function. This optimization problem is non-convex and typically solved using the expectation–maximization algorithm. This algorithm consists of a fixed-point iteration that never increases the empirical risk.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows a photograph of a mountain that is cut into small square patches, and each patch is described by two numbers: how green and how blue it is on average. Vegetation, mountain and haze, and bright sky form three clusters of such patches, which are data points characterized by a feature vector x ∈ Rd. A GMM is a probabilistic model for the generation of such data points. The idea of a GMM is to assume that each data point is generated by first drawing a latent cluster index I ∈ 1, …, k according to cluster probabilities \mathbb{P}\left(I=c\right) = p_{c}, \qquad \sum_{c=1}^{k} p_{c}=1\text{.} Given the choice I=c, the feature vector x is drawn from a multivariate normal distribution P(c)= N(μ(c),C(c)), with mean μ(c) and covariance matrix C(c). The resulting marginal distribution of x is therefore a weighted sum of multivariate normal distributions (Fig.~1), i.e., \mathbb{P} =\sum_{c=1}^{k} p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right)\text{.} A GMM is parameterized by the cluster-specific probability pc = P(I=c), mean μ(c), and covariance matrix C(c) for c=1, …, k. These model parameters can be learned from a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) by maximum likelihood. The resulting optimization problem has no closed-form solution, and the standard method for solving it approximately is the expectation–maximization algorithm, which alternates between two steps. The E-step computes, for every data point x(r) and every cluster index c, the posterior distribution under the current model parameters, \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} := \mathbb{P}\left(I = c \mid {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\right) = \frac{p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})} {\sum_{c'=1}^{k} p_{c'} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c')},\mathbf{C}^{(c')}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})}\text{,} \end{equation} and the M-step re-fits the model parameters as averages weighted by these posterior distributions, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} p_{c} &:= \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)}, \qquad {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)} := \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)}} {\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)}}, \mathbf{C}^{(c)} &:= \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)} ({\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)}) ({\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)})^{\top}} {\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)}} \quad \text{for } c = 1, \ldots, k\text{.} \end{aligned} \end{equation} The two steps are repeated until the model parameters stop changing. Trained by expectation–maximization on the 972 patches of Fig.~1, a three-component GMM separates vegetation, mountain and haze, and bright sky. Every patch it assigns to the bluest component lies in the upper half of the photograph. The learned model parameters define a soft clustering: the posterior distribution P(I = c | x) is the probability that a data point belongs to cluster c, and it provides a principled way to quantify the degree of belonging to cluster c. In contrast, hard clustering methods assign each data point to exactly one cluster. Fig.~2 shows these degrees of belonging on the photograph itself. The maximum likelihood optimization problem for the model parameters of a GMM is an instance of empirical risk minimization with a particular choice for the loss function. Assume that every covariance matrix C(c) is invertible, so that the GMM has a probability density function on Rd. The loss incurred by a feature vector x is the negative logarithm of this probability density function at x, L\left({\mathbf x},\mathbb{P} \right) = - \ln \sum_{c=1}^{k} p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right) ({\mathbf x}) \text{.} The empirical risk of a GMM is then obtained as the average loss over the entire dataset. Minimizing it maximizes the likelihood function, since the logarithm is increasing and the sign is flipped. Fitting a GMM is therefore empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space of mixtures of k multivariate normal distributions. The loss function is a non-convex function of the model parameters, so no closed form solves the optimization problem. The expectation–maximization algorithm is an approximate method for the maximum likelihood optimization problem: it never increases the empirical risk. Since the expectation–maximization algorithm might converge to a local minimum of the empirical risk, it is typically run several times with different initializations, keeping the run with the smallest empirical risk. A common construction of the initial model parameters runs k-means first and starts from its cluster centroids. Like k-means, the expectation–maximization algorithm is a fixed-point iteration. Collect the model parameters of a GMM in one vector w. One iteration, the E-step \eqref{equ_gmm_estep_dict} followed by the M-step \eqref{equ_gmm_mstep_dict}, applies an operator F to the current model parameters, so the method is the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(w(t)). The fixed points of F are model parameters at which the gradient of the empirical risk vanishes, i.e., the stationary points of the empirical risk (see zero-gradient condition). Convergence follows from monotone descent rather than from a contractive operator property: applying F never increases the empirical risk, so the sequence of empirical risk values converges, and under mild continuity conditions the iterates w(t) approach a fixed point. On the patches of Fig.~1, the empirical risk never increased in any of the 300 iterations of expectation–maximization. The expectation–maximization algorithm for learning the model parameters of a GMM reduces to Lloyd's algorithm for k-means under additional constraints. Fix every cluster probability at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix with one common σ2. The posterior distribution then depends on x only through its Euclidean distances to the means, and as σ2 shrinks towards 0 it concentrates on the closest one. In the limit (σ2 → 0), the E-step \eqref{equ_gmm_estep_dict} becomes an assignment of every data point to its nearest mean, and the M-step \eqref{equ_gmm_mstep_dict} re-centers the means on the data points assigned to them. That is Lloyd's algorithm for k-means. Fig.~3 shows the effect of the common σ2 on the degree of belonging to the vegetation cluster. With σ2 = 10-4, every patch obtains a degree of belonging of 0 or 1, and the grading coincides with the k-means assignment on more than 99% of the patches. With σ2 = 2 · 10-2, 63% of the patches obtain a degree of belonging between 0.2 and 0.8. On the patches of Fig.~1, with σ2 = 1 the three means collapse onto the average of all patches and every patch obtains the same degree of belonging 1/3. Leaving the covariance matrices and the cluster probabilities free is what lets a GMM provide a degree of belonging where k-means assigns each data point to one cluster.

terms.name: gradient
terms.abstract: The gradient of a real-valued function is a vector that determines the local linear approximation of the function. The entries of the gradient are the partial derivatives of the function. Their existence does not by itself make the function differentiable: the vector they form need not give a local linear approximation. For a convex function, the existence of all partial derivatives at a point already makes it differentiable there.
