The resulting optimization problem has no closed-form solution, and the standard method for solving it approximately is Lloyd's algorithm, which alternates between two steps. The assignment step assigns every data point to its nearest cluster centroid, \begin{equation} \widehat{c}^{(r)} := \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2} \quad \text{for } r = 1, \ldots, m\text{,} \end{equation} and the averaging step moves each cluster centroid to the mean of the data points assigned to it, \begin{equation} {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} := \frac{1}{\big|\{r: \widehat{c}^{(r)} = c\}\big|} \sum_{r: \widehat{c}^{(r)} = c} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \quad \text{for } c = 1, \ldots, k\text{.} \end{equation} The two steps are repeated until the assignment \eqref{equ_kmeans_assign_dict} stops changing. Algorithm~1 states the method in full. \begin{algorithm}[H] a̧ption{k-means, Lloyd's algorithm } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Require feature vectors x(1), …, x(m), cluster count k, initial cluster centroids w(1), …, w(k) \Repeat \State assignment: for each r = 1, …, m, assign x(r) to the cluster argminc = 1, …, k ‖ x(r) - w(c) ‖2, as in \eqref{equ_kmeans_assign_dict} \State averaging: for each c = 1, …, k, set w(c) to the mean of the feature vectors assigned to cluster c, as in \eqref{equ_kmeans_average_dict} \Until{no assignment changes} \Ensure cluster centroids w(1), …, w(k) and the assignment they induce \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Run on the 972 patches of Fig.~1 with k = 3, k-means separates vegetation, mountain and haze, and bright sky. Every patch it assigns to the bluest cluster centroid lies in the upper half of the photograph. The learned cluster centroids define a hard clustering: every data point belongs to exactly one cluster, the one with the nearest cluster centroid. In contrast, soft clustering methods assign the same data point to several clusters, with varying degrees of belonging. Fig.~2 shows this assignment on the photograph itself. The k-means principle is an instance of empirical risk minimization with a particular choice for the hypothesis space and the loss function. The hypothesis space Hk consists of all maps h: Rd → Rd of the piecewise-constant form h({\mathbf x}) = {{\mathbf w}}^{( c^{\star}({\mathbf x}))}, \qquad c^{\star}({\mathbf x}) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}\text{,} parameterized by the k cluster centroids w(1), …, w(k) ∈ Rd. Each such hypothesis maps every feature vector to its nearest cluster centroid. The region of feature space mapped to one cluster centroid is bounded by hyperplanes, one for each other cluster centroid (the dashed lines of Fig.~1). Thus, every cluster found by k-means is a convex region. The loss incurred by a feature vector x is the squared Euclidean distance to its nearest cluster centroid, L(x,h ) = ‖ x - h(x) ‖22. The clustering error is then obtained as the average loss, i.e., the empirical risk, over the entire dataset. Minimizing the clustering error is therefore empirical risk minimization over Hk. The clustering error is a non-convex function of the cluster centroids: with a single data point at x = 0 and two scalar cluster centroids w(1), w(2) ∈ R, it is min((w(1))2, (w(2))2), so both (1, 0) and (0, 1) are global optima with value 0, but their midpoint (0.5, 0.5) gives 0.25. Solving the optimization problem exactly is NP-hard. Lloyd's algorithm is an approximate method for the k-means optimization problem: it never increases the clustering error. Since Lloyd's algorithm might converge to a local minimum of the clustering error, it is typically run several times with different initializations, keeping the run with the smallest clustering error. A variant of k-means referred to as k-means++ uses a specific construction of the initial cluster centroids. Like the expectation–maximization algorithm for a Gaussian mixture model, Lloyd's algorithm is a fixed-point iteration. Collect the cluster centroids in one vector w := (w(1), …, w(k)). One iteration, the assignment step \eqref{equ_kmeans_assign_dict} followed by the averaging step \eqref{equ_kmeans_average_dict}, applies an operator F to the current cluster centroids, so the method is the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(w(t)). The fixed points of F are cluster centroids that each coincide with the mean of the data points assigned to them. Convergence follows from monotone descent rather than from a contractive operator property: each of the two steps minimizes the clustering error over one set of variables with the other held fixed, so applying F never increases the clustering error. A finite dataset admits only finitely many partitions, so the iterates reach a fixed point after finitely many iterations. On the patches of Fig.~1, Lloyd's algorithm reached a fixed point after 12 iterations, and the clustering error never increased along the way. Lloyd's algorithm for k-means is the limit of the expectation–maximization algorithm for a Gaussian mixture model under additional constraints. Fix every cluster probability of the Gaussian mixture model at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix with one common σ2. The posterior distribution of the cluster index then depends on x only through its Euclidean distances to the means, and as σ2 shrinks towards 0 it concentrates on the closest one. In the limit (σ2 → 0), the E-step of expectation–maximization becomes the assignment step \eqref{equ_kmeans_assign_dict} and the M-step becomes the averaging step \eqref{equ_kmeans_average_dict} of Lloyd's algorithm. On the patches of Fig.~1 with σ2 = 10-4, the expectation–maximization algorithm assigns 99.4% of the patches like k-means. Leaving the covariance matrices and the cluster probabilities free is what lets a Gaussian mixture model provide a degree of belonging where k-means assigns each data point to one cluster. The loss function is what separates k-means from its generalizations, and it decides what the averaging step of Lloyd's algorithm computes. Replacing the squared Euclidean distance by the Euclidean distance itself, L(x,h ) = ‖ x - h(x) ‖2, gives the k-medians optimization problem. The assignment step \eqref{equ_kmeans_assign_dict} is unchanged, since the nearest cluster centroid is the same under both losses, but the averaging step \eqref{equ_kmeans_average_dict} becomes the geometric median of the data points assigned to a cluster, which has no closed form and is computed by Weiszfeld's fixed-point iteration. The gain is robustness to outliers: adding 10 far-away patches to the 566 patches of the vegetation cluster of Fig.~1 moves their mean by 0.044 but their geometric median by 0.004, while k-medians assigns 98.5% of the patches like k-means. The averaging step is not tied to the squared Euclidean distance alone: for any Bregman divergence L(x,h ) = xh(x)φ as loss, the mean of the assigned data points still minimizes their summed loss, so only the assignment step changes. The Euclidean distance is not a Bregman divergence, which is why it changes the averaging step. Restricting each cluster centroid to be one of the data points assigned to it gives k-medoids, which uses only the pairwise distances between data points and therefore applies to data points without numeric feature vectors. Fig.~3 shows the effect of the number k of clusters on the patches of Fig.~1. Each patch is painted with the average color of its cluster, which is image segmentation. With k = 2, the sky and the mountain are separated from the vegetation. With k = 3, the mountain and haze form their own cluster. With k = 4, the vegetation splits into the sunlit meadow and the dark foliage. The clustering error decreases with k, from 0.034 for k = 2 to 0.018 for k = 3 and 0.011 for k = 4, and it reaches 0 when every data point is its own cluster centroid.

terms.name: label
terms.abstract: A label is an attribute of a data point that represents a quantity of interest and that typically requires human expertise to determine. Predicting the label of a data point from its features is the goal of supervised learning. Determining the label of a data point is error-prone and often involves human annotation. The choice of label determines the learning task: whether the task is classification or regression depends on the label space together with the loss function. In self-supervised learning, the label is constructed from the features themselves, so that no manual annotation is required.
terms.description: A label of a data point z is one of its attributes that represents a higher-level fact, or quantity of interest, and that typically requires human expertise or domain knowledge to determine. Unlike a feature, which can be computed or measured easily, a label is usually harder to obtain. For a data point that represents a patient, a feature could be the body weight, while the label could be the presence of a disease. Whether a given attribute serves as a feature or a label is often a design choice that depends on the resources available in a given machine learning application. If an oncologist is readily available, a cancer prognosis can serve as a feature. On the other hand, if no oncologist is available, the cancer prognosis is a label that needs to be predicted from patient features. One way to make the notion of a label precise is by introducing a labeling function h: Z → Y. The domain of this function is the data point space Z, the set of all possible data points that can occur in a given machine learning application. Its values lie in the label space Y, the set of all possible values the label of a data point can take on. The function assigns each data point z its label y = h(z). Note that the labeling function h acts on the data point z itself, that is, on the whole patient. A trained model (or learned hypothesis) h instead acts on the feature vector x, a fixed list of recorded features such as the patient's body weight and age. The feature vector usually captures only part of a data point. For example, in a health-care application, the data point space Z contains patients, whereas the feature space X contains only their recorded feature vectors. Two patients with the same feature vector may therefore carry different labels, since they can differ in information that was never recorded as a feature. No hypothesis h that reads only x can then deliver perfect predictions. In practice, the true label h(z) of a data point is rarely known exactly. Even with full access to the data point, its label must be determined by human judgment or measurement, which is imperfect. The available label is then a noisy version of h(z), as in the additive error model of Hastie et al. (2009, Sect. 2.6). For instance, an object category assigned by a human annotator or a diagnosis obtained from a clinician may be wrong, even though the annotator or clinician examines the data point directly. The discrepancy between such an observed label and the true label is called label noise and can degrade training and raise the risk of the learned hypothesis. This source of error differs from the incompleteness of the recorded features discussed above: here the data point is accessible, but its label is determined imperfectly. Label noise also matters for regulation. The EU AI Act requires the training set of a high-risk artificial intelligence system to be, to the best extent possible, free of errors and the system to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy; erroneous labels are one such error. When labels are personal data, the general data protection regulation requires them to be accurate. One way to reduce the effect of label noise is label smoothing, which slightly perturbs the labels of data points used for model training. It is a form of data augmentation that acts as regularization. The choice of label (or labeling function h) determines a specific learning task. For the image of a cow herd in Fig.~1, the label could be a binary indicator of whether the image contains cows (binary classification). Other choices are the number of cows or the average green level (regression), and a masked center pixel predicted from the surrounding pixels (self-supervised learning). Whether a learning task is a classification problem or a regression problem depends not only on the label space Y but also on the loss function. For example, the label space Y = 0,1,2,3,… can be used for a classification method that uses the 0/1 loss as the loss function. The same label space can also be used for a regression method that uses the squared error loss as the loss function. In self-supervised learning, the label is constructed from the features themselves, so no manual annotation is required. A prominent example is large language model training: consider the sentence ``All human beings are born free and equal,'' tokenized as the sequence (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'', ``are'', ``born'', ``free'', ``and'', ``equal''). The label for the subsequence (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'') is the next token ``are,'' the label for (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'', ``are'') is ``born,'' and so on. By sliding through the sequence, a single sentence produces many labeled data points from plain text alone.

terms.name: learning rate
terms.abstract: A learning rate is a hyperparameter of an iterative machine learning method that controls the extent of a single update of the current hypothesis. A prime example for a learning rate is the step size of gradient descent. A learning rate that is too small makes little progress within the available number of iterations, and one that is too large can result in divergent iterations. For a fixed number of iterations, the learning rate bounds the effective hypothesis space of a machine learning method, which makes it a means of regularization. The learning rate can be chosen by the validation error of the learned hypothesis.
terms.description: Consider an iterative machine learning method for learning a useful hypothesis h ∈ H. Such a method repeats similar update steps that modify the current hypothesis to obtain an improved one. A learning rate is a parameter of such a method that controls the extent to which the current hypothesis can be modified during a single iteration. A prime example for a learning rate is the step size η of gradient descent, \begin{equation} {\mathbf w}^{(t + 1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) \text{.} \end{equation} Here, the objective function f(w) is the empirical risk incurred by a hypothesis h(w) on a training set, and each gradient step moves the model parameters against its gradient ∇ f(w(t)) by a distance proportional to η. Fig.~1 illustrates one gradient step \eqref{equ_def_basic_gradstep_lrate_dict} of gradient descent for a linear model, started from the same hypothesis with three choices of the learning rate. The learning rates are given as multiples of 1/L, with L the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian of f. For the squared error loss, a gradient step lowers f for every learning rate below 2/L; the largest learning rate of Fig.~1 lies above that threshold, and its step raises f. Each iteration of a machine learning method should make large progress towards a useful hypothesis, so the learning rate should not be too small. However, it can also be too large: if the step size of gradient descent is too large, the gradient steps can overshoot a minimum of the objective function. Fig.~2 illustrates both cases. Consider an iterative machine learning method that learns a hypothesis from some underlying hypothesis space H by running a fixed number T of iterations. Varying the learning rate can be used to implement regularization via effectively pruning H. For example, each gradient step above \eqref{equ_def_basic_gradstep_lrate_dict} moves the model parameters by η ∇ f(w(t)). By the triangle inequality, \begin{equation} \Vert {{\mathbf w}^{(T)} - {\mathbf w}^{(0)}} \Vert \leq \eta \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \Vert {\nabla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)})} \Vert \text{.} \end{equation} Together with T, the learning rate thus determines the region of the parameter space that the method can reach, and thereby the effective hypothesis space: the hypotheses h(w) whose model parameters w lie in that region. Fig.~3 draws the balls around w(0) with the radius \eqref{equ_learnrate_reach_dict} for T = 10 gradient steps and three learning rates. Reducing the learning rate shrinks the effective hypothesis space that can be reached by the gradient steps. Choosing the learning rate too small or too large can then result in underfitting or overfitting. As a hyperparameter, the learning rate can be chosen by validation: the hypotheses learned with different learning rates are compared by their validation error on a validation set.

terms.name: linear classifier
terms.abstract: A linear classifier is a classifier whose decision regions are separated by hyperplanes. Each linear classifier is obtained by comparing the value of a linear hypothesis map against a threshold. For binary classification, the sign of the value can be used to determine the predicted label, and the absolute value measures the distance of the data point from the decision boundary. The model parameters of a linear classifier are the weight vector of the underlying hypothesis map and the threshold. They are learned by empirical risk minimization with different loss functions: logistic regression uses the logistic loss and the support vector machine the hinge loss. For multi-class classification, a linear classifier is characterized by several linear model hypothesis maps, one per label value, and the resulting decision regions are intersections of halfspaces.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows a scatterplot of data points that represent geographical areas. Each area is characterized by two features, which are obtained from an aerial photograph. The label of each area indicates whether the area belongs to a vineyard (y = 1) or not (y = -1). A linear classifier is a classifier whose decision regions are separated by hyperplanes in Rd. For binary classification, with label space Y = -1, +1, each linear classifier can be written as the thresholding rule y = sign(h(x)) with the hypothesis \[ h({\mathbf x}) = {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x} + b \text{.} \] The hypothesis map is parameterized by the weight vector w ∈ Rd 0 and the threshold b ∈ R. A data point with feature vector x is classified as y = 1 if h(x) ≥ 0 and as y = -1 otherwise. The resulting decision boundary is the hyperplane \[ \{ {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}: {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x} + b = 0 \} \text{,} \] with normal vector w. This boundary separates two halfspaces, which are the decision regions R1 = x: h(x) ≥ 0 and R-1 = x: h(x) < 0. Consider a feature vector x and any vector x' on the decision boundary, h(x') = 0. Subtracting wᵀ x' + b = 0 from h(x) gives \[ h({\mathbf x}) = {\mathbf w}^{\top} \big( {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf x}' \big) \text{.} \] The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds the right-hand side in magnitude by ‖ w ‖2 ‖ x - x' ‖2. Every vector of the decision boundary is therefore at distance at least |h(x)| / ‖ w ‖2 from x. That distance is attained by the orthogonal projection \[ {\mathbf x}' = {\mathbf x} - \frac{h({\mathbf x})} {\left\lVert {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}} {\mathbf w} \text{.} \] The distance of x from the decision boundary is thus |h(x)| / ‖ w ‖2, and the hypothesis value h(x) is that distance multiplied by ‖ w ‖2. Fig.~1 illustrates the distance to the decision boundary for one data point. The value |h(x)| is a measure of the noise tolerance at the feature vector x. Perturbing x by a vector δ changes the hypothesis value by wᵀ δ, which the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds in magnitude by ‖ w ‖2 ‖ δ ‖2. The sign of h(x), and with it the prediction, therefore survives every perturbation with ‖ δ ‖2 < |h(x)| / ‖ w ‖2. Multiplying h(x) by the label y gives the margin, which is positive exactly on the correctly classified data points. For a linearly separable training set and a sufficiently small regularization parameter α, the support vector machine learns the linear classifier whose smallest margin is largest. The model parameters (w, b) are learned from a training set D(train) = (x(r), y(r)) r = 1m by empirical risk minimization. Using the 0/1 loss results in an objective function that is piecewise constant, and minimizing it is computationally hard in general. Practical methods replace the 0/1 loss by a convex loss of the margin: logistic regression uses the logistic loss and the support vector machine uses the hinge loss. Both learn the model parameters of a linear classifier by minimizing a convex objective function: gradient descent minimizes the smooth objective function of logistic regression, and subgradient descent the non-smooth objective function of the support vector machine. For multi-class problems, with label space Y = 1, …, K and K > 2, a linear classifier uses one linear model hypothesis gc(x) = ( w(c) )ᵀ x + b(c) per label value c ∈ Y and predicts the value with the largest score, y = argmaxc ∈ Y gc(x). The decision region Rc is then an intersection of K - 1 halfspaces and is therefore a convex set. The border between two decision regions Rc and Rc' lies in the hyperplane on which the two scores agree. The resulting partition of the feature space is shown in Fig.~2 for a linear classifier with K = 3 classes. A linear classifier can be generalized to allow for non-linear decision boundaries by using a feature transformation. Applying a feature transformation φ: Rd → Rd' first and a linear classifier to φ(x) afterwards gives a decision boundary that is a hyperplane in Rd' but can be highly non-linear in the original feature space. A kernel method constructs such a feature transformation from a kernel, and a deep net uses its first layers as a trainable feature transformation.

terms.name: linear regression
terms.abstract: Linear regression is a regression method that learns a linear hypothesis map for predicting the numeric label of a data point from its features. Its least squares variant chooses a map that minimizes the average squared error loss on a training set. Linear regression is an instance of empirical risk minimization that is obtained by using the linear model and the squared error loss. The optimal model parameters are determined by the normal equations. This system can be solved in closed form or iteratively, for example, by gradient descent. Adding a penalty term to the average squared error loss yields regularized variants such as ridge regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator.
terms.description: Linear regression methods learn a linear hypothesis map that delivers a prediction of the numeric label of a data point. The prediction is based solely on the features of the data point, which are fed as input to the learned hypothesis map. Linear regression can be used to predict tomorrow's temperature from weather measurements recorded over the last five days, using them as features and tomorrow's temperature as the label. Formally, linear regression learns a linear hypothesis map h(w)(x) = wᵀx to predict the numeric label y ∈ R of a data point from its feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ ∈ Rd. Here, d denotes the number of features of a data point. The model parameters w are learned from a training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m of data points. Appending a constant feature to x lets one entry of w act as an intercept, so wᵀx represents an affine function of the original measurements. In what follows, x denotes the feature vector that is fed to the linear hypothesis map. It can be either the original or the augmented feature vector. The least squares variant of linear regression measures the quality of a linear hypothesis map by the average squared error loss on the training set. As an instance of empirical risk minimization, it learns the model parameters w by solving the optimization problem \[ \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big)^{2} \text{.} \] Fig.~1 illustrates this linear regression problem for a training set with a constant scalar feature x(r)=1 for r=1,…,m. The optimization problem can be written more compactly using the feature matrix X and the label vector y, \[ {\mathbf X} = \big({\mathbf x}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf x}^{(m)}\big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d} \text{,} \qquad {\mathbf y} = \big( y^{(1)}, \ldots, y^{(m)} \big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{m} \text{.} \] In terms of X and y, the optimization problem reads \[ \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \underbrace{\frac{1}{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf y} - {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}}_{f({\mathbf w})} \text{.} \] The average squared error loss f(w) is a convex and differentiable function of w. By the zero-gradient condition, a vector w solves this optimization problem if and only if it satisfies the system of linear equations \begin{equation} {\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X} \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = {\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf y} \text{.} \end{equation} The normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict} always have a solution because Xᵀy lies in the column space of XᵀX. However, the solution of the normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict} is unique only if the feature matrix X has full column rank. This requires at least as many data points as features, m ≥ d. When this holds, and the columns of X are linearly independent, the matrix XᵀX is invertible and the normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict} have the unique closed-form solution w = (XᵀX)-1 Xᵀ y. If instead m < d (more features than data points), X cannot have full column rank, XᵀX is singular, and the optimization problem has infinitely many solutions. All of them incur the same minimal average squared error loss on the training set, but their predictions for data points outside the training set can differ arbitrarily. Choosing among them is therefore a matter of generalization (see overfitting). A unique solution can be selected, for example, by picking the minimum-norm solution X+ y given by the pseudoinverse X+. A common remedy is regularization: adding a penalty term to the average squared error loss. The penalty term can be interpreted as an estimate of how much higher the loss is on data points outside the training set than on it. This yields regularized variants of linear regression, with ridge regression using the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 and the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator using the penalty term α ‖ w ‖1, where α > 0 is a hyperparameter that sets the weight of the penalty term. Linear regression also has a statistical interpretation. Consider a probabilistic model with a joint probability distribution P(x, y) over the features and the label. Under the squared error loss, the Bayes estimator (i.e., the hypothesis with minimum risk) is the conditional expectation Ey | x. In this statistical interpretation, x denotes the original feature vector. Let the features and the label be jointly Gaussian RVs with zero mean and invertible covariance matrix C(x) = Exxᵀ. This Bayes estimator is then \[ h^{*}({\mathbf x}) = \big({\mathbf w}^{\star}\big)^{\top}{\mathbf x} \text{, with } {\mathbf w}^{\star} = \big(\mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})}\big)^{-1} \mathbf{c}^{({\mathbf x},y)} \text{.} \] Here, c(x,y) = E is the covariance between the features x and the label y. This Bayes estimator is linear in x. Without the zero-mean assumption, it is an affine function of x. However, as for the linear hypothesis map above, the intercept can be absorbed by appending a constant feature. Least-squares linear regression is the empirical risk minimization counterpart of this predictor. It replaces C(x) and c(x,y) with the sample-based estimates (1/m)XᵀX and (1/m)Xᵀy. For invertible XᵀX, this recovers the unique solution w = (XᵀX)-1Xᵀy of the normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict}. Instead of solving the normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict} directly (via the inverse matrix or pseudoinverse), machine learning methods often solve it by an iterative optimization method, as implemented in widely used machine learning software libraries such as scikit-learn and PyTorch. Starting from initial model parameters w(0), such a method repeatedly applies an update operator F, \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{F}\big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big) \text{, for } t = 0,1,\ldots \text{.} \] The operator F is designed such that the sequence of model parameters w(t) converges to a solution of the normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict}. One important example of such an iterative optimization method is gradient descent, which uses the gradient descent step operator \[ \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) = {\mathbf w} - \eta \nabla f({\mathbf w}) \text{.} \] Here, η > 0 is a step size that must be chosen small enough to ensure convergence. The superscript in F(η) makes the dependence of the operator on η explicit. Inserting the average training error into the general form of the gradient descent step yields the explicit update \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) &= {\mathbf w} + \frac{2\eta}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top}{\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big) {\mathbf x}^{(r)} &= \Big(\mathbf{I} - \frac{2\eta}{m}{\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X}\Big){\mathbf w} + \frac{2\eta}{m}{\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf y} \text{.} \end{aligned} \] The fixed points of F(η) are exactly the solutions of the normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict}, since F(η)(w) = w holds if and only if XᵀXw = Xᵀy. The update operator is affine, \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) = {\mathbf M} {\mathbf w} + {\mathbf b} \text{,} with linear part M = I - (2η/m)XᵀX and offset b = (2η/m) Xᵀy. When X has full column rank, so that XᵀX is positive definite, F(η) is a contractive operator with respect to the Euclidean norm for every step size 0 < η < m/λmax. Here, λmax is the largest eigenvalue of XᵀX. The eigenvalues of the linear part M are 1 - (2η/m) λj, with the positive eigenvalues λj of XᵀX. They lie strictly between -1 and 1 exactly for such step sizes (cf. which covers gradient descent for any smooth, strongly convex objective function and step sizes η ≤ m/(λmin + λmax), with the smallest eigenvalue λmin of XᵀX). The fixed-point iteration converges to the unique solution w. Moreover, the convergence speed of gradient descent is governed by the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of XᵀX, that is, by its condition number κ (XᵀX) = λmax/λmin. The gradient descent step above uses the entire training set to compute the gradient. When the data points instead arrive sequentially at time instants t=1,2,…, or the training set is too large to fit in memory, the model parameters can be learned by online gradient descent. At each time step t, it applies a single gradient descent step. That step uses only the arriving data point ( x(t),y(t) ), \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + 2\eta \big( y^{(t)} - \big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big)^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(t)} \big) {\mathbf x}^{(t)} \text{.} \] This is the gradient descent step on the loss function (y(t) - wᵀx(t))2 of the arriving data point alone, rather than on the average squared error loss f(w). It is the least mean squares update. It avoids storing the entire training set, and its per-iteration complexity is independent of the training set size m. The optimality condition \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict} allows one to study the stability of linear regression. Ideally, the learned model parameters are insensitive to limited perturbations of the training set. A label-only perturbation, for example, replaces a single label of the training set with an outlier or another corrupted value. A perturbed training set yields a feature matrix X = X + Δ X and a label vector y = y + Δ y, with perturbation matrix Δ X and vector Δ y. This gives the perturbed normal equations \begin{equation} \widetilde{{\mathbf X}}^{\top} \widetilde{{\mathbf X}} \widetilde{{\mathbf w}} = \widetilde{{\mathbf X}}^{\top} \widetilde{{\mathbf y}} \text{.} \end{equation} Matrix perturbation theory quantifies how much w deviates from a solution w of the clean normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict}. For a label-only perturbation, Δ X = 0, the perturbed and clean normal equations share the coefficient matrix XᵀX. Assume X has full column rank, so XᵀX is invertible and the solution is unique. Subtracting the clean normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_normal_eq_dict} from the perturbed normal equations \eqref{eq_linreg_perturbed_normal_eq_dict} yields \[ \widetilde{{\mathbf w}} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \big({\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X}\big)^{-1} {\mathbf X}^{\top} \Delta{\mathbf y} = {{\mathbf X}}^{+} \Delta{\mathbf y} \text{,} \] with the pseudoinverse X+. The effect of perturbing the training set is thereby quantified, \[ \left\lVert \widetilde{{\mathbf w}} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}} \right\rVert_{2} \leq \left\lVert {{\mathbf X}}^{+} \right\rVert_{2} \left\lVert \Delta{\mathbf y} \right\rVert_{2} \text{.} \] When X has full column rank, the pseudoinverse has the norm ‖ X+ ‖2 = 1/min(XᵀX) = κ (XᵀX)/‖ X ‖2, where κ (XᵀX) = λmax/λmin is the condition number of XᵀX (see pseudoinverse). In the setting of Fig.~1, X = 1 (the all-ones vector), so X+ Δy = (1/m) Σr=1m Δy(r). Fig.~2 illustrates such a label-only perturbation of the training set from Fig.~1: the single label perturbation Δy(3) = 6 gives w - w = 6/3 = 2, i.e., the outlier pulls the average of the labels upward, from w = 3 to w = 5. The effect of perturbations can also be studied on the level of a specific optimization method. For example, the update of online gradient descent becomes \[ \begin{aligned} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} &= {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + 2\eta \big( \widetilde{y}^{(t)} - \big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big)^{\top} \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{(t)} \big) \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{(t)} &= {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + 2\eta \big( y^{(t)} - \big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big)^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(t)} \big) {\mathbf x}^{(t)} + {\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(t)} \text{.} \end{aligned} \] Here, ε(t) is a perturbation term that depends on the data point perturbation ( Δ x(t),Δ y(t) ) and the current model parameters w(t).

terms.name: large language model (LLM)
terms.abstract: A large language model (LLM) is an artificial neural network, typically with billions of model parameters, that implements a hypothesis map from a prompt to a response. The training of an LLM often proceeds in stages: pretraining uses self-supervised learning, splitting raw text into overlapping fragments that yield data points without manual annotation, and fine-tuning uses a small dataset of manually curated prompt--response pairs. LLM agents extend LLMs beyond text: a program interprets the response, for example as code to run or as a tool to execute, and can append the result to the next prompt, so the LLM chooses actions that the surrounding program carries out.
terms.description: Consider a chat-based artificial intelligence system such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, or Mistral: a user types a question, the prompt, and receives a reply, the response. The system that produces the reply is an LLM: an artificial neural network, typically a transformer with billions of model parameters, trained to output text given input text. Each data point of this learning task is a pair of texts, and the trained LLM implements a hypothesis map from the prompt to the response (Fig.~1). A prompt and a response are sequences of tokens, so the feature space and the label space of this learning task are sets of token sequences. In contrast, a text classifier that maps a document to one of a fixed set of labels is not an LLM: it returns a label, not text. Most LLMs implement h autoregressively: the response is generated one token at a time, each drawn from a probability distribution over the vocabulary that the network computes from the prompt and all tokens generated so far. Alternative constructions exist: masked probabilistic models predict removed tokens and serve text analysis rather than generation, and diffusion language models generate many tokens in parallel. The training of an LLM consists of several stages. One stage typically uses self-supervised learning: a given text is split into overlapping fragments, and each fragment amounts to a data point whose label is one of its tokens and whose features are the remaining tokens. Training sets built from text fragments require no manual annotation; a next-token fragment construction is used by Brown et al. (2020) and a masked-token one by Devlin et al. (2019). Pretraining then minimizes the average loss over the fragments, i.e., it is empirical risk minimization, the aim being a small expected loss on text fragments outside the training set. Another stage is fine-tuning, which uses a small dataset of manually curated prompt--response pairs. An LLM whose model parameters are reused across many learning tasks is a foundation model. LLM inference, i.e., computing the response for a given prompt, is computationally much cheaper than its training. Still, the inference itself is computationally costly and is often implemented using cloud computing services. Local execution is catching up, however: open-weight LLMs, whose model parameters are published, can be compressed by quantization. Quantization stores each model parameter in a few bits instead of a 16-bit floating-point number. An LLM with billions of model parameters then runs on a laptop or phone (see edge computing). The output of an LLM by itself is nothing but a sequence of letters that constitute the response. An LLM (or coding) agent interprets the response of an LLM as instructions for computations to be executed. For example, the prompt can steer the LLM to produce a response that is valid source code in a programming language such as Python, as in the spelled-out data point of Fig.~1. The delivered source code can then be executed, and the result can be appended to the next prompt. The response can likewise be read as a call to an external tool, so that the LLM generates the text that specifies the actions the surrounding program carries out.

terms.name: logistic loss
terms.abstract: The logistic loss is a convex and smooth surrogate for the 0/1 loss in binary classification. Like the hinge loss, it depends on a data point only through the location of that data point relative to the decision boundary. Unlike the hinge loss it is differentiable everywhere, which suits it to gradient-based optimization methods such as gradient descent. Running empirical risk minimization with a linear model and the logistic loss gives logistic regression. The logistic loss is the negative logarithm of the conditional probability distribution of the label given the feature vector, so minimizing it is maximum likelihood estimation of the model parameters. A probabilistic model in which the features are jointly Gaussian RVs given the label induces exactly that conditional probability distribution, and it is not the only one that does.
terms.description: A spam filter is a binary classification method that learns a hypothesis which reads in the features of an email and predicts either spam or no spam. The performance of such a spam filter can be measured by counting the fraction of emails that are misclassified. This fraction is the average 0/1 loss. However, this average loss is flat almost everywhere as a function of the model parameters, so it gives gradient descent no direction to move in. Its shape is the step drawn in Fig.~1: flat on either side of margin 0 and with no slope anywhere to follow. Practical classification methods therefore use a convex and smooth surrogate for the 0/1 loss, which is less flat. One such surrogate is the logistic loss, defined next. Consider a binary classification problem with feature space X and a real-valued hypothesis h: X → R. The two classes are encoded below by the label y ∈ -1, +1. The logistic loss incurred by h on a data point (x, y) is \begin{equation} L\left(({\mathbf x}, y),h \right) := \ln\big(1 + \exp(-y ḑot h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{.} \end{equation} Like the hinge loss, the logistic loss \eqref{equ_log_loss_gls_dict} depends on the data point only via the margin y · h(x). Normalizing the logistic loss by ln 2 makes it a convex upper bound on the 0/1 loss, with equality at margin 0 (see Fig.~1). The rescaling is what makes it a bound: at margin 0 the logistic loss itself is ln 2 ≈ 0.69, below the 1 that the 0/1 loss charges there. Scaling a surrogate so that it passes through 1 at margin 0 is the usual convention when such loss functions are compared. The logistic loss \eqref{equ_log_loss_gls_dict} is written for the label space -1, +1. A binary classification problem that uses a different label space must translate it through a label encoding. Unlike the hinge loss, the logistic loss is everywhere differentiable. It is therefore well suited for gradient-based optimization methods such as gradient descent. Empirical risk minimization with a linear model and the logistic loss yields logistic regression. The logistic loss arises naturally from a simple probabilistic model in which the data points are independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution P(x, y). Conditioned on the label y, the feature vector x is a Gaussian random variable with mean vector μ(-1) for y = -1 and μ(+1) for y = +1. The conditional covariance matrix is the same for both, and fixed to I. Under that probabilistic model, the posterior probability of y = +1 is the sigmoid function σ(h(x)) with σ(z) = 1/(1 + e-z). The identity holds for one choice of model parameters, namely \[ {\mathbf w} = {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(+1)} - {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(-1)} \text{,} \quad b = - \tfrac{1}{2} \big( \left\lVert {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(+1)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} - \left\lVert {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(-1)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \big) + \ln \frac{\mathbb{P}\left(y = +1\right)} {\mathbb{P}\left(y = -1\right)} \text{.} \] It is the shared covariance matrix that makes h affine: the terms quadratic in x are the same under both labels and cancel in the ratio, leaving only the inner product with w. When the two labels are equally likely the logarithm vanishes and b is the midpoint term alone. The probability of y = -1 is then σ(-h(x)), because the sigmoid function satisfies σ(-z) = 1 - σ(z). The logistic loss is thus the negative logarithm of the conditional probability of the label given the feature vector, and minimizing the average logistic loss is maximum likelihood estimation of the weight vector w and the offset b of h under that conditional probability distribution. The Gaussian probabilistic model is not the only one that induces this conditional probability distribution. If, given the label, the feature vector has a density of the form h(x) exp( (w(y))ᵀ t(x) - A(w(y)) ), a member of an exponential family whose natural parameter w(y) depends on the label while the base measure h and the sufficient statistic t(x) do not, then the logarithm of the posterior odds of y = +1 is affine in t(x), and the posterior is again the sigmoid function of an affine function. Its weight vector is the difference of the two natural parameters, w = w(+1) - w(-1), which for the Gaussian model above, where t(x) = x and the natural parameter is the mean vector, is the identity w = μ(+1) - μ(-1) displayed there. Conditionally independent binary features, the model behind naive Bayes, are another case. A binary classification problem whose label space is some other pair a, b is covered by an encoding e: a, b → -1, +1 with e(a) = -1 and e(b) = +1. The logistic loss \eqref{equ_log_loss_gls_dict} is then evaluated at the encoded label, \[ L\left(({\mathbf x}, y),h \right) = \ln\big(1 + \exp(-e(y) ḑot h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{.} \] The label spaces 0, 1 and no spam, spam are both handled this way. Take the label space 0, 1, with e(0) = -1 and e(1) = +1. The loss can then be written out as \[ - y \ln \sigma\big(h({\mathbf x})\big) - (1 - y) \ln \big(1 - \sigma(h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{,} \] which is the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss: the cross-entropy between the label and the predicted probability σ(h(x)), with the label 1 leaving the second summand zero and the label 0 the first. Summed over a training set it is the cross-entropy error function of logistic regression. Written that way the loss no longer needs the label to be one of two values. Let y be a soft label, a number between 0 and 1 giving the probability that the data point belongs to the class encoded by 1. Putting y in place of y gives the cross-entropy loss \[ - \tilde{y} \ln \sigma\big(h({\mathbf x})\big) - (1 - \tilde{y}) \ln \big(1 - \sigma(h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{,} \] which reduces to the previous display at y ∈ 0, 1 and carries over to more than two classes through the softmax function. The value of the logistic loss is harder to read than the 0/1 loss, because it depends on the size of the margin and not only on its sign. Each hypothesis compared below is a linear classifier h(x) = wᵀ x + b. Take the three data points of Fig.~2, two of them with label +1 at (1,1) and (2,3) and one with label -1 at (3,1), and the linear classifier h(1)(x) = -0.1 x1 + 0.05 x2 + 0.15. Its margins are 0.1 on each of the three, so it classifies all three correctly and incurs an average logistic loss of 0.644. Multiplying its model parameters by 50 gives 50 h(1), which leaves the decision boundary exactly where it was and so changes no prediction, yet the average logistic loss falls to 0.0067, a factor of 96. Two hypotheses far apart in logistic loss can therefore make exactly the same decisions. The two numbers can also rank two hypotheses in opposite orders. A second linear classifier, h(2)(x) = -2.25 x1 + 1.125 x2 + 6.125, has a decision boundary parallel to the first but shifted, which leaves the data point at (3,1) on the wrong side. Its margins are 5, 5, and -0.5, an accuracy of 2/3 against 1 for h(1), and it still attains the smaller average logistic loss, 0.329 against 0.644. Its two large margins cost 0.0067 each, so even the single negative margin, at 0.974, totals less than the three small margins of h(1) at 0.644 each. Choosing between the two by logistic loss alone selects the less accurate one. Only one reading of the number is safe, the upper bound above: a small logistic loss forces a small 0/1 loss.

terms.name: logistic regression
terms.abstract: Logistic regression learns a linear hypothesis map for binary classification, that is, for data points whose label takes one of two values, y ∈ -1, 1. The predicted label is the sign of h(x), and the absolute value |h(x)| measures the confidence in the classification. The parameters are learned by empirical risk minimization with the average logistic loss on the training set. This is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation under a simple probabilistic model, under which σ(h(x)) is the probability of the label 1. When a data point carries this probability as a soft label instead of a class, the logistic loss is replaced by the cross-entropy between soft label and prediction, equivalently their Kullback–Leibler divergence. The resulting objective function is convex and smooth, so variants of gradient descent can be used to minimize it.
terms.description: Consider predicting whether it freezes tomorrow from recent temperature measurements. Records from a weather station turn this question into data: each day is a data point with two numeric features, the maximum temperature of the day and that of the preceding day, collected in the feature vector x = (x1, x2)ᵀ ∈ R2. The label y ∈ -1, 1 is y = 1 if the minimum temperature of the following day stays at or above 0∘C and y = -1 otherwise. Fig.~1 shows such data points. Logistic regression learns, for such a binary classification task, a linear hypothesis map h(x) = wᵀ x + b with weight vector w and offset b. Despite its name, the method solves a classification problem: the regression refers to fitting the real-valued map h, not to a numeric label. The prediction, i.e., the classification, is obtained from the sign of h(x), which makes the learned h a linear classifier whose decision boundary is the hyperplane wᵀ x + b = 0. The absolute value |h(x)| is used as a measure of the confidence in the classification: it grows with the distance of x from the decision boundary, and a value close to zero indicates low confidence. The parameters w and b of logistic regression are learned via empirical risk minimization. The loss it minimizes is the logistic loss. On a data point (x, y), a hypothesis h incurs \[ L\left(({\mathbf x}, y),h \right) = \ln\big(1 + \exp(-y h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{.} \] Fig.~2 shows this loss for a data point with y = 1 as a function of h(x). A correct classification with high confidence incurs a small loss. A wrong classification incurs a loss whose size grows with the confidence in the wrong classification. Averaging this loss over the training set D(train) = (x(r), y(r))r=1m of m data points, empirical risk minimization delivers \[ \begin{aligned} (\widehat{{\mathbf w}}, \widehat{b}) &\in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, b \in \mathbb{R}} f({\mathbf w}, b), \quad\text{with} f({\mathbf w}, b) &:= \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \ln\Big(1 + \exp\big(-y^{(r)} ({\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} + b)\big)\Big) \text{.} \end{aligned} \] The logistic loss is the negative log-likelihood of the label under a simple probabilistic model for the classification task. In this probabilistic model, given the label y, the feature vector x is a Gaussian random variable whose mean μ(y) depends on the label while its covariance matrix C does not; the two means μ(-1), μ(+1) ∈ Rd are the parameters of the model. The best linear classifier under this model assigns x to the label with the nearer mean, and its decision boundary is the hyperplane midway between the two means. Its weight vector is w = C-1(μ(+1) - μ(-1)). The factor 12 that puts the decision boundary midway belongs to the offset b and not to w: any positive multiple of w leaves the decision boundary where it is, but only this one reproduces the posterior probability below. Learning the parameters w and b of the linear classifier is thus the same as estimating the parameters of the probabilistic model, and maximum likelihood is the principled way to estimate them. Under the model, the posterior probability of y = 1 is the sigmoid function σ(wᵀ x + b) with σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e-z). Maximizing the likelihood function coincides with minimizing the average logistic loss f. The hypothesis value as a confidence. The probabilistic model gives the number h(x) a second interpretation beyond its sign: σ(h(x)) is the probability that the label of a data point with feature vector x is y = 1, and σ(-h(x)) = 1 - σ(h(x)) the probability of y = -1. A forecast h(x) = 2 thus says that 88 percent of the days with these temperatures are followed by a frost-free day, and a forecast of 0 that half of them are. Whether these numbers can be trusted is the question of calibration. In most applications a data point carries only its label, the class that occurred. The logistic loss is the loss for this case. It is the cross-entropy between the probability mass function concentrated on the observed label and the predicted probability mass function (σ(h(x)), 1 - σ(h(x))). Some data points carry more than a class: a soft label y ∈ [0, 1], the probability of y = 1 itself. It may be the frequency of frost among the recorded days with the same temperatures, the share of several annotators who chose the class, or the output of a larger classifier, as in knowledge distillation. For such a data point the logistic loss is replaced by the cross-entropy between the soft label and the prediction, \[ L\left(({\mathbf x}, \tilde{y}),h \right) = - \tilde{y} \ln \sigma(h({\mathbf x})) - (1 - \tilde{y}) \ln \big(1 - \sigma(h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{,} \] which for y ∈ 0, 1 is the logistic loss again. Learning then minimizes the average of this loss over the training set, as before. This cross-entropy equals the Kullback–Leibler divergence from the predicted probability mass function to the soft label probability mass function (y, 1 - y) plus the entropy of the soft label probability mass function, which does not depend on h. Minimizing either therefore learns the same h, and the loss on a data point is smallest exactly when σ(h(x)) = y, when the confidence of the prediction matches the probability of the class. A hard label can never be matched this way, since σ never reaches 0 or 1. This is why the logistic loss keeps decreasing as |h(x)| grows on a correctly classified data point. Minimizing the average loss. With hard or soft labels, the parameters are found by minimizing the average loss f. Unlike linear regression with the squared error loss, the minimization admits no closed-form solution. As in linear regression, however, the objective function f is convex and smooth, so gradient descent applies. The parameters are collected as the pair (w, b), and the gradient descent step reads \[ ({\mathbf w}, b)^{(t+1)} = T\big(({\mathbf w}, b)^{(t)}\big) \text{, with } T({\mathbf w}, b) := ({\mathbf w}, b) - \eta \nabla f({\mathbf w}, b) \text{,} \] with learning rate η. The gradient ∇ f of the average logistic loss has the weight part \[ \nabla_{{\mathbf w}} f = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} y^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \sigma\big(-y^{(r)} ({\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} + b)\big) \text{,} \] and analogously for b. The pair (w, b) is a fixed point of the operator T precisely when ∇ f(w, b) = 0, which by convexity of f is exactly when (w, b) is a minimizer. It can be shown that ∇ f is Lipschitz continuous with some constant L. For a constant learning rate η < 2/L, every gradient descent step decreases f and the values converge to the minimum, f((w, b)(t)) → min f; the choice η = 1/L is the standard one. The iterates (w, b)(t) themselves need not converge: on a linearly separable training set the minimum is not attained, and the norm of the iterates grows without bound while the training error tends to zero. Adding the penalty term α w 22, with a positive α, to f makes the objective function strictly convex, with a unique minimizer that the iterates then approach. In practice, plain gradient descent is seldom used to minimize f: the smooth convex objective function is minimized faster by Newton's method, equivalently iteratively reweighted least squares, by the quasi-Newton solver L-BFGS, and, for a large training set, by coordinate descent. What these solvers minimize is the average logistic loss, but that is not the only loss with which a linear classifier can be learned. In principle, the squared error loss serves too: with the label values encoded as the real numbers +1 and -1, the squared error (y - (wᵀx + b))2 is well defined. Minimizing the squared error loss, however, has a flaw: it penalizes a prediction wᵀx + b that is large, positive, and correct, while the logistic loss keeps decreasing as this margin grows (Fig.~3). The hinge loss of the support vector machine shares this behavior on a correctly classified data point but stays flat once the margin exceeds one. For more than two label values, logistic regression extends in two ways. A simple reduction trains one binary classification logistic regression per label, each separating that label from the rest, and predicts with the most confident of them; this is one-vs-rest classification. An alternative replaces the sigmoid function by the softmax function, which models the probabilities of all labels jointly, so that they sum to one and no label is left without one; fitting it by maximum likelihood yields multinomial logistic regression.

terms.name: loss
terms.abstract: The loss incurred by a hypothesis on a single data point is a scalar that quantifies the error of the hypothesis when evaluated on that data point. The ultimate goal of machine learning methods is to train a model such that the learned hypothesis delivers predictions with minimum loss. A key characteristic of machine learning applications and methods is the accessibility of loss values. In supervised learning, the loss can be evaluated for every hypothesis. In reinforcement learning, the loss is observed only for the action actually taken.
terms.description: In temperature forecasting, the quality of a predicted temperature is naturally measured by how far it deviates from the temperature actually measured the next day. The loss formalizes this idea. The loss incurred by a hypothesis h ∈ H on a single data point is a scalar that quantifies the error of h when evaluated on that data point. A smaller loss value indicates a smaller error. In supervised learning, this error is the discrepancy between the prediction h(x) delivered for the features x and the label y of that data point. Some losses (e.g., the squared error loss) take a continuum of values, while others (e.g., the 0/1 loss) are binary, indicating only whether the prediction matches the label. For the temperature forecast, the loss on a given day can be the squared difference between the predicted temperature (the prediction) and the measured one (the label); see Fig.~1. Loss values are typically nonnegative: many losses are built from a norm or metric and are therefore bounded below by zero. Nonnegativity is not required, however: the logarithmic loss (negative log-likelihood) underlying maximum likelihood methods can take negative values, since a probability density function can exceed one. The loss is also not specific to supervised learning. In unsupervised learning there is no label: a clustering loss measures how far a data point lies from its assigned cluster centroid, and the loss of an autoencoder is the reconstruction error between a data point and its reconstruction. Machine learning methods use observed loss values to construct an objective function for model training. The average loss across a training set of data points is the empirical risk that empirical risk minimization minimizes. Machine learning applications can be categorized by how the loss values are accessible. In supervised learning, the loss can, in principle, be evaluated for every hypothesis in the hypothesis space, since the true label of each training data point is observed. In reinforcement learning, the situation differs. At each time step, the machine learning method (implemented by an agent) selects an action via the currently used hypothesis. The agent then observes the loss incurred by the action actually taken. The loss that would have been incurred by the other actions is not revealed. This limited accessibility of loss values is known as bandit (or partial) feedback. For example, a route-planning system learns the actual travel time only for the route the driver took, not for any alternative route. Similarly, a self-driving car selects a steering direction, and the incurred loss can be measured from onboard sensors such as collision detectors and lane-departure warnings, but only for the trajectory actually driven.

terms.name: matrix
terms.abstract: A matrix is a two-dimensional array of numbers, arranged in rows and columns. The entry Ar,j of a matrix A ∈ Rm × d sits in row r and column j. A prominent example in machine learning is the feature matrix of a dataset, obtained by stacking the feature vectors of m data points row-wise. A matrix represents several distinct mathematical objects. One is a system of linear equations, such as the normal equations of linear regression. Another is a linear map between two vector spaces, after fixing a basis for each. A third is a tabular dataset with one row per data point and one column per feature.
terms.description: Consider a spreadsheet of daily weather records at one station: each row holds a single day, each column one measurement such as temperature or humidity. Such a tabular dataset holds m data points, each described by d numerical features. The features of the r-th data point are collected in its feature vector x(r) = (x(r)1, …, x(r)d)ᵀ ∈ Rd, one entry per column of the spreadsheet. Stacking these m feature vectors row-wise, so that the r-th row is (x(r))ᵀ, produces an m × d rectangular array of numbers. Its entry in row r and column j is the j-th feature of the r-th data point. This two-dimensional numeric array is referred to as the feature matrix X of the dataset; Fig.~1 carries out the construction on three days of the weather example. More generally, a matrix of size m × d is a two-dimensional array of numbers denoted by {\mathbf A} = \begin{pmatrix} A_{1,1} & A_{1,2} & \dots & A_{1,d} A_{2,1} & A_{2,2} & \dots & A_{2,d} \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots A_{m,1} & A_{m,2} & \dots & A_{m,d} \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}\text{.} Here, Ar,j denotes the matrix entry in the r-th row and the j-th column. A digital image is a matrix of exactly this kind. Recording how green each pixel is turns a 16 × 16 image into a 16 × 16 matrix G whose two indices are pixel positions (Fig.~2). Matrices represent several distinct mathematical objects, including the following: \begin{itemize} \item Systems of linear equations: A matrix collects the coefficients of a system of linear equations, \begin{pmatrix} A_{1,1} & A_{1,2} A_{2,1} & A_{2,2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 x_2 \end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix} b_1 b_2 \end{pmatrix} \text{, written compactly as } {\mathbf A} {\mathbf x} = {\mathbf b} \text{.} Here, x is the vector of unknowns and b the right-hand side. One important example is the normal equations XᵀX w = Xᵀy, whose solutions are the model parameters that minimize the training error in linear regression. \item Linear maps: Consider two vector spaces U and V, of dimension d and m, respectively. Fixing a basis u(1), …, u(d) for U and a basis v(1), …, v(m) for V, each matrix A ∈ Rm × d defines a linear map f(A): U → V (see Fig.~3) via f^{({\mathbf A})}\big({\mathbf u}^{(j)}\big) = \sum_{r=1}^{m} A_{r,j} {\mathbf v}^{(r)}\text{.} Taking U = Rd and V = Rm with the standard bases, the image of a vector x under f(A) is the matrix-vector product f(A)(x) = Ax. \item Datasets: As in the opening example, a matrix can represent a dataset with each row holding a single data point and each column a specific feature or label. \end{itemize} Written with the feature matrix, the training error that empirical risk minimization-based linear regression minimizes becomes a succinct algebraic expression. Collecting the labels of the training set in y ∈ Rm, the training error of the hypothesis h(w)(x) := wᵀx is (1/m) \left\lVert {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} - {\mathbf y} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{,} with gradient (2/m) Xᵀ(X w - y). Each gradient descent step is therefore one multiplication by X followed by one by Xᵀ, and equating the gradient to zero leads back to the normal equations from the first example above. Matrices recur across machine learning beyond the feature matrix. The Jacobian matrix and the Hessian collect the first- and second-order partial derivatives of a multivariate function and drive gradient-based training. The covariance matrix records the pairwise covariances of a probability distribution over features. Principal component analysis, singular value decomposition, and a random projection factor or compress the feature matrix to lower its dimension. A kernel method replaces explicit feature vectors by a matrix of pairwise inner products, and a tabular Markov decision process stores its transition probabilities as a matrix. A graph is represented by matrices as well: its adjacency matrix lists which nodes are joined and with what edge weight. The Laplacian matrix assembled from those weights is the matrix whose eigenvectors graph clustering uses to split the nodes into clusters.

terms.name: mean
terms.abstract: The mean of a random vector x is its expectation, the Lebesgue integral of x with respect to its probability distribution. The term also refers to the sample mean, i.e., the average of the data points in a dataset. The two usages are consistent: the sample mean is the mean of the random vector obtained by drawing a data point uniformly from the dataset. Both usages share a further characterization: for a random vector with a finite second moment, the mean is the unique solution of a risk minimization problem under the squared error loss. For the random vector from a dataset, this optimization problem reduces to empirical risk minimization in the simplest regression setting: predicting a numeric label without features, for which the learned hypothesis is the sample mean of the labels.
terms.description: A weather station records the daily maximum temperature for a year. Adding the 365 numbers and dividing by 365 returns a single value that summarizes the whole record. This is the mean of the recorded numbers, and the same word names the corresponding quantity for a probability distribution. The mean of a random vector x, which takes on values in a Euclidean space Rd, is its expectation Ex. It is the Lebesgue integral of x with respect to its probability distribution P (e.g., see Billingsley (1986) or Rudin (1987)), i.e., \[ \mathbb{E}\{{\mathbf x}\} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}} {\mathbf x} \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf x}) \text{.} \] Here, P is the probability distribution that x induces on Rd, so the integral runs over the values x takes rather than over the underlying sample space. No probability density function need exist for the mean to be defined; when one does, denoted by p, it is ∫Rd x p(x) dx. The term is also used to refer to the sample mean of a finite dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) ∈ Rd. These two usages are consistent. A dataset defines a discrete random variable x(D)=x(I) on the sample space 1, …, m. Here, the index I is chosen uniformly at random, i.e., P(I=r)=1/m for all r=1,…,m. The mean of x(D) is precisely the sample mean \[ ({1}/{m}) \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \text{.} \] The probability distribution of x(D), which places mass 1/m on each data point, is the empirical distribution of the dataset. Fig.~1 shows both readings for a real-valued random variable and a dataset of seven numbers, with the empirical distribution drawn as its cumulative distribution function. The two readings are further connected by a shared characterization. Consider any random vector with a finite second moment, i.e., E ‖ x ‖22 < ∞. Its mean is the unique solution of the following risk minimization problem: \[ \mathbb{E}\{{\mathbf x}\} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf c} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \mathbb{E} \big\{\left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf c} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}\big \} \text{.} \] The objective function of this problem is a strictly convex function of the optimization variable c ∈ Rd. This risk-minimization characterization applies directly to the simplest machine learning problem, predicting a numeric label without any features. Consider a training set D(train) = y(1), …, y(m) that consists of labels y(r) ∈ R only. A hypothesis is then a single number h ∈ R that serves as the prediction for every data point. Empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss searches over candidate hypotheses h' ∈ R and learns \[ \widehat{h} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h' \in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big(y^{(r)} - h'\big)^{2} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} y^{(r)} \text{,} \] i.e., the learned hypothesis is the sample mean of the labels (see Fig.~2). This setting coincides with linear regression for data points that carry the constant scalar feature x = 1. Squaring the deviations also makes the mean sensitive to outliers. Moving one of m data points by an amount δ shifts the sample mean by δ / m, so a single corrupted data point can move the mean arbitrarily far. The trimmed mean that discards a fraction γ at each end stays bounded however far at most γ m data points are moved, and the median stays bounded however far up to half of the m data points are moved. Both are therefore preferred when features or labels may be unreliable (pythondemos/mean.py).

terms.name: membership inference attack
terms.abstract: A membership inference attack decides whether a given data point belonged to the training set of a published hypothesis. The signal it uses is memorization: empirical risk minimization drives the loss down on the training set and nowhere else, so a small loss at a candidate data point is evidence of membership. An adversary queries the hypothesis and compares the loss of its prediction against a threshold. What the attack can learn is therefore bounded by the gap between training error and validation error, which makes it a privacy cost of overfitting rather than a separate failure. Differential privacy bounds the leak by construction, at a cost in accuracy.
terms.description: A clinic trains a hypothesis on the records of a few hundred patients, which are personal data, and publishes it. A patient asks whether their own record was among them. A membership inference attack is the privacy attack that answers such a question: an adversary with access to h decides whether a given data point belonged to the training set. The signal is memorization. Empirical risk minimization drives the loss down on the training set and nowhere else, so a small loss at a candidate data point is evidence of membership. The adversary queries h at the feature vector and compares the loss of its prediction against a threshold. Fig.~1 shows why the attack works: a hypothesis flexible enough to pass through five data points reproduces each of their labels exactly, while a data point it never saw is missed by a visible margin. The attack is therefore bounded by what separates the training error from the validation error: a hypothesis that generalizes leaks little, and one that memorizes leaks much. Differential privacy bounds the leak by construction, at a cost in accuracy.

terms.name: machine learning pipeline (ML pipeline)
terms.abstract: A machine learning pipeline (ML pipeline) is the composition of the functions by which a machine learning system turns raw data into predictions. Its stages typically are data preprocessing, feature learning or hand-designed feature extraction, model training, and inference on new data points. Each stage is a function whose output is the input of the next, so the whole pipeline is one map from raw data to predictions and is applied identically during training and in deployment. Fitting stages such as feature scaling inside the pipeline, on the training set only, prevents data leakage from the validation set or test set.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau reports eight measurements of each day to the GeoSphere Austria data hub. Turning that stream into a forecast of tomorrow's minimum temperature takes four steps: cleaning the records, extracting features, training a model, and computing the prediction. The sequence of such steps is an ML pipeline: a composition (i.e., concatenation) of several functions within a machine learning system. The individual functions include data preprocessing, feature learning or hand-designed feature extraction, model training, and inference on new data points. By combining them, a machine learning system turns raw data into predictions (Fig.~1). Written as math, a pipeline of three stages is the concatenation \begin{equation} h = h^{(3)} i̧rc h^{(2)} i̧rc h^{(1)} \text{,} \end{equation} with h(1) the feature map, h(2) the hypothesis applied to the resulting features, and h(3) the post-processing of its output. Each factor is chosen from a hypothesis space of its own, h(j) ∈ H(j) for j = 1, 2, 3. The concatenations \eqref{equ_mlpipeline_dict} are themselves a hypothesis space, \[ \mathcal{H} = \bigl\{ h^{(3)} i̧rc h^{(2)} i̧rc h^{(1)} : h^{(j)} \in \mathcal{H}^{(j)}, j = 1, 2, 3 \bigr\} \text{,} \] so training the pipeline is empirical risk minimization over H rather than over any one stage. The pipeline object of a software library is this bundling made explicit. Each stage is a function whose output is the input of the next, so the pipeline is one map from raw data to predictions, applied identically during training and in deployment. Stages with their own parameters, such as feature scaling, are fitted on the training set only. Fitting them on all available data leaks information from the validation set or the test set into the learned hypothesis, so that the validation error or the error on the test set underestimates the risk (see data leakage). Software libraries therefore bundle the stages into one object that is trained as a whole on the training set. The pipeline is the computational part of a machine learning system, which additionally comprises data storage, deployment, and monitoring.

terms.name: model
terms.abstract: In machine learning, the word model is used in different ways. Formally, a model is a hypothesis space H: the set of candidate hypothesis maps from which a machine learning method picks (or learns) one. In applied machine learning literature and in software libraries, the word model also refers to the trained predictor, i.e., to the learned hypothesis returned by a machine learning algorithm; the EU AI Act uses this sense in the compound term general-purpose AI model. A different type of mathematical model is a probabilistic model, which specifies a family of probability distributions that characterize a data generation process.
terms.description: Consider the problem of predicting tomorrow's maximum daytime temperature from today's morning temperature. Machine learning methods learn a hypothesis map h that reads in today's morning temperature and delivers an accurate prediction of tomorrow's maximum temperature. This learned hypothesis is chosen from a (typically large) set of candidate hypothesis maps, i.e., a hypothesis space H. The hypothesis space underlying a machine learning method is its model: the set of candidate hypothesis maps, chosen in advance, from which the method picks one. For example, linear regression and logistic regression use the linear model as their hypothesis space. A decision tree method uses a hypothesis space that consists of hypothesis maps generated by a flow chart. Large language model systems use a hypothesis space consisting of non-linear maps represented by an artificial neural network. Model training refers to the process of finding a hypothesis in the hypothesis space that yields accurate predictions. A trained (or fitted) model is a learned hypothesis h = A(D(train)), the output of the map A by which the machine learning method turns a training set D(train) into a hypothesis. In applied machine learning literature and in software libraries, the word model typically refers to a trained model, i.e., to a specific hypothesis map h. The EU AI Act uses the word model in the same sense (i.e., a learned hypothesis) in the compound term general-purpose AI model. A different type of mathematical model is a probabilistic model, which specifies a family of probability distributions. Each such probability distribution defines a data generator: data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with the given probability distribution. Fig.~1 illustrates these three uses of the word model: the hypothesis space, the trained model, and the probabilistic model.

terms.name: model selection
terms.abstract: Model selection chooses among several alternative machine learning methods by comparing their validation errors. Each machine learning method delivers a learned hypothesis via some training method such as empirical risk minimization. A core design choice for a machine learning method is the underlying hypothesis space, or model. The effective hypothesis space can also depend on hyperparameters of the optimization algorithms used to solve empirical risk minimization. The training error of a machine learning method is a poor criterion for model selection, as it would always choose the largest hypothesis space. The validation errors can be obtained as the average loss on a single validation set or via k-fold cross-validation. The ultimately chosen hypothesis must be assessed on data points that have neither been used by any individual machine learning method nor for choosing among them.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows the morning minimum temperature x and the maximum daytime temperature y of six days. It also shows two hypothesis maps learned via empirical risk minimization from the training set D(train) of those six days. One is a linear hypothesis, learned over a linear model; the other is a degree-five polynomial, learned over the larger hypothesis space of polynomial regression. The polynomial passes through every day of D(train), so its training error, the average squared error loss over D(train), is zero. The linear hypothesis misses each of them and its training error is 0.47. The training error therefore ranks the polynomial first, and following that ranking would pick the candidate that predicts worst on a day that did not belong to D(train). Model selection ranks instead by the validation error on a validation set D(val) that empirical risk minimization did not use, which reverses the order. It leaves a test set D(test) untouched for estimating the risk of the selected hypothesis. Model selection is the step of a machine learning workflow that chooses among several alternative machine learning methods by comparing their validation errors. Consider C candidates h(c), c = 1, …, C, obtained from empirical risk minimization with a different effective hypothesis space H(c). The effective hypothesis space can also depend on hyperparameters of the optimization algorithm used to solve empirical risk minimization. Typical hyperparameters include the learning rate of a gradient-based method, the strength α of a regularization penalty term, and the depth of a decision tree. The training error of the learned hypotheses h(c) is a poor criterion for choosing between them: it trivially chooses the largest hypothesis space, even when that results in overfitting. Model selection therefore follows model training, e.g., via empirical risk minimization, and model validation, e.g., via k-fold cross-validation. It re-runs training once per candidate and reads the validation error that validation returns. The basic workflow has three stages. \begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*)] \item For each candidate c = 1, …, C, run empirical risk minimization on the training set with hypothesis space H(c) and the corresponding hyperparameter setting. This yields a trained hypothesis h(c) ∈ H(c). \item Compute the validation error Ev(h(c)) of each h(c) on a validation set held out from empirical risk minimization. k-fold cross-validation is the standard estimator of the validation error when the training set is too small to spare a validation set. \item Select the candidate with the smallest validation error. Its index is c⋆ = argminc Ev(h(c)). The selected hypothesis is h(c⋆). \end{enumerate} The selected hypothesis h(c⋆) must be evaluated on a test set. A test set consists of data points that have neither been used for learning any individual h(c) nor for choosing between them. Under an independent and identically distributed assumption for the data generation, the average loss on D(test) is an unbiased estimator of the risk of h(c⋆).

terms.name: norm
terms.abstract: A norm on a vector space is a function that assigns each vector a nonnegative number, its length. A norm is definite and homogeneous, and it satisfies the triangle inequality.
