Every norm defines a metric via the norm of the difference of two vectors, and every inner product induces a norm, but not every norm is induced by one. The ℓp-norms on Rd include the ℓ1-norm, the Euclidean norm, and the ℓ∞-norm; among them only the Euclidean norm is induced by an inner product. In machine learning, norms are used to construct loss functions and regularizers.
terms.description: Consider a data point that is represented by a feature vector x ∈ Rd, e.g., the hourly temperature recordings of one day at a weather station. Many machine learning methods use a measure for the size of such a vector or for the distance between two of them. A norm provides both: it assigns each vector a length, and the length of the difference of two vectors is their distance. Formally, a norm ‖ · ‖ on a vector space V over the field R is a function ‖ · ‖: V → R+ that satisfies the conditions below. These conditions hold for all vectors u, v ∈ V and all scalars β ∈ R, with |β| the absolute value of β: \begin{itemize} \item Definiteness: ‖ u ‖ = 0 u = 0; \item Homogeneity: ‖ β u ‖ = |β| · ‖ u ‖; \item Triangle inequality: ‖ u + v ‖ ≤ ‖ u ‖ + ‖ v ‖. \end{itemize} The same conditions define a norm on a vector space over the field of complex numbers C, with β ∈ C and |β| its modulus. A function that satisfies homogeneity and the triangle inequality but assigns the value zero to some nonzero vector is a seminorm, not a norm: on R2, the map u = (u1, u2)ᵀ ↦ |u1|, which keeps only the first entry, is a seminorm that is zero on (0,1)ᵀ. Every norm defines a metric by d(u,v) := ‖ u - v ‖, making ( V,d(·,·) ) a metric space. Conversely, some norms come from an inner product ⟨ ·, · ⟩, a function of two vectors that is symmetric, linear in each argument, and positive-definite (on Rd, ⟨ u, v ⟩ = uᵀ v). On an inner product space, ‖ u ‖ := ⟨ u, u ⟩ is a norm, and the norm of a Hilbert space is of this form. An induced norm satisfies the parallelogram identity ‖ u + v ‖2 + ‖ u - v ‖2 = 2 ‖ u ‖2 + 2 ‖ v ‖2, obtained by expanding ⟨ u ± v, u ± v ⟩. For the vector space V = Rd of feature vectors x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ and a number p ≥ 1, the ℓp-norm of x is defined as ‖ x ‖p = ( Σj=1d |xj|p )1/p. Its instances include the ℓ1-norm ‖ x ‖1 = Σj=1d |xj| and the ℓ2-norm ‖ x ‖2 = ( Σj=1d xj2 )1/2 (the Euclidean norm); the limit p → ∞ yields the ℓ∞-norm ‖ x ‖∞ = maxj = 1, …, d |xj|. The ℓ2-norm is induced by the inner product uᵀ v, and it is the only ℓp-norm induced by an inner product. The ℓ1-norm on R2 violates the parallelogram identity for u = (1, 0)ᵀ and v = (0, 1)ᵀ, where the left-hand side equals 8 and the right-hand side 4; the ℓ∞-norm violates it for the same pair, with the left-hand side 2. The distinction matters for machine learning methods. Only an induced norm defines angles and orthogonal projections and gives the least squares problem a closed-form solution; this is why the ℓ2-norm is the norm of the loss function of linear regression, while the ℓ1-norms of the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator penalty and of a residual need iterative solvers. The three norms differ in which vectors they count as having unit length. The unit sphere S(1) := u ∈ R2: ‖ u ‖ = 1 of a norm on R2 contains those vectors, and Fig. 1 shows it for the ℓ1-, the ℓ2-, and the ℓ∞-norm. Machine learning methods use norms to construct loss functions and regularizers. In linear regression, the label vector y ∈ Rm stacks the labels of a training set of size m and the feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d stacks its feature vectors. The average squared error loss of a linear hypothesis with model parameters w is then the scaled squared Euclidean norm (1/m) ‖ y - X w ‖22 of the residual y - X w. Ridge regression adds the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 to this training error, with a hyperparameter α > 0, while the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator adds α ‖ w ‖1. The choice of the norm determines the learned hypothesis by empirical risk minimization. Consider the two optimization problems \[ \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \left\lVert {\mathbf y} - {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2} \quad \text{ and } \quad \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \left\lVert {\mathbf y} - {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{1} \text{,} \] which differ only in the norm of the residual. Squaring the ℓ2-norm does not change the set of minimizers, so minimizing the ℓ2-norm of the residual is equivalent to minimizing the average squared error loss. Fig.~2 shows a training set of four data points, one of which is an outlier, and two linear hypotheses h(x) = w x learned from it. Minimizing the squared ℓ2-norm of the residual gives the slope w = 46/30. This solution is moved toward the outlier because squaring makes the largest residual the main part of the training error. Minimizing the ℓ1-norm yields w = 1, which predicts the three remaining data points exactly and leaves a single large residual at the outlier. The hypothesis learned with the ℓ1-norm is robust to the outlier in the sense that one unusual data point barely moves it, while the one learned by minimizing the squared ℓ2-norm is not (see robustness). Both slopes are learned from the training set; which of the two hypotheses has the smaller risk on data points outside it depends on whether outliers are present there as well.

terms.name: online learning
terms.abstract: Online learning refers to machine learning methods that continuously update the model parameters as new data points arrive over time. This contrasts with offline methods such as linear regression, which solve empirical risk minimization once over a fixed training set. The updates are based on some form of feedback: examples are an entire loss function determined by the new data point, or a reward signal. Online gradient descent uses an entire loss function as feedback; bandit and reinforcement learning methods replace the unavailable gradient by an estimate from the feedback. The figure of merit is the regret: the accumulated loss minus that of fixed model parameters chosen in hindsight. A method is successful if its regret per round vanishes as the number of rounds grows.
terms.description: A weather station reports one temperature reading per hour, and a forecast for the next hour must be issued before that reading arrives. An offline method such as linear regression first collects readings into a training set and trains a model on it once. It then forecasts with the learned model parameters for good: while it collects, it issues no forecast, and after it has trained, it no longer learns. An online learning method instead adapts its model parameters every time a new reading arrives; Fig.~1 shows both on three days of readings. Online learning proceeds in rounds: in each round, a machine learning method commits to model parameters, receives a feedback signal from its environment, and updates. The updates are based on some form of feedback. For the weather station, the feedback is the new data point itself. Any new temperature reading allows to compute the squared error loss against the current model parameters, and the loss can be evaluated for any possible choice of the model parameters. The feedback is therefore an entire loss function w ↦ L(z(t),w ). Online gradient descent is the online learning method for feedback by an entire loss function: it updates the model parameters by a gradient step on that loss function. Some online learning applications provide only a single loss or reward value as feedback (Fig.~2). For example, a clinic that gives one of several treatments observes the outcome of that treatment alone, which is a multiarmed bandit. A thermostat whose heating decision changes the temperature it faces in the next hour receives a reward together with a new state, which is reinforcement learning. Consider model parameters w from a convex closed set W ⊆ Rd, the parameter space, and rounds at consecutive time instants t = 1, 2, …. At time t, the environment fixes a function f(t): W → R, and the current model parameters w(t) incur the loss f(t)(w(t)). Only then is a feedback signal r(t) about f(t) revealed. Three kinds of feedback occur. With full information, the data point z(t) is revealed, and it determines f(t)(w) = L(z(t),w ) for every w ∈ W. On the temperature stream, the data point z(t) = (x(t), y(t)) has as features, collected in the feature vector x(t), the readings of the previous hours, and as label the reading of hour t. Its loss function f(t) is the squared error loss of the forecast h(w)(x(t)). With bandit feedback, only the value f(t)(w(t)) is revealed. In a multiarmed bandit with A actions, the model parameters w(t) ∈ ΔA-1 form the probability mass function from which the action a(t) is drawn. The environment fixes a loss vector ℓ(t) ∈ [0,1]A, whose entry ℓ(t)a is the loss of action a in round t, so the expected loss of the draw is f(t)(w) = ⟨ ℓ(t), w ⟩. The clinic observes the single entry ℓ(t)a(t), the loss of the action drawn, and no other entry. With reinforcement learning feedback, the immediate reward r(s(t), a(t)) of the action taken and the next state s(t+1) of a Markov decision process are revealed. The loss f(t)(w) is the negative expected reward of the policy with model parameters w in the state s(t). That state depends on the actions of the earlier rounds, so the environment's losses depend on the method's own past. The method then updates the model parameters using the feedback, \begin{equation} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} := \mathcal{F}^{(t)}\big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}, r^{(t)}\big) \text{,} \end{equation} with an update operator F(t) specific to the method, the counterpart of the operator F of a fixed-point iteration (Fig.~3). The feedback signal is written r(t), in the reward notation of reinforcement learning, although with full information it is a data point and with bandit feedback a loss value. The time index is also the iteration index: one update for any newly arriving data point. This contrasts with batch learning, which solves empirical risk minimization once over a fixed training set and then uses the learned hypothesis. The update \eqref{equ_def_onlinelearning_update_dict} at time t applies an operator that depends on the feedback signal r(t). By contrast, gradient descent applies a fixed gradient step operator in every time step. An online learning method is therefore not a fixed-point iteration of one fixed operator. Instead, it concatenates operators that vary over the time steps. Unlike stochastic gradient descent, which uses one data point per step to approximate the gradient of one fixed objective function, an online learning method faces a different loss function in every round. With full information, online gradient descent uses the gradient g(t) := ∇ f(t)(w(t)) in a projected gradient step. Online mirror descent replaces the Euclidean distance of the projection by a Bregman divergence, e.g., the Kullback–Leibler divergence on the probability simplex, which gives the Hedge update of the probability mass function over the actions. Follow-The-Regularized-Leader commits, in every round, to a minimizer of the accumulated loss of all rounds so far plus a regularizer. With bandit feedback, the gradient of f(t) is not available, since only one entry of ℓ(t) is observed. Exp3 forms an unbiased estimate of ℓ(t) by dividing the observed entry by the probability of the drawn action, and applies the online mirror descent update to the estimate. With reinforcement learning feedback, Q-learning changes one entry of a table of action values, the entry of the state visited and the action taken. The entry moves by a fixed fraction of the difference between its target, the reward received plus the discounted largest value of the next state, and its current value. This is a stochastic step of the Bellman operator, a contraction, so Q-learning, unlike online gradient descent, does have a fixed point interpretation. Policy gradient methods instead estimate the gradient of the expected reward from the rewards collected along the visited states. The figure of merit of an online learning method is not the decrease of an objective function along the iterates, which measures the progress of gradient descent: online learning has no fixed objective function. The loss function f(t) of round t is evaluated once, around w(t), and the next round brings a different loss function. Instead, an online learning method is evaluated by its regret. The regret is the excessive accumulated loss compared to that of a fixed choice w ∈ W of the model parameters. This fixed choice w is kept for all rounds t = 1, …, T and can be chosen after all losses are known. After T rounds, the regret relative to w ∈ W is \[ \mathrm{Regret}_{T}({\mathbf w}) := \sum_{t=1}^{T} f^{(t)}({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) - \sum_{t=1}^{T} f^{(t)}({\mathbf w}) \text{.} \] In a multiarmed bandit, the fixed w of interest is the probability mass function concentrated on one action. The regret is then measured against the best single action in hindsight; in reinforcement learning, against the best fixed policy. No assumption is made on how the losses are generated: the regret is defined for every sequence f(1), f(2), …, even one chosen by an opponent who has seen w(t). An online learning method is successful if its regret per round, RegretT(w)/T, vanishes as T grows for every w ∈ W. Regret bounds. The rate at which the regret per round vanishes depends on the feedback. With full information and convex losses whose gradients have norm at most G on a parameter space of diameter D, online gradient descent with the learning rate η(t) = D/(G√(t)) has RegretT(w) ≤ 32 DG√(T). No online algorithm can guarantee a regret below a constant times DG√(T) for every sequence: for each algorithm there is a sequence of losses on which its regret is at least that. With bandit feedback over A actions, the expected regret of Exp3 is at most 2√((e-1) T A ln A): observing one entry of ℓ(t) instead of all of them costs the factor √(A). With reinforcement learning feedback in a Markov decision process with S states and A actions, the UCRL2 method has regret at most a constant times S √(A T ln T), the constant depending on how many steps it takes to reach any state from any other. In each case the regret per round vanishes as T grows. Fig.~4 shows the regret per round of online gradient descent and of follow-the-leader, which commits in every round to a minimizer of the accumulated loss so far, on a year of hourly temperature readings. For linear regression with the squared error loss, that minimizer is computed by the recursive least-squares update, which carries the least-squares solution from time t - 1 to time t in closed form. Fig.~5 turns the same stream into a multiarmed bandit. The actions are five fixed forecasters, each a rule that needs no training. They forecast the previous reading, the reading of the same hour one day earlier, the mean of the three previous readings, the linear extrapolation of the two previous readings, and the mean of all readings of the year so far. The loss of an hour is the scaled absolute error of the forecaster used, and the regret is measured against the best single forecaster in hindsight. With full information, all five errors are observed after each hour and Hedge updates the probability mass function; with bandit feedback, only the error of the forecaster used is observed and Exp3 updates the probability mass function from its estimate of the loss vector. The regret of Hedge after T rounds is at most √(2 T ln A) for losses in [0,1], a weakening of the bound ln A / η + η T / 8 of Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2006, Thm. 2.2) at the learning rate η = √(2 ln A / T); the expected regret of Exp3 is at most 2√((e-1) T A ln A). Both regrets per round vanish, and the regret of Exp3 stays several times that of Hedge, the increase in regret caused by bandit feedback.

terms.name: overfitting
terms.abstract: Overfitting is the failure mode of a machine learning method that fits its training set too closely: the learned hypothesis incurs a small empirical risk on the training set but a large risk, i.e., the expected loss on data points drawn from the underlying probability distribution. Consequently, the learned hypothesis has a large generalization gap. Validation detects overfitting by comparing the training error with the validation error obtained on a validation set. Overfitting typically arises when the hypothesis space is too large for the number of data points in the training set; the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension and the Rademacher complexity measure that size. Regularization counteracts overfitting by pruning the model, adding a penalty term to the empirical risk, or augmenting the training set.
terms.description: An image classifier that memorizes every photograph in its training set but fails to correctly classify unseen images is overfitting. In general, consider a machine learning method that uses empirical risk minimization to learn a hypothesis h ∈ H with minimum empirical risk L(h|D(train)) on a given training set D(train). The method overfits D(train) if the empirical risk L(h|D(train)) is small while the risk L ( h ), i.e., the expected loss on data points drawn, independently of D(train), from the underlying probability distribution, is large. Consequently, an overfitting machine learning method learns a hypothesis with a large generalization gap. A large generalization gap alone does not imply overfitting. Consider a linear model fitted to a small training set whose labels are noisy and depend nonlinearly on the features. It can incur a large training error and a still larger risk, so the generalization gap is large while the training error is not small. The opposite failure is underfitting, where a hypothesis space holding no hypothesis that represents the relation between the features and the label of a data point leaves both quantities large. Fig.~1 shows why a small training error is on its own no evidence against overfitting. Three data points lie on a straight line. None of the three curves is drawn by hand: each is a hypothesis h delivered by empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss on those same three data points. What separates them is the hypothesis space that empirical risk minimization searched, and the three are nested, H(1) ⊂ H(2) ⊂ H(3): H(1) is the constants h(x) = b, H(2) the linear model, whose hypotheses are h(x) = w x + b, and H(3) all continuous functions on R. On H(1), empirical risk minimization has a unique solution: the constant whose value is the average of the three labels. That constant meets the middle data point and misses the other two, and no member of H(1) does better. The hypothesis space is too small here, and the method underfits. On H(2), the solution is unique as well and attains a training error of zero; the hypothesis space matches the relation between feature and label, and the method neither underfits nor overfits. On H(3), every continuous function through the three data points attains a training error of zero, and there are infinitely many of them: empirical risk minimization has infinitely many solutions there, and Fig.~1 draws one of them. The training error cannot separate that curve from the solution on H(2), the linear hypothesis that passes through the three data points, and it cannot choose among the solutions on H(3) either. The two hypotheses agree on the training set but differ at feature values between those of the training data points, and the risk registers this difference, since data points drawn from the probability distribution also fall in that region. The hypothesis space is too large here, and the method overfits. Validation detects overfitting, because the generalization gap that defines it can be estimated: a machine learning method that overfits delivers a small training error but a large validation error on a validation set held out from training. Fig.~2 illustrates overfitting for polynomial regression. Each data point carries a single feature x and a noisy label y, drawn from a probability distribution described in the caption. Polynomials of degree p = 0, …, 9 are fitted, using empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss, to training sets of m = 5, 10, and 20 data points; each panel of Fig.~2 shows the training error and the validation error for one size. The training error decreases with increasing degree in every panel: the polynomial of degree 9 has 10 model parameters and interpolates the m = 10 data points; for m = 5, every degree from 4 on interpolates; for m = 20, no degree shown interpolates. The validation error is obtained on a shared validation set of 100 data points. It is in contrast smallest at a moderate degree and grows by several orders of magnitude for larger degrees. The high-degree polynomials overfit the training set, and the gap between validation error and training error estimates their large generalization gap. Comparing the three training set sizes shows that the smaller the training set, the lower the degree at which the validation error departs from the training error. For m = 5, the validation error jumps by nearly three orders of magnitude already at degree 4. That is the lowest degree whose 5 model parameters suffice to interpolate the training set. For m = 20, the validation error varies by less than one order of magnitude across all degrees shown. At degree 9, it is smaller than the m = 10 validation error by a factor of more than 100. Overfitting typically occurs when the hypothesis space H is too large relative to the number of data points in the training set (as for H(3) in Fig.~1). Counting model parameters is the obvious way to measure that size, but not always the right one: the hypotheses h(w)(x) = 0.5 sin( w x ) carry a single model parameter yet form a hypothesis space with infinite Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension. The count is exactly right, in contrast, for the classifiers h(x) = sign( w0 + w1 x + … + wp xp ) obtained by thresholding the polynomials of maximum degree p in a single feature. Their hypothesis space has Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension p + 1, the number of model parameters and one more than the maximum degree. These thresholded classifiers concern a different case than Fig.~2, which fits polynomials of the same degrees to a regression task. The feature map x ↦ (x, x2, …, xp) turns these classifiers into linear classifiers on Rp, whose hypothesis space has Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension p + 1. Conversely, any p + 1 data points with distinct features are shattered. The classifiers realize every possible assignment of binary labels to these data points, since a polynomial of degree at most p interpolates arbitrary labels on them. The Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension of H and its Rademacher complexity measure the size of H without counting model parameters. Both enter the upper bounds on the generalization gap, which grow with them and shrink with the number of data points in the training set. Regularization counteracts overfitting in three elementary forms: pruning the model, adding a penalty term to the empirical risk, or augmenting the training set via data augmentation.

terms.name: principal component analysis (PCA)
terms.abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is the linear case of feature learning: it maps the feature vector of a data point to a vector of fewer entries by a linear map, chosen so that a second linear map rebuilds the original as well as possible. The criterion is the reconstruction error on a dataset whose labels, if it has any, are not used, since what has to be reproduced is the data point itself, which makes PCA an instance of empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss. The linear map that minimizes this error is given by the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix belonging to its largest eigenvalues, so PCA is computed by an eigenvalue decomposition. The error left is the sum of the eigenvalues that are dropped, which prices every choice of the number of retained directions in advance. Each eigenvalue is the variance along its eigenvector, so the first direction is the one of largest variance. An autoencoder keeps the same criterion with ANNs in place of the two linear maps.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau records eight numbers for each day of 2024: the lowest, highest and mean air temperature, precipitation, sunshine duration, humidity, air pressure and wind speed. Eight numbers per day are more than a scatterplot can show, and one of them, the mean temperature, is the midpoint of two others to within the precision of the archive. PCA replaces the eight by fewer, chosen so that a second linear map rebuilds the originals from the few with the smallest average squared error. PCA is the linear case of feature learning, and its criterion is the reconstruction error. The encoder is a linear map {\mathbf \Phi}^{({\mathbf W})}: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d'}: {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x} \text{,} given by a matrix W ∈ Rd' × d with d' < d, and the decoder is a linear map R ∈ Rd × d' that rebuilds the raw feature vector from the code, the lower-dimensional representation z = W x of the data point. The usefulness of a specific W is the minimum reconstruction error it leaves on a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) of feature vectors x(r) ∈ Rd with sample mean zero, the decoder being learned alongside the encoder: \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d'}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf R} {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} Minimizing over R and W jointly yields the same pair; the inner minimum is taken first so that the reconstruction error becomes a loss function of W alone. No labels appear in the reconstruction error \eqref{eq:pca_reconstruction}: the decoder has to reproduce the data point itself. PCA is therefore an instance of empirical risk minimization whose loss function is the squared error loss L(x,W ) = ‖ x - R W x ‖22, for the decoder R that attains the minimum. The eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix solve the reconstruction problem \eqref{eq:pca_reconstruction}. The feature vectors are centered, i.e., their sample mean is zero, which is what makes the following matrix the sample covariance matrix: \widehat{\mathbf{Q}} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big)^{\top} \text{,} and it is positive semi-definite, so its eigenvalue decomposition is a spectral decomposition, Q = Σj=1d λj u(j) ( u(j) )ᵀ with eigenvalues λ1 ≥ ≥ λd ≥ 0 and eigenvectors u(1), …, u(d) forming an orthonormal basis of Rd. Restricting the decoder R to orthonormal columns costs nothing, since the products R W range over the matrices of rank at most d' either way. For such an R the encoder attaining the minimum is the transpose W = Rᵀ: the best code holds the inner products Rᵀ x of x with the orthonormal columns of R. The reconstruction R Rᵀ x is therefore the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace they span. That projection is orthogonal to the error it leaves, and \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf R} {\mathbf R}^{\top} {\mathbf x} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} = \left\lVert {\mathbf x} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} - \left\lVert {\mathbf R}^{\top} {\mathbf x} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} Averaging over all data points in D turns the reconstruction error \eqref{eq:pca_reconstruction} into tr (Q) - tr (Rᵀ Q R). The first trace does not depend on R, so minimizing the error is maximizing the second over matrices with orthonormal columns. That maximum is Σj=1d' λj, attained by the eigenvectors belonging to the d' largest eigenvalues. A matrix W = ( u(1), …, u(d') )ᵀ whose rows are those eigenvectors therefore minimizes the criterion \eqref{eq:pca_reconstruction}, paired with the decoder R = Wᵀ. The minimum reconstruction error is Σj=d'+1d λj, the eigenvalues left out, so the spectrum of Q gives the reconstruction error of every code length in advance. The eigenvalues of Q are the variances of the data along its eigenvectors, so u(1) is the direction of largest variance. Fig.~1 shows the two directions for the days at Krems taken with two features, the lowest and the highest temperature of the day (both centered). Their eigenvalues are 130.9 and 7.9 squared degrees, whose square roots are the standard deviations along them, and no direction among two thousand drawn at random carries more variance than u(1). On all eight measurements, each scaled to unit sample variance because temperatures, precipitation and pressure are measured in different units, the two largest eigenvalues carry 64% of the total variance. A code of two numbers leaves a reconstruction error of 2.91, exactly the sum of the six dropped eigenvalues, and no encoder among fifty drawn at random reconstructs better. Fig.~2 plots the error left by every code length. These numbers are averages over the dataset the eigenvectors were computed from. Whether the subspace also rebuilds data points outside it is the question of generalization. The answer turns on how well Q estimates the covariance matrix of the data points the method will meet. The code length d' is a hyperparameter, and the spectrum of Q prices every choice of it in advance. The error left is the sum of the eigenvalues dropped. Each number added to the code therefore buys exactly the next eigenvalue, and the ones bought first are the largest (see Fig.~2). No choice is optimal on the criterion itself, which falls to zero at d' = d, where nothing is compressed. What picks d' is the use the code is put to: a scatterplot needs two, a later learning task can be given the validation error of each length to choose from, and a storage budget fixes it outright. The same criterion compresses images. Cutting a photograph into patches of 64 × 64 pixels makes each patch a data point with 12288 features, three color values per pixel, and PCA replaces those by a code of d' numbers (see Fig.~3). At d' = 5 the mountain and the meadow are already in place while the patch boundaries still show; at 15 the reconstruction is close to the original. The smallest eigenvalue reveals as much as the largest. It is 6.5 · 10-6 against 3.62, and its eigenvector loads on the three temperatures alone: the mean temperature of a day is the midpoint of its lowest and its highest, to within the 0.05 degrees the archive records. A direction of almost no variance is a dependency among the features, and PCA reports it without being asked. This is what makes PCA a dimensionality reduction method rather than only a feature learning one: the features it drops are the ones the others already determine. Three variants of PCA change one thing each. Probabilistic principal component analysis keeps the subspace but replaces the criterion by a probabilistic model. The code is a Gaussian random variable, and the data point is its linear image plus isotropic Gaussian noise. Maximum likelihood, computed by expectation–maximization, recovers the PCA subspace as the noise variance tends to zero. Sparse principal component analysis keeps the criterion but adds a penalty on the entries (loadings) of an eigenvector. Each direction then involves few features and can be read as a named combination of them. On the eight measurements, four loadings, the three temperatures and the sunshine duration, keep 81% of the variance of u(1). Robust principal component analysis replaces the squared error loss, which a single grossly corrupted entry can dominate. In its place comes a decomposition of the data matrix into a part of low rank plus a part with few nonzero entries. A small number of faulty measurements then ends up in the second part instead of tilting the directions. An autoencoder keeps the reconstruction error \eqref{eq:pca_reconstruction} as its criterion and replaces the two linear maps by ANNs, which is the nonlinear counterpart of PCA. With a linear decoder and the squared error loss it reconstructs into the same subspace as PCA.

terms.name: policy (reinforcement learning)
terms.abstract: A policy in reinforcement learning is a function that maps the current state to an action. Sometimes a policy is stochastic and defined by a conditional probability distribution over the actions given the state. The policy of a reinforcement learning method can be viewed as the hypothesis of a machine learning method. It reads in the features that characterize the current state of the agent and delivers a prediction of the best action to take. Instead of an average loss on a training set, reinforcement learning methods use the rewards observed after taking actions to guide the learning of a policy.
terms.description: In reinforcement learning, an agent interacts with an environment. At each time instant t = 1, 2, …, the agent observes the state st of the environment, takes an action at, and receives the next state st+1 together with a reward rt+1. Fig.~1 shows three time instants of a self-driving car: the state is the position and heading of the car, the action is the steering direction, and the reward tells how well the car follows the road. In its simplest form, a policy is a function that specifies which action at to take in this Markov decision process when the current state is st. A policy differs from a plan, a fixed sequence of actions: a policy reacts to the state it meets. Such a deterministic policy is a special case of a stochastic policy: it defines a conditional probability distribution P(a | s) over the actions given the state, a probability distribution from which the action is drawn. A policy can be viewed as a hypothesis map h(x) that predicts the best action to take. The feature vector x fed into the hypothesis is either the state itself, when the state is fully observed, or some indirect measurements of it, when the state is only partially observed. What sets supervised learning apart from reinforcement learning is how the usefulness of a hypothesis is assessed. Instead of computing the average loss on a dataset of labeled data points, reinforcement learning methods use the expected return obtained when the policy is applied to a Markov decision process. The return at time instant t is the discounted sum of the rewards received afterwards, \[ G_{t} := \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^{k} r_{t+k+1} \text{,} \] with a discount factor γ ∈ [0,1]. The expected return, as a function of the starting state, is the value function of the policy. It can be estimated by actually executing the policy: the agent starts from the state several times, follows the policy for a number of time instants, records the rewards, and averages the observed returns.

terms.name: pretraining
terms.abstract: Pretraining is the training of a model on a large, generic dataset to produce model parameters that are reused as the starting point for a later learning task. The loss minimized is typically self-supervised, so no manual annotation labour is needed. For a large language model, pretraining minimizes the average next-token prediction loss over a large text corpus. While transfer learning is the reuse of what was learned on one learning task for another, pretraining is the stage that produces what is reused, with a proxy task chosen for that purpose. The reuse takes several forms, by fine-tuning all model parameters from the pretrained ones, or by training only a subset of them on top of a pretrained feature transformation.
terms.description: Before a deep net is asked to detect tumors in a few hundred annotated scans, it is fitted to millions of ordinary photographs that have nothing to do with tumors. That first step is pretraining: the training of a model on a large, generic dataset to produce model parameters that are reused as the starting point for a later learning task. The loss minimized during pretraining is typically self-supervised (see self-supervised learning): the label of a data point is constructed from the raw data itself, so no manual annotation labour is needed. For a large language model, pretraining minimizes the average next-token prediction loss over a large text corpus. The model parameters learned during pretraining are then adapted separately for each task-specific dataset by fine-tuning (Fig.~1). In the tumor example, the task-specific data points are the annotated scans, while the generic dataset is ImageNet, a corpus of more than three million labeled images at its release. One approach to pretraining learns a feature transformation φ X → Rd, which is then concatenated with a task-specific model. In a deep net, the first layers are the pretrained φ and the final layers are trained separately for each learning task (Fig.~2). The same φ serves every learning task, so generic features are learned once, and each later learning task starts from an informative initialization instead of from scratch. A worked example. A piece of an aerial photograph of the Wachau, 2.4 km by 1.2 km at 0.79 m per pixel, is cut into 4608 patches of 25 m. A parcel register labels a patch as vineyard when more than half of its pixels lie on vineyard parcels, which is the case for a third of them. The western half is the training set, the eastern half the test set. At this resolution the rows of vines are visible stripes, while the mean color of a patch tells little: vineyards, meadows and gardens are all green (Fig.~3). Pretraining uses the photograph alone, never the labels. The central 8 × 8 pixel block of a western patch is blanked. A convolutional neural network of two convolutional layers, each with eight 3 × 3 filters and a rectified linear unit, is followed by a linear readout at the blanked block. It is trained to predict the mean color of the blanked pixels from their surroundings. On the eastern patches the trained network predicts the blanked color with a squared error of 0.0008, a quarter of the error of the mean color of the rest of the patch (Fig.~4, top). A second pretext task trains the same network to tell whether a patch was rotated by 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees. The direction of the rows and of the shadows answers that question. The network recognizes the rotation of 37 percent of the eastern patches, against 25 by chance. The two convolutional layers are then frozen: they are the feature transformation φ, and their output on the original patch, averaged over a 4 × 4 grid, gives 128 features. Logistic regression on these features is a linear classifier of vineyard against no vineyard. It is trained on as few as 8 and at most 128 labeled data points of the western half, and its accuracy is measured on the eastern half (Fig.~4, bottom). Labels are scarce on purpose: this is the regime in which pretraining decides the outcome. With so few labels a linear classifier on the pixels themselves is prone to overfitting. It has 768 features and at most 128 patches to fit them to, and its accuracy stays below the majority baseline of 0.69 until 128 labels are available, where it reaches 0.72. The mean color of a patch hovers at that baseline too, from 0.72 with eight labels down to 0.67 with 128. The control that every pretraining claim needs is the same two layers with their random initial weights, never trained: they reach 0.72 with eight labels and 0.76 with 128, since random convolutional filters with pooling already respond to texture. The color-pretrained layers are ahead of that control from 32 labels on, 0.76 against 0.73, and the rotation-pretrained layers beat it at every number, 0.77 against 0.72 with eight labels and 0.82 against 0.76 with 128. Two lessons follow. Pretraining pays when the labeled dataset is too small to learn what the pretext task already taught the layers. The pretext task matters too. A task that needs the direction of the stripes yields features that a classifier of vineyards needs, while predicting a color from its surroundings is largely solved by averaging. The numbers are computed by pythondemos/pretraining.py.

terms.name: probability distribution
terms.abstract: A probability distribution of a random variable is the probability measure that the random variable induces on the set of its values: it assigns a probability to every measurable set of values. A machine learning method reads in a dataset and delivers an output, such as a learned hypothesis or the prediction for a given data point, and should work well for any dataset that could arise in the machine learning application at hand. The independent and identically distributed assumption models such a dataset as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution, which is postulated from domain knowledge or estimated from a dataset. The probability distribution of a binary random variable is fully specified by a single probability, that of a discrete random variable by a probability mass function, and that of a real-valued random variable with a probability density function by that probability density function.
terms.description: Consider a machine learning method that reads in a dataset D = z(1), …, z(m) and delivers an output, such as a learned hypothesis h or the prediction for a given data point. Feeding a different dataset into the same method can deliver a different output. In general, the method should work well for any dataset that could arise in the machine learning application at hand. The independent and identically distributed assumption models such a dataset as independent and identically distributed RVs z(1), …, z(m) ~ P with a common probability distribution P (see Fig.~1). The outputs obtained from different such datasets are themselves realizations of a random variable, whose probability distribution depends on P and on the method. How much the outputs spread, i.e., how much they differ from one another, is therefore determined by P and the method. Formally, a random variable is a measurable function z: Ω → Z from a probability space (Ω, Σ, P) to a measurable space Z, the set of values that z can take. The probability distribution of z is the probability measure P(z) that z induces on Z. This probability measure assigns to every measurable subset B ⊆ Z the probability \[ \mathbb{P}^{({\mathbf z})}(\mathcal{B}) := \mathbb{P}\left({\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{B}\right) = \mathbb{P}\big( \{ \omega \in \Omega: {\mathbf z}(\omega) \in \mathcal{B} \} \big) \text{,} \] the probability of the event that z takes a value in B (see Fig.~2; ;; ). That event is the preimage z-1(B) = ω ∈ Ω: z(ω) ∈ B, the set of outcomes ω of the sample space Ω that z sends into B. Measurability of z guarantees that z-1(B) belongs to the σ-algebra Σ, so that P assigns z-1(B) a probability. The superscript of P(z) names the random variable whose distribution is meant, as in P(x,y) for a data point with features x and label y. When only one random variable is in play, the superscript is dropped, and z ~ P states that P is the probability distribution of z. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the probability distribution P of the data points decides how likely each dataset is: a dataset of realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs is likely when its data points lie where P assigns large probability. This distribution is generally unknown; only the dataset is observed. In practice, P is postulated based on domain knowledge or estimated from a dataset, e.g., by its empirical distribution or histogram, or by maximum likelihood within a parametric family. A parametric family is a set of probability distributions indexed by a few numbers, such as the normal distributions indexed by mean and variance. A probability mass function or a probability density function is a compact way of specifying a probability distribution. The probability distribution of a binary random variable y ∈ 0,1 is fully specified by the single probability P(y = 0), since P(y=1) = 1-P(y=0); more generally, the probability distribution of a discrete random variable is specified by its probability mass function. The probability distribution of a real-valued random variable x ∈ R that has a probability density function p(x)(·) is specified by that probability density function. The probability of a value in an interval [a,b] is the integral \[ \mathbb{P}\left( x \in [a,b] \right) = \int_{a}^{b} p^{(x)}\left(x\right) \mathrm{d}x \text{,} \] which is approximately p(x)(a) |b-a| for a short interval [a,b]. Because the probability density function says how much probability sits near a value, it can be drawn. For data points z = (x, y) with a single numeric feature x and a numeric label y, a probability distribution can be visualized in the plane R2. Fig.~3 shows one as a grayscale over the feature--label plane: the darker a region, the larger its probability density function, i.e., the more likely a data point drawn from P falls in it. The depicted probability density function is a weighted sum of two Gaussian pdfs, i.e., a Gaussian mixture model. Paralleling Fig.~1, three datasets D(1), D(2), D(3), each consisting of m = 40 realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with this distribution, are shown together with the three hypotheses h(1), h(2), h(3) learned from them by the same polynomial regression method. The three learned hypotheses differ most where the probability density function is small. Empirical risk minimization chooses the hypothesis by its average loss over the dataset, and a region in which the datasets contain few or no data points contributes little to that average. Hypotheses that differ only there have nearly the same training error, so the dataset does not decide between them.

terms.name: projection
terms.abstract: The projection of a vector onto a closed non-empty subset of a Euclidean space is a point in the subset that is closest to the vector in the Euclidean norm. If the subset is convex, this closest point is unique and the solution of a convex optimization problem. If the subset is a subspace, the projection is a linear map, namely the orthogonal projection onto the subspace. Every projection is idempotent, and a linear map of a Hilbert space into itself is an orthogonal projection if and only if the map is idempotent and self-adjoint. In machine learning, projections enforce constraints on model parameters during training: projected gradient descent alternates gradient steps with projections onto the constraint set, e.g., the ℓ1-ball in an equivalent formulation of the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator.
terms.description: Training a machine learning model must sometimes keep the model parameters w inside a constraint set, such as the set of vectors whose ℓ1-norm does not exceed a prescribed bound. A gradient step can move w outside this set, and the result must then be replaced by a closest admissible vector. The projection formalizes this replacement. Consider a non-empty closed set W ⊆ Rd in the d-dimensional Euclidean space. The projection PW( w) of a vector w ∈ Rd onto W is \[ P_{\mathcal{W}}\big( {\mathbf w}\big) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w}' \in \mathcal{W}} \left\lVert {\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}' \right\rVert_{2}\text{,} \] a vector in W closest to w in the Euclidean norm. The minimum exists for every non-empty closed set W, but several closest vectors can exist. For the two-point set W = (-1,0)ᵀ, (1,0)ᵀ, both elements are closest to (0,0.7)ᵀ, and likewise to every other point on the vertical axis, which consists of exactly the points equidistant from the two elements. If W is closed and convex, the closest point in the Euclidean norm is unique. The construction extends beyond the Euclidean space: a non-empty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space contains, for each point of the space, a unique closest point. If W is a subspace, that is, a subset that contains all sums and scalar multiples of its elements (such as a line through the origin), the map w ↦ PW( w) is a linear map: it is the orthogonal projection onto W. The projection is distinct from the proximal operator: the proximal operator minimizes, over all of Rd, the sum of a convex function f(w') and half the squared Euclidean distance to w, while the projection minimizes the distance alone, over the given set W. Every projection is idempotent: the vector PW( w) lies in W, so its closest point in W is itself and PW( PW( w)) = PW( w). A linear map P of a Hilbert space into itself is the orthogonal projection onto the range of P if and only if P is idempotent and self-adjoint, i.e., ⟨ Pu, v ⟩ = ⟨ u, Pv ⟩ for all u, v. For a matrix P ∈ Rd × d acting on the Euclidean space, idempotence reads as P2 = P and self-adjointness amounts to the condition Pᵀ = P. Idempotence alone is not sufficient for a linear map to be an orthogonal projection: an idempotent linear map that is not self-adjoint is an oblique projection. For example, the matrix P = pmatrix 1 & 1 0 & 0 pmatrix on R2 satisfies P2 = P but Pᵀ ≠ P. Its range is the horizontal axis, and it maps w = (0,1)ᵀ to P w = (1,0)ᵀ, while the point of the axis closest to w is the origin (0,0)ᵀ. In machine learning, projections enforce constraints on model parameters during training. Linear regression with the constraint ‖ w ‖1 ≤ τ, for a prescribed constant τ > 0, is an equivalent formulation of the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. This constrained problem can be solved by projected gradient descent. Each iteration takes a gradient step on the training error and then projects the result onto the ℓ1-ball W = w' ∈ Rd: ‖ w' ‖1 ≤ τ. The projection step is what enforces the constraint: without it, basic gradient descent on the training error can produce iterates with ‖ w ‖1 > τ, and the result solves the unconstrained problem instead of the constrained one. Since W is not a subspace (scaling the vector (τ,0)ᵀ ∈ W by 2 yields a vector outside the ball), this projection is not a linear map but amounts to solving a convex optimization problem (see Fig.~1).

terms.name: random experiment
terms.abstract: A random experiment is a physical or computational process that produces an outcome ω from a known set of possibilities, the sample space of the experiment. Probability theory represents the process by a probability space (Ω, Σ, P), where the σ-algebra Σ collects the measurable events and the probability measure P(·) assigns each event a probability. This representation is a probabilistic model of the process, not a property of it. A measurement of the outcome is represented by a random variable, a measurable function x: Ω → X, and the measured value x(ω) is a realization. Repeating the experiment m times is itself a random experiment on the product sample space, and the measurements of the runs are modeled as independent and identically distributed RVs. In machine learning, the collection of a training set, the draw of a subset of it by stochastic gradient descent, and the noise added for differential privacy are random experiments.
terms.description: A random experiment is a physical or computational process that produces an outcome ω from a set Ω of possibilities, the sample space of the experiment. Its defining characteristic is that the outcome is uncertain, and a key conceptual property is that it can be repeated under identical conditions. Fig.~1 shows the minimum and the maximum temperature of every day of January 2023 at the weather station Krems an der Donau: the weather of a day is a random experiment, and the two temperatures are measurements of its outcome. Rolling a die, reading the maximum temperature of a day at Krems, or drawing a handful of data points from a training set for one iteration of stochastic gradient descent: each of these is a random experiment. Its outcome is not known before the process is carried out, while the set of possible outcomes is. Probability theory represents a random experiment by a probability space (Ω, Σ, P). The sample space Ω collects the possible outcomes. The σ-algebra Σ collects the events, those subsets A ⊆ Ω to which a probability is assigned. The probability measure P(·) assigns to each event A ∈ Σ a number P(A) ∈ [0,1] such that P(Ω) = 1 and the probability of a countable union of pairwise disjoint events is the sum of their probabilities. Choosing Ω, Σ and P(·) is a modeling step: the probability measure is a property of the probabilistic model, not of the process. For a die, the sample space is 1, …, 6 and the uniform probability measure is the model of a fair die; whether a given die is fair is a question about the process, answered by the relative frequencies of its outcomes in many rolls. What is observed of an outcome is a measurement, a function x: Ω → X of the outcome. Such a measurable function is a random variable, and the value x(ω) it takes for the actual outcome ω is a realization of it. The temperature read at 13:00 is a random variable on the weather of a day, and the number read on one day is a realization. The probability measure on Ω induces the probability distribution of the random variable, P(x)(B) = P(x ∈ B) for every measurable set B ⊆ X. Machine learning methods work with the RVs and their probability distributions; the sample space behind them rarely needs to be written down. Fig.~2 depicts the two layers, the process and its mathematical representation. Repeating a random experiment m times defines a new random experiment whose outcomes are sequences (ω(1), …, ω(m)) of outcomes of the original one (Fig.~3). Its sample space is the product Ω × × Ω, and repetition under identical conditions, with no run influencing another, is represented by the product probability measure: the measurements x(1), …, x(m) of the runs are then independent and identically distributed RVs. While the outcome of a single run is uncertain, the long-run behavior of repeated runs becomes predictable: the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem make this precise. Random experiments arise in machine learning in three places: \begin{itemize} \item Data collection: the data points of a training set are modeled as RVs, i.e., as functions of the outcome ω ∈ Ω of a random experiment, and the independent and identically distributed assumption models their collection as the repetition of one experiment. This is what makes the risk of a hypothesis, an expectation under P(z), a meaningful target for empirical risk minimization. \item Stochastic algorithms: stochastic gradient descent runs a random experiment at each iteration, the draw of a subset of the training set; the bootstrap draws resamples of the training set. \item Privacy protection methods run a random experiment to perturb the outputs of a machine learning method, which is what differential privacy requires. \end{itemize}

terms.name: random forest
terms.abstract: A random forest is the instance of bagging whose base learners learn decision trees. Each decision tree is trained on randomly selected data points of the training set, and each base learner also uses only a randomly selected subset of the features. The predictions of the base learners are aggregated by a majority vote in classification or by averaging in regression. The random selection of data points and of features aims at a decorrelation, so that aggregating reduces the variance of the returned prediction. The aggregation of base learners is a form of regularization and counteracts overfitting. A random forest also yields a feature importance score per feature: the fraction of the overall splits that use that feature.
terms.description: A bank must decide, for each loan application, whether the applicant is creditworthy. A random forest answers with the majority vote of many different decision trees. A random forest is the instance of bagging whose base learners learn decision trees. As in bagging, each decision tree is trained on randomly selected data points of the training set. Besides the random selection of data points, each base learner also uses only a randomly selected subset of the features of the original data points. The predictions of the base learners are aggregated by a majority vote in classification or by averaging in regression. The scatterplot of Fig.~1 shows a regression example: each data point is one of the 366 days of 2020 at the weather station Krems an der Donau, its feature the minimum and its label the maximum air temperature of the day. Three decision trees, each trained on its own random selection of the days, yield three different piecewise constant hypotheses; the random forest delivers their average. This construction works because averaging many high-variance predictions yields one of lower variance, provided the errors of the individual predictions are weakly correlated. A deep decision tree is well suited as a base learner here: it can fit the training set closely (small bias), but its prediction varies strongly with the training set (large variance). Averaging reduces this variance. Consider M identically distributed predictions, each with variance σ2 and with pairwise correlation ρ. The averaged prediction has variance \rho \sigma^{2} + \frac{1-\rho}{M} \sigma^{2} \text{,} which decreases with the number M of trees toward the lower bound ρ σ2 set by the correlation. The random selections are drawn independently of each other once the training set is fixed, which is what makes the predictions identically distributed. They are not independent when the underlying dataset is itself a random variable: every decision tree is grown from the same training set, and that shared dependence results in a nonzero correlation ρ in general. The random selection of data points and the random selection of features both aim at a decorrelation of the predictions that the base learners deliver for a feature vector x (Fig.~2; ). While withholding features lowers the correlation ρ between the base learners, it raises the variance σ2 of each of them. The number of features offered to each base learner is therefore worth tuning: too many and the decision trees agree, too few and each of them predicts poorly. The aggregation of base learners is a form of regularization and counteracts overfitting. A random forest naturally yields a feature importance score for each feature: the fraction of the overall splits that use that feature. Fig.~3 computes these scores for a forest grown on four features of a day at Krems an der Donau.

terms.name: regularization
terms.abstract: Regularization refers to modifications to a machine learning method that improve its generalization. Three routes are distinguished by which component of the method is modified: pruning the hypothesis space, adding a penalty term to the loss function, and augmenting the training set with perturbed copies of its data points. The three routes often yield the same learned hypothesis. As a case in point, augmenting the training set of linear regression with Gaussian feature perturbations is equivalent to adding the ridge regression penalty term to the training error.
terms.description: Training a large deep net (such as a large language model) on a fixed training set via plain empirical risk minimization typically leads to overfitting: the learned hypothesis h performs well on the training set but poorly outside it. Regularization refers to modifications to a machine learning method to ensure the learned hypothesis performs nearly as well on unseen data points as on the data points of the training set. For empirical risk minimization-based methods, regularization can be done in three ways: \begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*)] \item {Model pruning:} shrink the hypothesis space H (the set of candidate hypotheses h) to a smaller H'. For a parametric model, the shrinkage can be implemented via constraints on the model parameters (e.g., w1 ∈ [0.4,0.6] on the weight of feature x1 in linear regression). \item {Loss penalization:} add a penalty term to the training error of empirical risk minimization. For the squared error loss, the penalty term can be read as an estimate of how much the risk exceeds the average loss on the training set; for other losses it controls the generalization gap without estimating it (see support vector machine). \item {Data augmentation:} enlarge the training set D(train) with perturbed copies of its data points (e.g., adding the realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs to the feature vector of each data point). \end{enumerate} Fig.~1 illustrates the three routes. These routes can yield the same learned hypothesis. As an example, consider data augmentation for linear regression that adds zero-mean perturbations with covariance matrix σ2 I to the feature vector of each data point. Asymptotically in the number of perturbations, the resulting learned hypothesis coincides with the one obtained from ridge regression. Ridge regression adds the penalty term σ2 ‖ w ‖22 to the training error of linear regression. According to Lagrangian duality, adding this penalty term is equivalent to shrinking the hypothesis space to the set of hypotheses with ‖ w ‖22 ≤ C for some constant C. The above regularization techniques are not limited to empirical risk minimization-based methods but can also be applied to other types of machine learning algorithms. For example, in online learning, the Follow-The-Leader method can be regularized by adding a regularizer to the per-round objective function of Follow-The-Leader. The resulting Follow-The-Regularized-Leader method achieves lower regret than plain Follow-The-Leader. Another instance of regularization is the use of a prior distribution over H in Bayesian inference. The prior distribution acts as a regularizer: the maximum a posteriori estimate of the model parameters of linear regression under a Gaussian prior distribution is the ridge regression solution.

terms.name: reinforcement learning (RL)
terms.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is the task of learning to act optimally within some environment. The actions are taken by an agent based on observations about the environment. The standard mathematical model of the interaction between agent and environment is a Markov decision process. An MDP includes a transition function, the conditional probability distribution of the next state given the current state and action. Another component of an MDP is a reward function that maps each pair of state and action to a reward value, which can be interpreted as a negative loss value. RL differs from supervised learning in the construction of the loss function: at each time step, the reward is observed only for the action taken, and it depends on previous actions, which forces a trade-off between exploring new actions and exploiting the ones found best.
terms.description: Consider a robot on the 4 × 4 gridworld of Fig.~1: a grid of cells, the cell in row r and column c written ⟨ r, c ⟩, with a wall at ⟨ 2, 2 ⟩ and a goal at ⟨ 3, 3 ⟩. At each time step, the robot moves up, down, left or right. A move into the wall or the boundary leaves it in place. Every move yields a reward of -1, while the move that enters the goal yields a reward of +1 and results in a stand still. RL is the task of learning, from such interaction, to choose actions that eventually reach the goal. The learner is not told which action is correct but must discover the actions that yield the most reward by trying them, and an action affects not only the immediate reward but also the next state and, through it, all later rewards. These two properties, trial-and-error search and delayed reward, distinguish RL from other forms of learning. The standard mathematical model of an RL application is a Markov decision process: a state space S, an action space A, the conditional probability distribution of the next state and reward given the current state and action, and a discount factor γ ∈ [0, 1]. The conditional probability distribution of the next state alone is the transition function. An agent interacts with its environment in time steps t = 1, 2, …: it observes the state st, chooses an action at, and receives the reward rt+1 and the next state st+1. The actions are chosen by a policy π, which for a stochastic policy is a conditional probability distribution P(a | s) over the actions given the state. The quantity to be maximized is the return, the discounted sum of the rewards to come, Gt = Σk=0∞ γk rt+k+1, where the discount factor γ weighs later rewards less. The state-value function of a policy, \[ v_{\pi}(s) := \mathbb{E}_{\pi} \big\{ G_{t} \mid s_{t} = s \big\} \text{,} \] is the expected return from a state when the actions are chosen by π. An optimal policy π* is one whose state-value function is at least that of every other policy at every state. In the gridworld with γ = 1, a shortest route of d moves earns -1 for each of its first d - 1 moves and +1 for the last, so vπ*(s) = -(d-1) + 1 = 2 - d. As a special case of machine learning, RL also trains a model on data: a policy is the hypothesis of RL. Two things set it apart from supervised learning. The first is the construction of the loss function. A supervised learning method holds the label of each data point and can evaluate the loss of every candidate hypothesis and its predictions. An RL method can evaluate the loss, the negative reward, only for the action it took, since the rewards of the actions not taken are not observed. The second is that the loss at time step t depends on the previous actions. RL is not unsupervised learning either: it maximizes a reward signal instead of finding structure in unlabeled data points. Within RL itself, methods differ in the amount of information about the environment required upfront, from a known Markov decision process to nothing beyond the observed rewards. If the Markov decision process is known, methods such as value iteration and policy iteration compute an optimal policy before the agent executes it. A policy is greedy with respect to a value function v if it maximizes, at every state s ∈ S, the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state. It therefore chooses an action in argmaxa ∈ A E rt+1 + γ v(st+1) | st = s, at = a. Both methods use two facts. The state-value function of a policy is the fixed point of its Bellman operator, which iterative policy evaluation reaches from any starting value function. And the policy that is greedy with respect to vπ is at least as good as π. When the Markov decision process is not known, an RL method has to learn from the interaction itself, and every reward it observes is one it paid for by taking the action. This forces a trade-off between exploration, trying actions whose reward is unknown, and exploitation, choosing the actions found best so far. Q-learning learns the action-value function qπ*(s, a), the expected return of taking a in s and following π* afterwards, from the rewards of the actions it tries, updating after each time step. Other methods learn the policy directly, or estimate a model of the environment and plan with it. Two special cases of the Markov decision process remove the delayed reward and leave only the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. The first has a single state: the transition function yields that state whatever the action, so the return is a sum of rewards that each depend on the current action alone. This is the multiarmed bandit. An ad server that shows one of ten banners and observes the clicks of the banner shown, but not of the nine it withheld, faces this case. The upper confidence bound method handles it by adding to the sample mean of each action a confidence term that shrinks with the number of times the action was chosen. The second case keeps several states but draws st from a fixed probability distribution that does not depend on the actions taken. The action at time t then changes the reward rt+1 and nothing else, and the state is called the context. This is the contextual bandit. The learning task is to learn a hypothesis that maps a context to an action, which has the form of a supervised learning problem, except that the loss is still observed only for the action taken. News recommendation is an instance: the context is the visitor profile, the action is the article placed on the front page, and the reward is the click. RL is often a form of online learning: the agent learns while it acts, and the data points it learns from arrive one per time step and depend on its current policy. Offline RL instead learns a policy from a fixed dataset of recorded interactions, without acting in the environment during training. The exploration is then fixed by whoever collected the dataset.

terms.name: reward
terms.abstract: A reward is an observed quantity that allows a machine learning method to estimate the loss incurred by the prediction of a hypothesis. One example of such a quantity is the label of a data point itself. Many machine learning applications, however, do not allow the label to be observed, but only a noisy estimate of it; some allow only the prediction error of one specific prediction to be observed. Reinforcement learning methods learn a sequence of hypothesis maps from the rewards obtained by their predictions. For example, a self-driving vehicle predicts, at each time instant, a steering direction, and derives a reward from a collision sensor that assigns a low reward to a direction moving the vehicle toward an obstacle.
terms.description: The ultimate goal of machine learning is to learn a hypothesis that predicts the label of a data point well from its features. Choosing among different hypothesis maps requires a measure of the prediction error that a hypothesis incurs. Such a measure is the loss, which can be defined, for example, by comparing the prediction h(x) with the actual label value y. In some machine learning applications, however, the label of a data point cannot be accessed at all. Consider a self-driving car, where a data point is the current time instant and the label is the optimal steering direction. That optimal direction is never observed; what is observed is whether the steering direction predicted by the hypothesis keeps the car on its lane (Fig.~1). A reward is an observed quantity from which a machine learning method estimates the loss incurred by the prediction of a hypothesis. One example of such a quantity is the label of a data point itself. Many machine learning applications, however, do not allow the label to be observed, but only a noisy estimate of it. Some allow only the prediction error of one specific prediction to be observed. In the machine learning application to self-driving vehicles, the hypothesis predicts, at each time instant, a steering direction. A reward is constructed from the measurements of a collision sensor that indicate whether the vehicle is moving toward an obstacle, and a low reward is assigned to the steering direction h(x) if the vehicle moves dangerously toward an obstacle. A reward replaces the label of supervised learning: it does not reveal the correct prediction, only how good the chosen action was, and it may arrive delayed, several time steps after the action that caused it, or corrupted by noise. Reinforcement learning methods learn a sequence of hypothesis maps from the rewards obtained by their predictions: the negative reward is the loss of the action taken, and the actions chosen are those that maximize the cumulative reward, the return. In the self-driving car of Fig.~1, the state st is the position and orientation of the car on the road at time instant t, and the action at is the steering direction predicted there. Fig.~2 shows how states, actions and rewards follow one another over two time steps.

terms.name: robust principal component analysis (robust PCA)
terms.abstract: Robust principal component analysis (robust PCA) decomposes a data matrix into the sum of a matrix of low rank and a matrix with few nonzero entries. A small number of grossly corrupted entries then lands in the second part instead of tilting the principal directions, which the squared error loss of principal component analysis lets a single such entry do. Principal component pursuit computes the decomposition by minimizing the sum of the singular values of the first part plus a weighted sum of the absolute entries of the second. That is a convex problem whose solution is the true decomposition under conditions on the low-rank part and on the positions of the corrupted entries. The alternating direction method of multipliers solves it by alternating singular value thresholding and soft thresholding. Uses are the separation of a static background from moving objects in video and the detection of faulty measurements.
terms.description: The hourly air temperature at Krems an der Donau in 2024, arranged as a matrix with one row per day and one column per hour, has 366 rows and 24 columns, and every row is the daily cycle on top of that day's level. Three singular values carry 99.5% of its energy: the matrix is nearly of rank three. Now let 5% of the entries be sensor faults, each off by 20 to 40 degrees. Principal component analysis of the corrupted matrix, its best rank-three approximation by a truncated singular value decomposition, ends up 19% away from the clean matrix, since the squared error loss lets the faults tilt the directions. Robust PCA decomposes the corrupted matrix into a low-rank part and a part with few nonzero entries: the first is 6% away from the clean matrix, and the entries of the second at the scale of a fault are exactly the faults (Fig.~1). Let X ∈ Rm × d be the data matrix whose rows are the feature vectors of m data points. Principal component analysis finds the matrix of rank d' nearest to X in the sum of squared entries, which is the truncated singular value decomposition. A single entry of X that is off by a large amount changes every singular vector, since the squared error grows with the square of that amount. Robust PCA assumes instead that \begin{equation} {\mathbf X} = {\mathbf L} + \mathbf{S} \text{,} \end{equation} with a matrix L of low rank and a matrix S with few nonzero entries of arbitrary size, and recovers both. Minimizing the rank of L plus the number of nonzero entries of S subject to \eqref{equ_rpca_model_dict} is intractable, and principal component pursuit replaces each count by its convex surrogate: \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf L}, \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}} \left\lVert {\mathbf L} \right\rVert_{*} + \alpha \left\lVert \mathbf{S} \right\rVert_{1} \quad \text{ subject to } {\mathbf L} + \mathbf{S} = {\mathbf X} \text{,} \end{equation} with the nuclear norm ‖ L ‖*, the sum of the singular values of L, in place of the rank, and the ℓ1 norm ‖ S ‖1, the sum of the absolute entries, in place of their count, as for the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. Both are penalty terms, the loss-penalization route of regularization. The weight α = 1/maxm, d needs no tuning: if the singular vectors of L are spread over all rows and columns rather than concentrated on a few, and the nonzero entries of S sit at positions chosen uniformly at random and are not too many, then the minimizer of \eqref{equ_rpca_pcp_dict} is the true pair (L, S) with high probability. On the temperature matrix the first condition fails only mildly, since the rows are not exactly of rank three, and the pursuit then assigns the small remainder of the daily curves to S as well; the faults are still the entries of S at their own scale. The alternating direction method of multipliers solves \eqref{equ_rpca_pcp_dict} by alternating two proximal operators: the proximal operator of the nuclear norm, which computes a singular value decomposition and shrinks every singular value toward zero by a threshold, and the proximal operator of the ℓ1 norm, which shrinks every entry toward zero by a threshold, followed by an update of the multiplier of the constraint. Each iteration applies the same operator to the triple of L, S and the multiplier, so the method is a fixed-point iteration, whose fixed points are the saddle points of the augmented Lagrangian and therefore the solutions of \eqref{equ_rpca_pcp_dict}; the operator is averaged, which is what guarantees convergence for a convex problem. On the temperature matrix the recovered L has rank nine out of 24 and the pursuit takes a few thousand iterations, each a singular value decomposition of a 366 × 24 matrix. The sparse part is as useful as the low-rank part. In a video from a fixed camera, with one frame per column, the static background is the low-rank part and the moving people are the sparse part, so robust PCA separates the two without a model of either. In a matrix of sensor readings, the sparse part flags the faulty entries, which is anomaly detection with the low-rank structure as the model of normal behavior. If entries of X are missing rather than corrupted, the same nuclear-norm criterion with the constraint restricted to the observed entries recovers L, which is the matrix-completion problem.

terms.name: random variable (RV)
terms.abstract: A random variable (RV) is a measurable function that maps each outcome of a random experiment to an element of a measurable space. Important types of RVs include binary RVs, discrete RVs, real-valued RVs, random vectors, and random matrices. The analysis of machine learning methods often relies on probabilistic models that represent data sources as RVs. The most widely used probabilistic model assumes that data points are independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution, which is unknown in general.
terms.description: The weather on a given day in the Austrian city Krems an der Donau is the outcome of a random experiment. Each possible outcome ω is characterized by a maximum daytime temperature, the temperature at 13:00, and reading off this temperature assigns a real number x(ω) to the outcome. This assignment is an RV x. The temperatures recorded on consecutive days are realizations of this RV (see Fig.~1). More generally, an RV maps the outcomes of a random experiment to elements of a measurable space. Mathematically, an RV is a measurable function x: Ω → X whose domain is the sample space Ω of a probability space and whose co-domain is a measurable space X. Measurability refers to the σ-algebras of the two spaces: the preimage x-1(B) of every measurable set B ⊆ X must belong to the σ-algebra of the probability space, so that the probability of x taking a value in B is defined. The value x(ω) ∈ X that x assigns to an outcome ω ∈ Ω is the image of ω under x (see Fig.~2). The sample space and the RVs on it are a modeling choice, not fixed by the data. The daily Krems temperatures admit two standard constructions (Fig.~3). In the first, each day r has its own probability space with sample space Ω(r), and the temperature of that day is an RV x(r): Ω(r) → R; the recorded value is one realization x(r)(ω(r)). In the second, one probability space with sample space Ω carries the whole reality: a single outcome ω ∈ Ω fixes the temperatures of all days simultaneously, and each day is an RV x(r): Ω → R on this common space. The independent and identically distributed assumption is a statement about the second construction: the x(r) share one probability distribution and are independent. The common-space construction is the one used for learning from data, because a single probability distribution then governs an entire dataset.
