Different types of RVs include \begin{itemize} \item {binary RVs}, which map each outcome to an element of a binary set (e.g., -1,1 or cat, no cat); \item {discrete RVs}, which take on values in a countable set (which can be finite or countably infinite; e.g., the number of heads in ten coin flips, with values in 0,1,…,10); \item {real-valued RVs}, which take on values in the real numbers R (e.g., the maximum daytime temperature in Krems); \item {random vectors}, which map outcomes to the Euclidean space Rd (e.g., the red-green-blue (RGB) values of a pixel, which form a vector in R3); \item {random matrices}, which map outcomes to a space of matrices Rm × d (e.g., the data matrix of a dataset). \end{itemize} In machine learning, RVs represent data sources, so that the behavior of learning methods can be analyzed. For example, the generation of a training set or validation set is represented by independent and identically distributed RVs sharing one underlying probability distribution; this is the common-space construction, in which a single probability distribution governs the whole dataset. This probability distribution is either postulated or estimated from actual datasets, for example via maximum likelihood. Ideally, a machine learning method should work well on datasets that arise as realizations of high probability. This is the generalization goal that empirical risk minimization pursues, minimizing the average loss on the training set as a proxy for the expected loss of the learned hypothesis on a new data point drawn from the common probability distribution.

terms.name: sample size
terms.abstract: The sample size is the number m of data points in a sample. Many machine learning methods model the data points as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs and judge a hypothesis by its expected loss, the risk; since the probability distribution is unknown, the risk is estimated by the average loss on the sample, for training by empirical risk minimization and for validation. How close that average is to the risk depends on the sample size. A concentration inequality such as Hoeffding's inequality bounds the deviation of the average from the risk and turns a required accuracy ε and confidence 1 - δ into a sample size of order ln(1/δ) / ε2 for validation; for training, the sample size must also be compared with the size of the model. For data points recorded in sequence, autocorrelation lowers the effective sample size. The same reasoning sizes the sample for a statistical test, such as whether two features are correlated: the sample size needed to detect a correlation grows as the inverse square of that correlation.
terms.description: A frost warning for Krems an der Donau predicts, from the minimum and the maximum temperature of a day, whether the next day brings frost. Whether a hypothesis h for this task is any good is judged by its expected loss, the risk L ( h ) = E L(z,h ), where the expectation is over a data point z drawn from the probability distribution P(z) of the days. Many machine learning methods use the independent and identically distributed assumption: the data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs z(1), …, z(m) ~ P(z). In practice, P(z) is unknown, and a method observes only these m data points, a sample. Their number m is the sample size. With the probability distribution unknown, the risk is estimated by the average loss on the sample, \begin{equation} \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}\big) := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},h \right) \text{,} \end{equation} which is the empirical risk. Empirical risk minimization minimizes this average over the hypotheses of a model on a training set, and validation compares the learned hypotheses by the same average on a validation set. Both uses require the average to be close to the risk, and how close it is depends on the sample size: by the law of large numbers, the average \eqref{equ_samplesize_emprisk_dict} converges to L ( h ) as m grows. Fig.~1 shows this for the frost warning: the sample average of the 0/1 loss of one fixed hypothesis, computed on samples of m = 10 to 1000 days, scatters around the risk 0.118 with a spread that falls like 1/√(m). How large should the sample be? One approach uses a concentration inequality, which bounds the probability that the average deviates from the risk by more than a given amount. For a loss function with values in [0, 1], such as the 0/1 loss, Hoeffding's inequality gives, for every ε > 0, \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}\left( \big| \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}\big) - \bar{L} \big( h \big) \big| > \epsilon \right) \leq 2 \exp\big( -2 m \epsilon^{2} \big) \text{,} \end{equation} see Hoeffding (1963) and Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014, Lemma 4.5). The bound holds for a hypothesis chosen before the sample is drawn, which is the situation of validation: the hypothesis was learned on the training set, and the validation set is a fresh sample. Setting the right-hand side to a tolerated failure probability δ and solving for m turns a required accuracy ε and confidence 1 - δ into a sample size: \begin{equation} m \geq \frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2 \epsilon^{2}} \text{,} \end{equation} and this many data points make the validation error lie within ε of the risk with probability at least 1 - δ. For the frost warning, ε = 0.05 and δ = 0.05 give m ≥ 738 days; at that sample size all of 2000 drawn samples in Fig.~1 land within 0.05 of the risk. The bound is loose, since it holds for every probability distribution and every loss function in [0, 1]; the sample size \eqref{equ_samplesize_choice_dict} is therefore enough, but not always needed. Its shape is what carries over: halving ε quadruples the sample size, while a smaller δ costs only a logarithm. For training, the same question has a second answer. The hypothesis is then chosen by looking at the sample, so the bound \eqref{equ_samplesize_hoeffding_dict} for a fixed hypothesis no longer applies to the learned one. The sample size then has to be compared with the size of the model. For a model of Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension d, a sample size proportional to d / ε2 makes the training error of every hypothesis in the model lie within ε of its risk at once. A sample that is small against the effective dimension of the model is the typical cause of overfitting, and the learning curve shows the validation error of the learned hypothesis as a function of the sample size. The sample sizes above assume independent and identically distributed RVs. Data points recorded in sequence, such as consecutive days, often show autocorrelation: a frost day is more likely after a frost day, and so is a wrong prediction. Dependent data points carry less information than independent ones. For a stationary sequence with autocorrelation ρℓ at lag ℓ, the variance of the average of m consecutive values is that of m independent values multiplied by \begin{equation} 1 + 2 \sum_{\ell=1}^{m-1} \Big( 1 - \frac{\ell}{m} \Big) \rho_{\ell} \text{,} \end{equation} see Brockwell and Davis (1991, Sect. 7.1). The average is therefore as accurate as that of m divided by \eqref{equ_samplesize_acf_dict} independent values, the effective sample size. For the 0/1 loss of the frost warning, the sample autocorrelation of consecutive days is 0.24 at lag 1 and stays positive for a week, and the factor \eqref{equ_samplesize_acf_dict} is 4.2 for m = 30. The average over 30 consecutive days therefore scatters as much as that over 7 days drawn at random: a month of consecutive days is worth a week of random ones. A sample of consecutive data points must then be larger than \eqref{equ_samplesize_choice_dict} or \eqref{equ_samplesize_corr_dict} say, by the factor \eqref{equ_samplesize_acf_dict}, or be drawn at random from the whole record, as the days of Fig.~1 are. Sample size enters a third task, hypothesis testing: are two features of a data point correlated? For the days of 2024 at Krems, is the minimum temperature of a day correlated with its diurnal range, the maximum minus the minimum? Over the whole year, the Pearson correlation coefficient of the two features is ρ = 0.16. A test sees a sample of m days and computes the sample correlation r, a function of sample means. Under the hypothesis that the two features are uncorrelated, r scatters around 0 with a standard deviation close to 1/√(m), whatever their probability distribution. For features that are Gaussian RVs, Fisher's transformation artanh(r) is approximately a Gaussian random variable with mean artanh(ρ) and standard deviation 1/√(m - 3). The test rejects ``uncorrelated'' when |artanh(r)| √(m - 3) exceeds the quantile z1-α/2 of the standard Gaussian random variable, which bounds the probability of a false rejection by the significance level α. A correlation ρ is then detected with probability at least 1 - β, the power of the test, once \begin{equation} m \geq 3 + \bigg( \frac{z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}} {\operatorname{artanh}(\rho)} \bigg)^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} For ρ = 0.16, α = 0.05 (z0.975 = 1.96) and a power of 0.8 (z0.8 = 0.84), the sample size \eqref{equ_samplesize_corr_dict} is 304 days. Fig.~2 shows the power of the test against the sample size: 0.84 at m = 304, and 0.10 for a sample of 30 days. The shape is that of \eqref{equ_samplesize_choice_dict} again: halving the correlation to be detected quadruples the sample size, so a weak correlation needs a large sample before ``uncorrelated'' can be rejected.

terms.name: self-supervised learning
terms.abstract: Self-supervised learning constructs the labels of a training set from the data points themselves. Some features of a data point are withheld and used as its label while the rest remain features, so what results is an ordinary supervised learning problem, solved by empirical risk minimization on data that no annotator has touched. In natural language processing the withheld feature is the next token, which is how a large language model is trained. In computer vision it is a set of pixels, deleted from an image and predicted from the patches left visible.
terms.description: An open image database returns thousands of photographs for a keyword such as cat, and a web crawl yields billions of sentences. Neither comes with a label saying what should be predicted. A prediction task can be made from any one of them: hide the last word of a sentence, and the words before it become a question whose answer is already known. Self-supervised learning constructs labels this way, from the data point itself. de Sa (1993) uses the term for a classifier whose label for one sensory modality is derived from a co-occurring input in another. In general, some of the features of a data point are withheld and used as the label; the remaining ones stay as the features. The result is an ordinary supervised learning problem, solved by empirical risk minimization, and its training set needs nothing beyond the raw data. A single unlabeled collection yields as many training sets as there are ways of hiding part of a data point (see Fig.~1). The withheld feature can be a token. In natural language processing a data point is a stretch of text, its features are the n tokens v(1), …, v(n) of a context window of length n, and its label is the token v(n+1) that follows. Every position in every document is one labeled data point, so a corpus of m tokens gives on the order of m of them. This is the training task of a large language model such as GPT-3, an autoregressive language model, i.e., one trained to predict the next token. Masking a token in the middle and predicting it from both sides withholds a different feature of the same data point. Similarly, in computer vision the withheld features are pixels: an image is split into patches, most of them are deleted, and the method predicts the missing pixel values from those that remain. He et al. (2022) delete 75% of the patches and still recover recognizable content. A deep net solving either task computes a composition h = s ∘ φ. The feature transformation φ X → Rd, with X the set of raw inputs (texts or images), sends a data point to a vector of activations, and the map s predicts the withheld feature from that vector. That feature can be predicted only from what φ has kept: a next token cannot be recovered from a vector that has discarded the context, nor a deleted patch from one that has dropped its surroundings. Fitting the composition is therefore what shapes φ, even though φ appears nowhere in the loss. He et al. (2022, Sect. 3) name the two halves: their encoder is φ and sees only the patches left visible, while their decoder is s and rebuilds the pixels from its output. What restricts φ there is the deletion of most of the input, not a narrow layer. In both domains it is φ that is carried over. The map s is dropped, and a small replacement for it is fitted on the output of φ using the few labels the later task does have (see transfer learning, foundation model). Self-supervised learning is therefore one answer to the same shortage that motivates semi-supervised learning: there, unlabeled data points assist a label-scarce problem directly; here, they are turned into a labeled problem of their own first. Unsupervised learning is the third answer, and it gives up the label entirely: it looks for structure among the feature vectors instead of predicting a withheld one.

terms.name: sigmoid function
terms.abstract: The sigmoid function maps the real line into the interval between 0 and 1. It translates the real-valued score of a binary classifier into an estimate for the probability of a specific label value. It is smooth and strictly increasing, with a derivative that vanishes for an argument with large magnitude. Machine learning uses it in two roles: as an activation function inside a neuron, and as part of the log-likelihood function for learning the model parameters of a probabilistic model.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows minimum daytime temperatures measured at Krems an der Donau. A classifier that warns of frost reads the recent measurements of a day, its feature vector x, and delivers a real-valued score h(x). The classification is a threshold: a frost warning for the next day is issued if and only if h(x) > 0, and the magnitude |h(x)| measures the confidence in that warning. In practice it is often more useful to state a probability. The sigmoid function translates the score h(x) into one, as Fig.~1 shows for its last day. The sigmoid function maps the real line into the interval between 0 and 1. It is the function σ: R → (0,1) given by \[ \sigma(z) := \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \text{.} \] It rises from σ(z) → 0 as z → -∞ to σ(z) → 1 as z → +∞, and passes through σ(0) = 1/2 (see Fig.~2). It is also called the logistic function, and it is the softmax function for two classes. Consider the classifier map h learned by logistic regression from the days of 2024 at Krems. Where its score is zero the sigmoid returns 1/2, so the warning is issued exactly where the probability passes one half. A score of 2.14 becomes a probability of 0.89 for frost tomorrow, and a score of -2.67 becomes 0.07. The sigmoid function is smooth and strictly increasing, and it satisfies the symmetry σ(-z) = 1 - σ(z). Its derivative is available in closed form, and in terms of the function itself, \[ \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big) \text{.} \] These properties make the sigmoid function a popular choice for the activation function of an artificial neural network. One challenge of that choice is that the derivative decreases quickly as the argument grows in magnitude, which slows the progress of gradient-based learning methods, the vanishing gradient problem. That is why the rectified linear unit replaced the sigmoid in the hidden layers of deep nets. A probabilistic model for a binary label uses the sigmoid function to turn a score into a probability. Let the label y be either 1 or -1, and let the score be wᵀ x with model parameters w. The model reads \[ \mathbb{P}\left(y = 1 \mid {\mathbf x}\right) = \sigma\big({\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}\big) \text{,} \qquad \mathbb{P}\left(y = -1 \mid {\mathbf x}\right) = \sigma\big(-{\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}\big) \text{,} \] where the second follows from the symmetry σ(-z) = 1 - σ(z). Both cases are the single expression σ(y wᵀ x), which is where the sigmoid function enters the log-likelihood. For a training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m of labeled data points, the log-likelihood of the model parameters is \[ \sum_{r=1}^{m} \ln \sigma\big( y^{(r)} {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big) \text{.} \] Maximizing it over w is maximum likelihood estimation, and it is logistic regression. Each summand is the negative of a logistic loss, so maximizing the log-likelihood and minimizing the average logistic loss are the same computation.

terms.name: Sobolev space
terms.abstract: A Sobolev space is a set of functions whose derivatives, taken in a generalized sense, have bounded size. Machine learning methods whose hypothesis space is a ball in a Sobolev space with a bound on the gradient enforce a well-defined quantitative notion of robustness. Any hypothesis map in such a ball can be locally approximated by a linear map with bounded slope. A small change of the features of a data point therefore changes the prediction by at most a proportional amount. The generalized derivative is needed because hypothesis maps such as those of a deep net with rectified linear unit activation functions have kinks. A decision tree, whose hypothesis map jumps, belongs to no Sobolev space and admits no such guarantee. Linear regression whose hypothesis space is a ball in a Sobolev space, rather than the linear maps, is nonparametric regression. Sobolev norms also serve as regularizers, and they describe the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a Matérn kernel.
terms.description: A weather service forecasts the maximum temperature of a day from its minimum temperature. Fig.~1(a) shows the 366 days of 2024 at the station Krems an der Donau of GeoSphere Austria as the data points of a scatterplot, with the minimum temperature of a day as its feature and the maximum temperature as its label. The panel also shows three hypotheses learned from these data points: the non-linear map of a deep net with rectified linear unit activation functions, the step function of a depth-2 decision tree, and the curve of linear regression with a Sobolev penalty term. A trustworthy forecaster must not change its prediction, the forecast, abruptly: a thermometer error of half a degree in the minimum temperature must not move the forecast by several degrees. Sobolev spaces make this requirement precise. They consist of the functions whose derivatives have bounded size. A bound on the derivative is a bound on how fast the forecast can change. The derivative is understood in a generalized sense, since the deep net of Fig.~1(a) has kinks and no classical derivative exists there. The generalized derivative starts from integration instead of differentiation. On the real line, a function with f(x) = f(a) + ∫ax g(t) dt is the integral of its slope g, the flow accumulated from a to x, and g is called a weak derivative of f. On an open set Ω ⊆ Rd, consider an infinitely differentiable test function that vanishes outside a bounded subset of Ω. A function gj is a weak partial derivative of f if, for every such , \[ \int_{\Omega} f({\mathbf x}) \frac{\partial \varphi({\mathbf x})}{\partial x_{j}} \mathrm{d}{\mathbf x} = - \int_{\Omega} g_{j}({\mathbf x}) \varphi({\mathbf x}) \mathrm{d}{\mathbf x} \text{.} \] This is integration by parts with all derivatives moved onto . It holds when f is the integral of gj along the jth coordinate, and it never asks for a derivative of f at a particular point. The slope of the deep net, the step function of Fig.~1(b), satisfies it for every test function tried (pythondemos/sobolevspace.py). For p ∈ [1,∞], the Sobolev space W1,p(Ω) consists of the functions whose weak derivatives exist and have finite Lp norm ‖ · ‖p. The case p = 2 gives the Hilbert space H1(Ω), and the spaces Wk,p(Ω) require weak derivatives up to order k. The case that matters most for machine learning is W1,∞, the functions with a bounded weak gradient. A function f belongs to it with supx ∈ Ω ‖ ∇ f(x) ‖2 ≤ L precisely when it is Lipschitz continuous with constant L. Perturbing a feature vector by δ then changes f by at most L ‖ δ ‖2. The deep net of Fig.~1 has L = 2.44, so an error of 0.5 ∘C in the minimum temperature moves its forecast by at most 1.22 ∘C; the largest change among 20000 random perturbations of that size was 1.21 ∘C. The bound also says that near almost every feature vector the hypothesis agrees with a linear map whose slope is at most L (Rademacher's theorem, ). This linear map is the explanation that gradient-based explainable artificial intelligence delivers and that local interpretable model-agnostic explanations fits from perturbed data points. For the forecast, it reads: one additional degree in the minimum adds s(x) degrees to the forecast, with the slope s(x) of Fig.~1(b) between 0 and 2.44. Since the deep net is piecewise linear, the approximation is exact whenever no kink lies between x and x + δ, which was the case for 98.0% of 20000 random pairs with |δ| ≤ 0.1 ∘C. The guarantee comes from the bound, not from the space: W1,∞ contains functions with every value of L. A machine learning method whose hypothesis space is the ball of functions with slope at most L learns a robust hypothesis by construction, whatever the training set. The choice p = ∞ is what makes the bound hold at every feature vector; H1 bounds the slope only on average. For the deep net, the weak gradient is bounded by the product of the spectral norms of its weight matrices, i.e., of their largest singular values, here 46.0 against the true 2.44: valid but loose. For a classifier that takes the sign of such an f, the bound certifies that no perturbation of Euclidean norm below |f(x)|/L changes the prediction. The decision tree of Fig.~1(a) has no such bound: at its root threshold of 5.5 ∘C, a change of 2 · 10-9 ∘C in the minimum temperature moves the forecast by 7.81 ∘C. A jump has no weak derivative that is a function, so no Sobolev space contains the tree. The bound concerns perturbations of the features only; robustness against perturbations of the training set is a property of the training map (see stability). Sobolev spaces also serve as hypothesis spaces in their own right. Plain linear regression minimizes the average squared error loss over the linear maps. Replacing the linear maps by a ball in H1, or equivalently adding the squared H1 seminorm ∫Ω ‖ ∇ f(x) ‖22 dx as a penalty term, a norm that ignores constant shifts of f (see regularization), gives nonparametric regression. The dotted curve of Fig.~1(a) minimizes the training error plus ten times that seminorm; it reaches a training error of 18.03, below the 18.66 of the deep net, with slope at most 3.05 (pythondemos/sobolevspace.py). A computer cannot search all of H1, and it need not. A minimizer of the training error plus the seminorm is piecewise linear with kinks at the m data points, since between two data points the straight line has the smallest seminorm for given end values (a consequence of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality). The search therefore runs over m numbers, the values at the kinks; this is kernel ridge regression with the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of H1. For a piecewise linear function the seminorm is a sum of squared slopes, one per segment and weighted by its length, so the normal equations of the penalized problem form one linear system. The demo places the kinks on 200 equally spaced points instead of the data points, which changes nothing in the arithmetic. The seminorm expresses the smoothness assumption. Its counterpart for a function on the nodes of a graph replaces the gradient by differences across edges, the form used by generalized total variation and generalized total variation minimization; penalizing the gradient in L1 instead gives total variation regularization, which allows jumps. The reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a Matérn kernel is a Sobolev space Ws,2(Ω) whose order s is set by the smoothness parameter of the kernel. A kernel method with that kernel is therefore again nonparametric regression over a Sobolev ball, the setting of Wainwright (2019, Ch. 13) above. Finally, a bound L is also of regulatory interest. Article~15 of the EU AI Act requires a high-risk artificial intelligence system to be robust and to have its accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use. A Lipschitz constant is such a metric: it states, as a single number, how much a perturbation of a feature vector can change the prediction.

terms.name: stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
terms.abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a variant of gradient descent in which the gradient of the objective function is replaced by a computationally cheaper stochastic approximation. Its main application in machine learning is empirical risk minimization on a training set that is large or stored in a distributed database: the gradient of the empirical risk requires an average over the entire training set. SGD approximates this average by the average over a randomly drawn batch of data points. The batch size trades the computational cost of a single update against the accuracy of the gradient approximation.

terms.name: supervised learning
terms.abstract: Supervised learning is the machine learning setting that needs the label values of some data points. That requirement is what sets it apart from other forms of machine learning, such as unsupervised learning or reinforcement learning. Two main types of supervised learning are regression, for a numeric label, and classification, for a label with finitely many values. Empirical risk minimization learns a hypothesis of a hypothesis space that minimizes the average loss on a training set of labeled data points. A label can be obtained from a sensing device, computed, or annotated by a person. These labeling processes typically involve errors, so a recorded label value is a noisy estimate of the true one.
terms.description: Supervised learning refers to machine learning methods that need the label values of some data points, the ones forming a training set. That requirement sets it apart from the other settings. Supervised learning methods evaluate the quality of a hypothesis by comparing its prediction against a known label value. Its two main types are regression, where the label is numeric, and classification, where the label takes one of finitely many values. Empirical risk minimization learns a hypothesis by comparing its predictions for the data points in a training set with their actual labels. The training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m consists of m labeled data points, each with a feature vector x(r) and a label y(r). Among the hypotheses of a hypothesis space H it chooses one that minimizes the average loss on the training set, \[ \widehat{h} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left(\left( {\mathbf x}^{(r)},y^{(r)} \right),h \right) \text{.} \] The loss of a data point can be evaluated on that data point alone, since its label supplies the value to compare with. In unsupervised learning, no such value is available, and the loss is defined through model parameters that summarize the whole dataset. In reinforcement learning, a reward signal measures the usefulness of a prediction instead. The label space Y, the set of values a label can take, decides which of the two types a learning task is: Y = R makes it regression, a discrete label space makes it classification. Both learning tasks can be built from the same data points. Fig.~1 shows two supervised learning tasks, one regression and one classification, obtained from the same data points. The data points represent daily weather conditions at Krems an der Donau, recorded by a weather station of GeoSphere Austria. With the maximum temperature of the day as label, the learning task is regression, and empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss learns the curve of panel (a). The second learning task uses both temperatures of the day as features. Its label is +1 if the next day is at least two degrees warmer and -1 otherwise, so the learning task is classification. The two classes overlap, so no straight line separates them: the same morning can be followed by a warmer or by a cooler day. The label values of data points can be obtained in different ways, such as physical sensing devices, computations, or human annotation. For example, the maximum temperature of a day at Krems can be read from a calibrated thermometer of the weather station. The label value can also be obtained by numerical computations. GeoSphere Austria runs INCA, which computes the temperature across Austria on a grid of one kilometer. INCA starts from the forecast of a numerical weather prediction model and corrects it with the differences between forecast and observation at the surrounding stations, so it returns a temperature value also for a location that has no station. The temperature recordings can be annotated by a person instead, a meteorologist or a panel of local residents. These labeling processes differ in the amount of required resources and in the resulting label quality. Each carries an error of its own, so a recorded label value is a noisy estimate of the true one. The station thermometer has a calibration tolerance. A computed label inherits the error of the equations and of the readings they were given. A layman might misreport temperatures. Human annotation also limits how large the training set can be, since it requires the expert whose judgment is to be reproduced. ImageNet, a dataset of 3.2 million annotated images at the time of its first publication, was assembled by annotators working through a crowdsourcing platform. An annotated label records a judgment rather than a measurement, and two annotators need not return the same value. ImageNet was assembled to limit this disagreement. Several annotators vote on each image, which is kept only on a convincing majority. The number of votes required is fixed per category, from an initial subset of its images.

terms.name: singular value decomposition (SVD)
terms.abstract: The singular value decomposition (SVD) factors any matrix into an orthogonal matrix, a matrix that is zero off its main diagonal, and a second orthogonal matrix. For A ∈ Rm × d it reads A = V Λ Uᵀ, and the nonnegative diagonal entries of Λ are the singular values. In contrast to an eigenvalue decomposition, which only exists for a square diagonalizable matrix, an SVD exists for every matrix. Truncating the SVD after the k largest singular values yields the best approximation by a matrix of rank k, which underlies dimensionality reduction. For linear regression, the SVD of the feature matrix splits the objective into one term per singular value plus an irreducible remainder. The solution with the smallest Euclidean norm divides each component of the label vector along a left singular vector by the matching singular value. The SVD delivers the pseudoinverse, the spectral norm, and the condition number of a matrix.
terms.description: A grayscale photograph with m rows and d columns of pixels is stored as a matrix of m × d intensities, that is, m d numbers. Most photographs can be stored with far fewer numbers: keeping only the k largest of the singular values of that matrix, defined below, costs k (m + d + 1) numbers. The SVD of a matrix A ∈ Rm × d is a factorization of the form \[ {\mathbf A} = \mathbf{V} {\boldsymbol \Lambda} \mathbf{U}^{\top} \text{,} \] with orthogonal matrices, whose columns are orthonormal vectors, \[ \mathbf{V} = \big({\mathbf v}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf v}^{(m)}\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}, \qquad \mathbf{U} = \big( {\mathbf u}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf u}^{(d)} \big) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} \text{.} \] The matrix Λ ∈ Rm × d is zero off the main diagonal, whose entries Λj,j = λj ≥ 0 are referred to as singular values and ordered as λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ … ≥ 0. The columns u(j) of U are the right singular vectors and the columns v(j) of V the left singular vectors; both families are orthonormal. Multiplying the factorization by u(j) gives A u(j) = λj v(j). The matrix A therefore maps each right singular vector u(j) to the left singular vector v(j) scaled by the singular value λj (see Fig. 1). In contrast to an eigenvalue decomposition, which only exists for square diagonalizable matrices, an SVD exists for every matrix. The existence of the SVD and its computation build on the spectral decomposition of the symmetric positive semi-definite matrix AᵀA. That matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors u(j) of Rd, with eigenvalues λj2 ≥ 0, the squares of the singular values. The left singular vectors are then v(j) := A u(j) / λj for λj > 0, completed to an orthonormal basis of Rm for λj = 0. The matrices U, Λ, and V built this way satisfy A = V Λ Uᵀ. If A is itself symmetric and positive semi-definite, its SVD coincides with its eigenvalue decomposition. The largest singular value λ1 equals the spectral norm ‖ A ‖2, and the ratio of the largest to the smallest nonzero singular value is the condition number κ (A). Retaining only the k largest singular values yields the truncated SVD \[ \widehat{{\mathbf A}} := \sum_{j=1}^{k} \lambda_{j} {\mathbf v}^{(j)} \big({\mathbf u}^{(j)}\big)^{\top} \text{,} \] a matrix of rank at most k. Among all matrices B of rank at most k, the truncation A minimizes the approximation error ‖ A - B ‖F. This property is what makes the truncation useful for storing the photograph of the opening. No matrix of rank at most k is closer to A, so the truncation loses as little as any storage by a rank-k matrix can. It requires only the k largest singular values with their left and right singular vectors, that is, k (m + d + 1) numbers instead of m d (pythondemos/svd.py). Principal component analysis is the same truncation applied to a centered feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d: a linear dimensionality reduction that replaces each feature vector by its coordinates along the k directions of largest variance. The right singular vectors u(j) of X are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix (1)/(m) Xᵀ X, whose eigenvalues are λj2/m. Principal component analysis therefore projects each data point onto the leading u(1), …, u(k). The SVD can also be used to analyze and to implement linear regression methods. Consider a feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d, whose r-th row is the feature vector of the r-th data point, and a label vector y ∈ Rm. Linear regression minimizes the squared Euclidean norm ‖ X w - y ‖22 of the residual over the model parameters w. That is the empirical risk minimization objective for the squared error loss, the least squares problem. This objective is a proxy: the goal is a small squared error on data points outside the training set (see generalization), and the training set is what is available. Let p be the number of nonzero singular values of X, its rank. A component of w along a right singular vector u(j) with j > p leaves X w unchanged, so expanding w = Σj=1p w(j) u(j) in the leading right singular vectors loses nothing. With X u(j) = λjv(j) and the orthonormality of the left singular vectors v(j), the objective of linear regression reads \[ \begin{aligned} \left\lVert {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} - {\mathbf y} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} &= \left\lVert \textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{p} \lambda_{j}\widetilde{w}^{(j)} {\mathbf v}^{(j)} - {\mathbf y} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} &= \sum_{j=1}^{p} \big(\lambda_{j}\widetilde{w}^{(j)} - ({\mathbf v}^{(j)})^{\top}{\mathbf y}\big)^{2} + \sum_{j=p+1}^{m} \big(({\mathbf v}^{(j)})^{\top}{\mathbf y}\big)^{2} \text{.} \end{aligned} \] The objective of linear regression depends on y only through its components (v(j))ᵀy along the left singular vectors. The second sum is the constant, irreducible error from the part of y outside the column space of X. The first sum is minimized termwise at w(j) = (v(j))ᵀy / λj for j ≤ p. In matrix form, this is w = X+ y with the pseudoinverse X+ = U Λ+ Vᵀ, where Λ+ inverts the nonzero singular values. The vector w is the solution of linear regression with the smallest Euclidean norm. A small singular value divides the corresponding component of y by a small number, which is why the condition number of X governs how noise in y reaches w.

terms.name: support vector machine (SVM)
terms.abstract: The support vector machine (SVM) is a binary classification method that learns a linear classifier by regularized empirical risk minimization, combining the hinge loss with a squared-norm penalty term. For a linearly separable training set and sufficiently weak regularization, the solution is the maximum-margin separating hyperplane. This hyperplane is fully determined by the feature vectors closest to it, which are called support vectors. The kernel SVM is obtained by combining the basic SVM with a feature transformation derived from a kernel function.
terms.description: The SVM is a binary classification method for data points with feature space X=Rd. In its simplest form, the SVM learns a linear classifier with decision boundary \{ {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}: {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x} + b = 0 \}. The linear classifier is parameterized by a nonzero vector w ∈ Rd 0 and an offset b ∈ R. The vector w is the normal vector to the decision boundary and the offset b shifts the decision boundary away from the origin. For a data point with feature vector x and label y ∈ -1, +1, the SVM delivers the prediction y = sign(wᵀ x + b). SVMs have been applied to text classification, where each document is first represented by a numeric feature vector of word frequencies and then categorized by topic. Another application is handwritten digit recognition, where digit images are classified from pixel-level features. The SVM can be formulated as an instance of regularized empirical risk minimization for learning a linear classifier from a training set that consists of m data points. The model parameters (w, b) of the linear classifier are obtained as \begin{equation} (\widehat{{\mathbf w}}, \widehat{b}) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, b \in \mathbb{R}} \underbrace{\frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \max\{0, 1 - y^{(r)} ({\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} + b)\} + \alpha \left\lVert {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}}_{:= f({\mathbf w}, b)}\text{.} \end{equation} The SVM objective function consists of the average hinge loss on the training set plus a penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 with regularization parameter α > 0. The penalty term in the SVM problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} is the scaled squared Euclidean norm α ‖ w ‖22, the same penalty term as in ridge regression. It does not involve the model parameter b, which is therefore left unpenalized. In linear regression, the penalty term can be interpreted as an estimate of how much higher the loss is on data points outside the training set than on it (see linear regression). This interpretation rests on the quadratic structure of the squared error loss and does not carry over to the hinge loss. For the SVM, the penalty term instead controls the generalization gap: the hinge loss is Lipschitz continuous in w, with a constant given by the Euclidean norm of the feature vector. Adding the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 to the average hinge loss has three effects: First, it makes the overall objective function in the SVM problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} strongly convex in w, so that its solution w is unique. Second, it controls how much that solution varies if the data points in the training set change. Third, it keeps ‖ w ‖2 small and therefore the margins wide. If the feature vectors in the training set have bounded Euclidean norm, the expectation of the difference between the risk and the empirical hinge loss of the learned linear classifier decreases in proportion to 1/(α m). The penalty term also has a geometric role: a small norm ‖ w ‖2 corresponds to a large margin 1/‖ w ‖2 of the learned linear classifier, as discussed below. Like logistic regression and linear regression, the SVM learns the model parameters (w, b) of a linear model. In contrast to logistic regression and linear regression, the SVM objective function f(w, b) is non-smooth because of the hinge loss. However, since the SVM objective function is convex, the optimization problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} can be solved by convex optimization methods. One such method is subgradient descent, which is obtained from gradient descent by replacing the gradient of the objective function with a subgradient. Starting from an initial choice w(0), b(0) of the model parameters, subgradient descent repeatedly applies the update \[ \big({\mathbf w}^{(t+1)}, b^{(t+1)}\big) = \big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}, b^{(t)}\big) - \eta^{(t)} {\mathbf g}^{(t)} \text{, for } t = 0,1,\ldots \text{,} \] with a step size η(t) > 0 and a subgradient g(t) ∈ ∂ f(w(t), b(t)) of the SVM objective function \eqref{eq:svm_rerm}. Inserting the SVM objective function \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} into the generic update yields the explicit update \[ \begin{aligned} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} &= \big(1 - 2 \eta^{(t)} \alpha\big) {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + \frac{\eta^{(t)}}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta^{(t)}_{r} y^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \text{,} b^{(t+1)} &= b^{(t)} + \frac{\eta^{(t)}}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta^{(t)}_{r} y^{(r)} \text{,} \end{aligned} \] with expansion coefficients β(t)r ∈ [0, 1], for r = 1, …, m. The coefficient β(t)r is nonzero only for data points that satisfy y(r) ( (w(t))ᵀ x(r) + b(t) ) ≤ 1, i.e., data points on which the hinge loss is nonzero or non-differentiable at the current model parameters. Each iteration scales w(t) by the factor 1 - 2 η(t) α (the effect of the penalty term) and adds corrections y(r) x(r) only from these data points. In particular, for the initialization w(0) = 0, every iterate w(t) is a weighted sum Σr=1m βr y(r) x(r) of the feature vectors in the training set. The solution w of the SVM problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} admits the same expansion, with coefficients that are nonzero only for the data points satisfying the same condition y(r) ( wᵀ x(r) + b ) ≤ 1 (see the discussion of support vectors below). For a suitably diminishing step size, e.g., η(t) = 1/(t+1), the iterates (w(t), b(t)) converge to a solution of the SVM problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm}. The solution of the SVM problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} has a clear geometric meaning when the training set is linearly separable, i.e., there is some choice for (w, b) such that sign(wᵀ x(r) + b) y(r)=1 for r=1, …, m. For a sufficiently small α, the solution of the SVM problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} determines the separating hyperplane that is farthest from the feature vectors in the training set (see Fig.~1). The distance between this hyperplane and the nearest feature vectors, which are precisely the support vectors discussed below, is referred to as the margin and is given by 1/‖ w ‖2. The margin of the learned hyperplane measures robustness against perturbations of the features of a data point. Perturbing a feature vector x by a vector δ changes the score wᵀx + b by wᵀδ, whose magnitude is at most ‖ w ‖2 ‖ δ ‖2 by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. A data point therefore stays correctly classified under every feature perturbation with ‖ δ ‖2 < γ, as illustrated by the dashed circle around a support vector in Fig.~1. Data points whose feature vectors lie farther from the decision boundary tolerate even larger perturbations: the tolerated radius equals the distance of the feature vector from the decision boundary, which is at least γ and equals γ precisely for the support vectors. Maximizing the margin maximizes this worst-case tolerated radius, so the maximum-margin classifier is the separating classifier that is robust against the largest feature perturbations. The same holds beyond the separable case: the SVM problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} is equivalent to minimizing the hinge loss under the worst case over bounded perturbations of the feature vectors. While the above discussion only applies when the SVM training set is linearly separable, every solution of the SVM problem \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} has a structure that holds in general. In particular, \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta_{r} y^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} with expansion coefficients 0 ≤ βr ≤ 1/(2 α m) that are nonzero only for the feature vectors with y^{(r)} (\widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} + \widehat{b}) \leq 1. These feature vectors are referred to as support vectors since they entirely determine the SVM solution (w, b). Applying a perturbation to any feature vector that is not a support vector leaves w, b unchanged, provided the perturbation is small enough to preserve the strict inequality y (wᵀ x + b) > 1 (see Fig.~2). An overly large regularization parameter α makes the SVM underfit: the above expansion of w implies ‖ w ‖2 ≤ ρ/(2α), with ρ the largest Euclidean norm of a feature vector in the training set, so w shrinks toward 0. Consider a training set with unequal class sizes. For sufficiently large α, the predictions approach the constant majority-class prediction sign(b) and every data point of the minority class is a misclassified support vector. The training set of Fig.~2 also has unequal class sizes, four data points labeled y = +1 and three labeled y = -1, but with the value α = 1/14 used there, the SVM misclassifies one data point that can be considered an outlier. Increasing the value of α to 50 for that training set shrinks ‖ w ‖2, makes every prediction on the training set equal to +1, and misclassifies all three data points of the minority class. The basic SVM \eqref{eq:svm_rerm} learns a linear classifier on the feature space X = Rd. It can be generalized to a classification method for data points whose feature vectors lie in an arbitrary feature space X by first applying a feature transformation φ: X → X' with X' = Rd and then learning a linear classifier on the transformed feature vectors. By choosing φ (and d) appropriately, any given training set with distinct feature vectors can be made linearly separable in X', e.g., by mapping each distinct feature vector to its own coordinate axis. A principled construction of a feature transformation φ is via a kernel k: X × X → R. In this construction, the transformed feature space is, in general, not Rd but a Hilbert space H, which can be infinite-dimensional (see kernel method). The resulting method is then referred to as a kernel SVM.

terms.name: tabular data
terms.abstract: Tabular data consist of data points that share a common, fixed set of attributes. The measured attributes serve as the features or as the label of a data point. The data points constitute the rows, or records, of a table, and the attributes are its columns. Every row has one cell per column, and the cells within one column hold values of the same attribute. The fixed attribute set separates tabular data from other types of data, such as text or graphs, whose data points carry no common set of attributes.
terms.description: Tabular data consist of data points that share a common, fixed set of attributes. As the name suggests, tabular data can be stored as a table: the rows of the table are the data points, and the columns of the table are the attributes. The weather measurements at a Finnish Meteorological Institute weather station are typically represented as a table (Fig.~1(a)): one row for each day. The table has four columns, one per attribute of a day: the date, the morning minimum temperature, the precipitation, and the maximum daytime temperature. The date identifies the data point, and the three measured attributes are the candidates for its features and its label. In Fig.~1(b), the learning task is to forecast the maximum daytime temperature of a day from its morning minimum temperature. A machine learning method reads the minimum-temperature column as the feature and the maximum-temperature column as the label, while the precipitation column is left unused. It learns a hypothesis from the 366 data points, shown as a scatterplot with the learned curve. The distinct characteristic of tabular data is the rigid shape of a table. Every row contains the same number of cells, one per column, and the cells within one column hold values of the same attribute of the data points. The value range must be clearly defined for each column, and every cell of a column holds a value from that range. The precipitation column of Fig.~1(a), for example, holds a daily amount in millimeters or the special value -1.0, which records that no precipitation was observed. A second, different use of a special value is a marker such as ``N/A'' reserved for an empty cell. Missing data are represented by an empty cell: an attribute that was not recorded for a data point leaves its cell empty, while the table keeps its shape. Data imputation fills such a cell with an estimate computed from the cells that were recorded. In database theory, the relational model formalizes a table as a relation. A relation is a set of tuples of attribute values. The relational model also provides the operations, such as selecting rows or joining tables, that database systems use to manipulate tabular data. The fixed attribute set is what separates tabular data from other data types. For the weather measurements, the station records the same quantities every day, so the attribute set is fixed by the measurement process and shared by every data point. A text, in contrast, is a sequence of tokens whose length varies from data point to data point, and a graph varies in its node and edge sets. Such data points carry no attribute set of their own. One can be imposed, for example the number of occurrences of each word from a fixed word list, but such a set discards the order of the tokens. The table of weather measurements loses nothing in this way, since a day is fully described by its four attributes, while a text with its tokens in another order is a different text. Instead, feature learning methods are developed that map such data points to feature vectors (or embeddings).

terms.name: trusted execution environment (TEE)
terms.abstract: A trusted execution environment (TEE) is a part of a computing system that runs code and holds data in isolation from the rest of the system. Neither the operating system nor the operator of the hardware can read or alter them, and the TEE can prove to another party which code it runs. Processor features such as Arm TrustZone and Intel SGX provide a TEE on an ordinary chip; a sealed, shielded embedded device without network connection is the physical extreme. In machine learning, a TEE protects three assets: the feature vectors handed to a learned hypothesis, the model parameters of that hypothesis, and the integrity of the computed prediction. It hides nothing about what the prediction reveals, which is the part that differential privacy addresses, and it protects against physical side channels only with hardware countermeasures. Compared with fully homomorphic encryption, a TEE runs at near-native speed but rests on trust in the chip vendor rather than on a mathematical proof.
terms.description: Consider a Raspberry Pi in a clinic that reads the signal of an electrocardiograph and computes, from the feature vector x of each heartbeat, the prediction h(x) of a learned hypothesis that flags an arrhythmia. The board sits in a sealed metal box with no network cable and no radio. The only inputs are the sensor cable and the power cable, and the only output is a display. The model parameters w of h and the recorded heartbeats never leave the box. A TEE is the part of a computing system that provides this kind of protection: code and data inside it cannot be read or altered from outside, and a party outside can verify which code runs inside. The sealed box is the physical extreme of a TEE. Most TEEs are instead a mode of an ordinary processor: Arm TrustZone splits the processor of the Raspberry Pi into a normal world, which runs Linux and the display software, and a secure world, which runs the prediction code and holds w and the heartbeats; the normal world cannot read the memory of the secure world even with root privileges. Intel SGX provides the same isolation for an enclave inside a process on a server, and remote attestation lets a client verify a signed digest of the enclave's code before it sends any data. Fig.~1 shows the Raspberry Pi and what each part can see. A TEE protects three assets of a machine learning system. The first is the data: the heartbeats are personal data that the clinic must not disclose. The second is the learned hypothesis: the model parameters w are the outcome of training on a costly dataset, and an attack that reads them out obtains the hypothesis without the dataset. The third is the integrity of the prediction: nobody can alter the code so that it flags fewer arrhythmias. A TEE does not protect what the prediction reveals. A membership inference attack that only observes predictions is unaffected by it, and differential privacy is the tool for that part. A TEE also does not, by itself, protect against side channels. The current drawn by the processor and the electromagnetic field it emits depend on the data it processes, and a probe held near the chip recovers secret keys from these traces. The same probe recovers the model parameters and the layer structure of an artificial neural network running on an embedded processor, one multiplication at a time. A short electromagnetic pulse or a glitch on the supply voltage can also skip an instruction, e.g., the check that rejects unsigned code. The metal enclosure of the Raspberry Pi attenuates the emitted field and blocks the pulse, tamper sensors erase w when the box is opened, and constant-time code makes the power trace independent of the data. Server TEEs face a software side channel instead: the memory access pattern of an enclave is visible to the operating system, so machine learning code inside an enclave must be data-oblivious, with access patterns that do not depend on the data, and speculative execution has leaked enclave memory outright. Two uses of TEEs beyond the sealed box are prediction in the cloud and federated learning. A hospital that rents a server can require an SGX enclave, verify by attestation that it runs the agreed prediction code, and send its feature vectors encrypted to the enclave's key, so that the cloud provider never sees them. In federated learning, an enclave on the server implements secure aggregation: the clients encrypt their model parameters updates to the enclave, which decrypts and sums them, and the server operator sees only the sum; the TrustZone secure world of each phone protects the local update in turn. A TEE, fully homomorphic encryption and differential privacy protect against different parties by different means. Fully homomorphic encryption hides the data from the computing party by mathematics, at a cost of orders of magnitude in time and memory, and needs no trust in the hardware. A TEE hides the data by hardware isolation at near-native speed, and rests on trust in the chip vendor and in the absence of side channels. Differential privacy bounds what the prediction reveals about any single data point and is combined with either.

terms.name: test set
terms.abstract: A test set consists of data points used to evaluate the performance of a hypothesis delivered by a machine learning method. These data points are used neither for training nor for model selection, which is why a test set is also called a hold-out set. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the average loss on the test set is an unbiased estimator of the risk of the learned hypothesis, and a concentration inequality bounds its deviation from the risk in terms of the test-set size. This yields a guideline for splitting a dataset: make the test set and the validation set just large enough for the required precision and train on the rest. The estimate stays valid only as long as no design choice depends on the test set; repeated evaluation with selection turns it into a validation set, and overlap with the training set constitutes test set contamination.
terms.description: Consider a machine learning method that reads in weather recordings from the station Krems an der Donau (Austria) and delivers a hypothesis h that predicts the next day's maximum temperature from the current day's. Assessing the quality of h requires applying it to data points that the method has not used: the method typically uses a training set for learning a hypothesis via empirical risk minimization and a validation set for comparing the hypotheses learned from different models. The data points of these two sets have tuned the learned hypothesis, which therefore typically incurs a smaller loss on them than on other data points. A test set D(test) is a dataset of data points used to evaluate the performance of a hypothesis delivered by a machine learning method. Its data points enter neither the training of a model, e.g., via empirical risk minimization on the training set D(train), nor the model selection based on a validation set D(val) (Fig.~1). Since its data points are held back from training and model selection, a test set is also referred to as a hold-out set; some texts use that name for the validation set instead. For a hypothesis h that was learned and selected without reference to D(test), the test error is the average loss \[ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm test)}|} \sum_{{\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{D}^{(\rm test)}} L\left({\mathbf z},\widehat{h} \right) \text{.} \] Interpreting the data points of D(train), D(val), and D(test) as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution p(z) (the independent and identically distributed assumption), the test error is an unbiased estimator of the risk of h. The distinction from the validation set is the direction of information flow: the validation error flows back into the choice of h, so it is an optimistic estimate for the chosen candidate. The test error is computed once, after all choices are frozen, and flows back into nothing. The sizes of the three sets are design choices (Fig.~2). Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the test error is an average of |D(test)| independent and identically distributed loss values, so a concentration inequality bounds its deviation from the risk: for a loss taking values in [0,1], with probability at least 1-δ the deviation is at most ln(2/δ)/(2 |D(test)|). The test set is therefore made just large enough for the required precision; the size of the validation set is chosen by the same argument, and the training set receives every remaining data point. No general rule fixes the proportions; a typical split is 50 percent for training and 25 percent each for validation and testing. The estimate stays valid only as long as the test set is used this way. Evaluating many candidate models on D(test) and keeping the best turns the test set into a validation set, and its error into a validation error; data points of D(test) that enter the training set constitute test set contamination. In a machine learning competition, the labels of the test set are therefore withheld from the participants: no design choice of theirs can then depend on the test data, and the reported error keeps its meaning as a risk estimate.

terms.name: training error
terms.abstract: The training error of a hypothesis is its average loss over the training set, the empirical risk of the hypothesis on the data points used for training. For a hypothesis delivered by empirical risk minimization, it is the smallest empirical risk that any hypothesis of the hypothesis space attains. Because the same data points selected the hypothesis, the training error is often far below the risk, by a gap that grows with the size of the hypothesis space, so a hypothesis with zero training error can have a large risk. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the training error of every hypothesis is a noisy estimate of its risk, and empirical risk minimization compares all of them at once, so a generalization guarantee for the empirical risk minimization solution requires the deviation to be small uniformly over the hypothesis space. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting, and a large training error indicates underfitting.
terms.description: Five years of days at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria), 2020 to 2024, are drawn in Fig.~1 as a scatterplot. Each day is a data point: its feature x is the morning minimum temperature, its label y the maximum temperature of the day. Three of the days, drawn in black, form a training set for two empirical risk minimization-based methods that deliver the hypotheses h(1) and h(2). The hypothesis h(1) is learned by empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss over the hypothesis space of affine maps h(x) = b + w x, the linear model. The dotted bars are its prediction errors on the three days, the differences between the recorded maximum and the value of h(1), and the average of the three squared bars is its training error, 7.91. The second hypothesis h(2) is learned by empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space of all polynomials of degree at most two. Although the training error of h(2) is zero, and therefore far below that of h(1), it is clearly the worse choice: averaged over all days of the five years, the loss of h(2) is 42.90 against 24.22 for h(1). Holding the intercept of h(1) at the value empirical risk minimization gave it and varying only its slope w leaves the training error a function of one number. Fig.~2 shows it with the risk, the expected loss over the probability distribution of a day, approximated by the average over the five years. The two functions have different minimizers: the training error is smallest at the slope that empirical risk minimization picked, the risk at a smaller slope. At the slope empirical risk minimization picked, the training error is a third of the risk. The training error is an average over the three days that determined the hypothesis; it does not measure the loss on a day outside the training set. The training error Et of a hypothesis h is its average loss over the training set D(train) = z(r)r=1m, \[ E_{t} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},\widehat{h} \right) \text{,} \] i.e., the empirical risk of h on the data points used for learning h. The hypothesis is the output of a training method, a map A that reads in a training set and delivers h = A(D(train)). For a hypothesis delivered by empirical risk minimization, the training error is the smallest empirical risk that any hypothesis of the hypothesis space attains on D(train), since empirical risk minimization minimizes this average. The training error is computed on the same data points that selected h, which limits its use as a measure of quality. The goal of a machine learning method is to learn a hypothesis that incurs a small loss on any data point, also those outside the training set. This goal can be formalized as the minimization of the risk, or expected loss, of a random data point, i.e., a random variable. The training error of the learned hypothesis is often a poor estimator for its risk, because the learned hypothesis has been adapted to the training set by minimizing the training error. A hypothesis with zero training error can therefore have a large risk, as h(2) of Fig.~1 does. The difference between the risk and the training error is the generalization gap. The validation error, computed as the average loss on data points not used in the training, is often a much better estimator for the risk of the learned hypothesis. As a case in point, let the data points of the validation set be realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, independent of the training set. Each summand of the validation error is then the loss on an independent draw from the probability distribution of a data point, whose expectation conditional on the training set is the risk of the learned hypothesis. The expectation of the validation error conditional on the training set is therefore that risk. Moreover, the validation error concentrates around the risk at a rate that depends only on the size of the validation set, not on how the hypothesis was learned. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the training error becomes a random variable, as it depends on the randomly generated training set. For one fixed hypothesis h ∈ H, the empirical risk L(h|D(train)) is an average of the m loss values L(z(1),h ), …, L(z(m),h ), which are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. It is therefore the realization of a random variable with expectation L ( h ) and a variance proportional to 1/m. Empirical risk minimization does not evaluate this estimate at one fixed hypothesis: it compares the estimates of all hypotheses in H and picks the smallest. The estimates form the family L(h|D(train)) h ∈ H, a stochastic process indexed by the hypothesis space: one random variable for each hypothesis, all realized by the single draw of D(train). The minimizer h of this process is itself a random variable, and its training error Et = L(h|D(train)) is the minimum of many noisy estimates, so it is below L ( h ) on average. A guarantee of generalization for the empirical risk minimization solution must therefore hold uniformly over the hypothesis space: if \begin{equation} \sup_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \big| \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}\big) - \bar{L} \big( h \big) \big| \leq \epsilon \text{,} \end{equation} then L ( h ) ≤ Et + ε, and the risk of h exceeds the smallest risk in H by at most 2ε. A hypothesis space for which the uniform deviation \eqref{eq_trainerr_uniform} falls below any ε with probability at least 1-δ once m is large enough has the uniform convergence property. For a finite hypothesis space and a loss with values in [0,1], a union bound over the hypotheses and Hoeffding's inequality give ε = ln(2 |H| / δ) / (2 m). For an infinite hypothesis space, ln |H| is replaced by a measure of its size such as the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension or the Rademacher complexity. The validation error estimates the risk of the single hypothesis that A delivered, and one Hoeffding bound without |H| suffices for it. Fig.~3 shows three deviations of a training error from a risk for one year of the Krems record: for one fixed hypothesis, for the hypothesis that empirical risk minimization learns, and the largest deviation over the hypothesis space. The 366 days of the year stand in for the probability distribution of a day, so the risk of a hypothesis is its average loss over the year, and a training set of m days is drawn at random from the year, 300 times for each m ∈ 10, 20, 40, 80. The hypothesis space is the linear model, which consists of all hypothesis maps h(x) = w1 x + w0 with w1, w0 ∈ R. The fixed hypothesis is the one with the smallest risk in the hypothesis space, the hypothesis learned by linear regression from all 366 days; it does not depend on the draw. The empirical risk minimization hypothesis is learned by linear regression from the drawn training set. The largest deviation over the hypothesis space, the uniform deviation \eqref{eq_trainerr_uniform}, is approximated by the maximum over a grid of 2500 hypotheses, 50 slopes w1 ∈ [0.8, 1.3] times 50 intercepts w0 ∈ [6, 15], together with the learned hypothesis. Over the repeated draws, the deviation of the fixed hypothesis has mean zero. The training error of the empirical risk minimization hypothesis is below its risk on average, and the largest deviation is several times the standard deviation of the fixed hypothesis' deviation. The gap of the empirical risk minimization hypothesis never exceeds the largest deviation, as the uniform deviation \eqref{eq_trainerr_uniform} requires, and both decrease as the training set grows (pythondemos/trainerr.py). The size of the gap L ( h ) - Et depends on the hypothesis space. The first day of each month from January to August 2024 forms a training set of eight days, and the rest of the year is held back. A hypothesis of the linear model learned from the eight days has a training error of 20.36, only slightly below its average squared error of 21.60 on the held-back days: the linear model has two model parameters and can adapt little to the particular eight days. Fig.~4 shows the two errors for polynomials of prescribed maximum degree p = 0, …, 7. Increasing the degree means a larger hypothesis space, a polynomial of degree p being one of degree p+1 with a zero leading coefficient, so the training error never increases with the degree. In contrast, the average loss on the held-back days is smallest at degree one and grows for larger degrees, where the polynomial oscillates between the eight days it was learned from. By comparing the training error of a machine learning method with the resulting validation error, two failures can be detected. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting. A large training error indicates underfitting: a hypothesis space too small, or an iterative optimizer that stopped too early, which restricts the effective hypothesis space. Fig.~4 also shows the effect of regularization by model pruning: restricting the hypothesis space by using a small polynomial degree raises the training error a little and lowers the average loss on the held-back days.

terms.name: training
terms.abstract: Training is the process of choosing a useful hypothesis out of a hypothesis space, or model. Mathematically, training is an optimization problem with an objective function that a training method builds from the data points it reads. In supervised learning the objective function is the average loss over data points whose label values are known, such as the average squared error loss. In unsupervised learning it measures structure instead, such as the clustering error incurred by a choice of cluster centroids. In reinforcement learning it is the expected cumulative reward collected by a policy. Training methods differ also in how they access data points. Offline methods require the training set up front, while online methods learn a hypothesis sequentially, updating it whenever new data points arrive.
terms.description: Training is the process by which a machine learning method picks one hypothesis out of a hypothesis space. The hypothesis space, or model, is the set of candidate maps the method may choose from. Training selects the single hypothesis h that the method then uses for inference: the training phase learns h, the inference phase uses it to deliver predictions for newly arriving data points. What makes one candidate better than another is an objective function, so training amounts to solving an optimization problem. Training methods differ along two axes. The first is the objective function. In supervised learning each data point carries a label, and the objective function is the average loss of a hypothesis over the training set, its empirical risk, such as the average squared error loss in linear regression. In unsupervised learning no label is given, so the objective function measures a structural quantity instead, such as the clustering error incurred by a choice of cluster centroids in hard clustering. In reinforcement learning there is no fixed training set at all: the objective function is the expected cumulative reward G collected by a policy that interacts with an environment. The second axis is the form of data access, offline or online. A training method is an algorithm A that reads in a dataset D of data points, constructs the objective function from them together with the chosen model and loss, and delivers the hypothesis making that objective function small, h = A(D). An offline algorithm reads in all data points at once, computes, and delivers h. An online algorithm reads in new data points as they arrive, updating the current hypothesis at each time instant t = 1, 2, … instead of waiting for a complete training set. The hypotheses it produces form a Markov chain, since each one depends on the dataset only through its predecessor and the data point that just arrived (Fig.~1). For a parametric model, each hypothesis h(w) is fixed by a choice of model parameters w, so training searches over w. Many training methods amount to iterating an operator on those model parameters, \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = T({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) \text{,} \] and the two forms of data access appear here as two forms of the operator. An offline method builds its objective function once, from the whole dataset, so T is fixed: the same map is applied at every step, and training stops at, or near, a fixed point of T, where a further iteration leaves the model parameters unchanged. An online method has no fixed objective function. Its operator reads in the arriving data point, \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = T\big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}, {\mathbf z}^{(t)}\big) \text{,} \] so the map changes from step to step, and in general there is no single fixed point to stop at. The model parameters keep changing for as long as new data points arrive. The learned hypothesis h is the one that the final model parameters define. What T does is decided by the shape of the objective function. When the objective function is differentiable in all model parameters at once, T is a gradient step, T(w) = w - η ∇ f(w) with step size η. The familiar methods are then one operator applied to three different objective functions, which is the data-access axis again. Offline empirical risk minimization takes the gradient of the average loss f(w) over the whole training set. When that training set is too large to pass through at every step, stochastic gradient descent replaces ∇ f(w) by the gradient of the average loss over a few data points. Its operator is drawn at random at each step, from a distribution that the training set fixes, so it is fixed in expectation rather than fixed outright. In online learning there is no training set at all, and online gradient descent takes one gradient step on the loss of the arriving data point alone. Some objective functions arising in training methods can be minimized easily once a subset of the model parameters is held fixed. Then T is one sweep of alternating optimization, a minimization over each subset in turn. The k-means algorithm alternates between assigning each data point to the nearest cluster and recomputing the cluster means. The expectation–maximization algorithm is the probabilistic instance: training a Gaussian mixture model, it alternates between the responsibilities of the mixture components for each data point and the parameters of those components. What separates expectation–maximization from a plain alternation is that each step minimizes a surrogate, a bound on the objective function rather than the objective function itself, which is why the likelihood function cannot decrease. Both are offline, so both reach a fixed point of their operator, and neither is guaranteed to reach the smallest loss available in H. A shop forecasts daily bread demand from the weather with a linear model. It trains that linear model by gradient descent on a year of past records. To let the forecaster follow a changing clientele instead, it trains the same linear model by online gradient descent on each new day's sales: the same model and the same objective function, moved from one form of data access to the other. One of the main challenges in machine learning is to control the discrepancy between the loss on the training set and the loss on data points outside it, and no choice of optimization method removes that challenge.

terms.name: training set
terms.abstract: A training set is a dataset used to train a model: it consists of data points for which the loss incurred by each candidate hypothesis can be evaluated, so that training methods can pick the hypothesis that performs best on it. Empirical risk minimization, for example, learns the hypothesis minimizing the average loss on the training set, the empirical risk, whose minimum value is the training error. Because the learned hypothesis is picked to perform well on the training set, a small training error can be misleading and result in overfitting. The validation error on a held-back validation set probes whether the learned hypothesis also predicts well outside the training set.
terms.description: The ultimate goal of a machine learning method is to learn a hypothesis (or to train a model) that incurs a small prediction error not only on the data points used for training but on any data point that is typical for the application. The prediction error is measured by some loss function: the loss is a number, typically nonnegative, that quantifies the error of a hypothesis on a single data point, such as the squared difference between the predicted and the true label. The goal is formalized probabilistically as a small risk: the expected loss under the probability distribution from which the data points are drawn (independent and identically distributed assumption). The method must therefore compare the candidate hypotheses from its hypothesis space on data points for which the loss can be evaluated. For example, in regression or classification, the loss can only be computed for data points with a known label. These data points form a dataset referred to as the training set, D(train) = z(r)r=1m. A training method is a map A whose input is the training set and whose output is a learned hypothesis, h = A(D(train)). Training evaluates this map on the given training set. For example, empirical risk minimization minimizes the average loss on the training set, the empirical risk, to learn a hypothesis \[ \widehat{h} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},h \right) \text{.} \] The empirical risk of the learned hypothesis is the training error. Consider three days of weather recordings: for each day, the morning minimum temperature is the feature and the maximum daytime temperature is the label. Fig.~1 shows a training set of these three days along with two hypotheses learned from it: the linear hypothesis h(1) delivered by empirical risk minimization on the linear model, and a degree-two polynomial h(2) that passes through all three data points and therefore attains a training error of zero. Which data points are contained in D(train) decides what is learned. The choice of the training set is therefore crucial for trustworthy artificial intelligence: a training set that underrepresents a group of data points can yield a learned hypothesis that incurs a larger loss on that group, a source of unfairness (see fairness). Since h is chosen to make the empirical risk small, the training error is typically smaller than the loss that the same hypothesis incurs on data points outside D(train). A small training error therefore does not guarantee a small loss outside the training set. Fig.~1 illustrates this: the polynomial h(2) has a smaller training error than the linear hypothesis h(1), so the training error prefers the polynomial. The figure shows no data points outside D(train), but it shows that the two curves predict different labels for feature values between and beyond the three training data points.
