At most one of the two curves can therefore incur a small loss on a new data point with such a feature value, and the training error cannot tell which one (see overfitting). A second subset of data points, the validation set D(val), is therefore held back from model training (Fig.~2): the average loss on D(val), the validation error, probes the learned hypothesis on data points it was not trained on. Comparing the two errors diagnoses the machine learning method: if both are small, the learned hypothesis is likely to predict well outside D(train) as well. A small training error paired with a validation error far above it indicates overfitting; one typical cause is a hypothesis space that is too large for the number of data points in D(train).

terms.name: transfer learning
terms.abstract: Transfer learning is the reuse of what was learned on one learning task to solve another learning task. A learning task can be characterized by a probability distribution of data points, and the effectiveness of transfer learning depends on the similarity of the corresponding probability distributions. Task similarity can be encoded as a similarity graph whose edge weights couple the learning tasks at its nodes; transfer learning methods can then be obtained by optimization over this graph.
terms.description: The weather stations Krems an der Donau and Melk in the Wachau valley each record the minimum and the maximum temperature of every day. Predicting the maximum temperature y of a day at one station from its minimum temperature x is a learning task. Each weather station defines a separate learning task. Fig.~1 shows the two tasks side by side, each with a decision tree of depth two, the hypothesis learned from a training set of five labeled days of 2020. A learning task can be characterized by the probability distribution of its data points: at the two stations those distributions are similar. Transfer learning uses such similarity. It couples the learning tasks so that what is learned at one station improves the predictions at the other, and its effectiveness depends on how similar the probability distributions of the coupled tasks are. The coupling in Fig.~1 is implemented by adding a penalty to the objective function of the model training at each station. Let h(1) and h(2) be the hypotheses of the two stations and T a test set of feature values selected at random from the range [-10, 10] of minimum temperatures. Transfer learning then minimizes the sum of the two training errors plus α 1|T| Σx ∈ T ( h(1)(x) - h(2)(x) )2, the mean squared disagreement of the two hypotheses on the test features. For decision trees, minimizing over one tree while the other is fixed is a weighted fit of that tree to its own days together with the test features labeled by the other tree, and alternating the two fits solves the coupled problem. With five labeled days per station, the coupled trees agree on the test features (mean squared disagreement 32.2 → 0.1), and their average error on the held-out days of the two stations falls from 47.4 to 33.5. The coupling of two tasks extends to a collection of learning tasks, one per node i = 1, …, n of an undirected weighted graph G, the similarity graph. A weighted edge i,i' with edge weight Ai,i' encodes the similarity between two learning tasks; a zero weight leaves them uncoupled. Each node i carries a local model, a local dataset, and the local hypothesis h(i) learned from them. Minimizing the sum of the local training errors plus α times the generalized total variation \sum_{\{i,i'\} \in \mathcal{E}} A_{i,i'} d^{(i,i')} \text{,} with d(i,i') a measure of the discrepancy between the local hypotheses h(i) and h(i'), is generalized total variation minimization. The coupling in Fig.~1 is generalized total variation minimization on a graph with two nodes, with the mean squared disagreement on the test features T as the discrepancy measure; this measure applies to any local model, the decision trees included. For local models with model parameters w(i), the squared distance ‖ w(i) - w(i') ‖22 is a common choice, and the network Lasso is the variant with the unsquared distance. Generalized total variation minimization learns all local hypotheses simultaneously and transfers knowledge between well-connected learning tasks, as in federated learning. Fig.~2 shows a similarity graph of nine stations in Lower Austria, with edge weights that fall off with the distance between stations. With five labeled days and a decision tree at every station, generalized total variation minimization with the disagreement on T lowers the average held-out error of the nine stations from 57.0 to 35.9 and the error at eight of them; at the ninth, Wien, whose edges are the weakest of the graph, the coupling raises it slightly, from 29.5 to 30.8. A special case of transfer learning is a node without any labeled data points. Its own training error is absent from the objective, so generalized total variation minimization determines its hypothesis through the generalized total variation alone, from the predictions of its neighbors on the test features. This is semi-supervised learning: the unlabeled node still has data points, and its position in the similarity graph is what lets them be used. A different form of transfer learning adapts a deep net trained on a large dataset to a small one: the features computed by its early layers are kept (see feature learning) and the remaining model parameters are adapted by fine-tuning. When the features useful for the first task are not useful for the second, the adapted hypothesis can have a larger risk than one trained from scratch, which is called negative transfer. The case in which the learning task stays fixed and only the probability distribution of the feature vectors changes is domain adaptation.

terms.name: transformer
terms.abstract: A transformer is an artificial neural network built by composing layers, each of which transforms the features of a data point made up of smaller units, so-called tokens, such as the words of a text or the patches of an image. The feature vectors of the tokens are stacked into a matrix; each layer maps this matrix to one of the same shape, so that layers can be composed freely into a deep artificial neural network. The layers alternate between token mixing, which combines information across tokens, and a position-wise multilayer perceptron, which transforms each token separately.
terms.description: Many machine learning applications involve data points that consist of smaller units, so-called tokens: a text consists of words, and an image consists of patches of pixels (see Fig.~1). A transformer is an artificial neural network that is built by composing layers, each of which transforms the features of such a token-based data point. The feature vectors (or embeddings) x(1), …, x(n) ∈ Rd of the n tokens are stacked into a matrix X = (x(1), …, x(n))ᵀ ∈ Rn × d. Each layer of the original transformer maps such a matrix to a transformed matrix of the same shape, so that layers can be composed freely into a deep artificial neural network. For example, a transformer that translates a sentence transforms the stacked word embeddings, layer by layer, into feature vectors from which the translated words are predicted; transformers also process images by taking patches as tokens. Contemporary LLMs, such as GPT-3, are transformers trained to predict the next token of a text. Some transformer variants reduce the number of tokens in deeper layers. The layers of a transformer alternate between two types of transformations of X (see Fig.~2). A token-mixing layer maps X to a new matrix X, each row of which is a weighted sum of the rows of X, with weights that can depend on X itself; the tokens thereby interact. In the original transformer, token mixing is implemented by multi-head attention; attention distinguishes transformers from RNNs, which process the tokens of a data point sequentially instead of in parallel. A position-wise multilayer perceptron then transforms each row of X separately. For each of the two transformations, a residual connection adds the input of the transformation to its output, and a subsequent layer normalization standardizes each row of the resulting matrix. The matrices produced by successive layers represent the tokens at increasingly abstract levels. This progression is measured by probing: a simple classifier is trained to predict a chosen property from the output of a single layer, and the depth at which the property becomes predictable locates it in the network. In a language transformer, word-level properties are predictable from the output of early layers. One example is a part-of-speech tag, which marks whether a word is a noun, a verb, or an adjective. Relations between tokens far apart in the text become predictable only in deeper layers. Deep CNNs show the same progression, from edges and textures in early layers to object parts in deeper ones. Vision transformers develop it too: their early layers split attention between nearby and distant patches, while the deeper layers attend across the whole image. In language and vision transformers alike, the most informative representations often arise in the middle layers, whose outputs can outperform those of the final layer as features for other tasks. The token mixing that produces the matrix of each layer is computationally expensive. Attention compares every pair of tokens, so its cost grows as n2 with the number n of tokens. This quadratic growth motivates alternative techniques for token mixing. Any transformation that combines the rows of X can replace attention: a multilayer perceptron applied across tokens, a fixed Fourier transform, or a state-space layer whose cost is linear in n.

terms.name: transparency
terms.abstract: Transparency is a key requirement for trustworthy artificial intelligence: it names the duties to close the information gaps between the provider of an artificial intelligence system, its deployer, and the persons affected by its predictions. For machine learning methods, transparency is often used interchangeably with explainability: explanations, delivered along with the predictions of a learned hypothesis, let a human user anticipate those predictions. The EU AI Act makes transparency a binding design requirement. Under the Act, the provider must design a high-risk artificial intelligence system so that its deployer can interpret the delivered predictions. Persons interacting with an artificial intelligence system must be informed of that fact. Affected persons may obtain an explanation of decisions based on the predictions delivered by a high-risk artificial intelligence system. The Act also requires documentation of the algorithm design, the training datasets, and the intended use of an artificial intelligence system, as well as a machine-readable marking of synthetic content as artificially generated.
terms.description: Consider a bank that uses an artificial intelligence system to score loan applications. The loan officer sees only the score, and the applicant might not even know that an artificial intelligence system was involved. Transparency names the duties to close such information gaps; it is a fundamental requirement for trustworthy artificial intelligence. In the context of machine learning methods, transparency is often used interchangeably with explainability: explanations, delivered along with the predictions of a learned hypothesis, let a human user anticipate those predictions. Some machine learning methods inherently offer this form of transparency. Classification methods quantify the confidence in an individual prediction via the distance of the feature vector from the decision boundary. A shallow decision tree does not require a separately constructed explanation: presenting the tree as a flow chart of explicit, human-readable decision rules is an explanation of every prediction it delivers (see interpretable machine learning). In the broader scope of AI systems, transparency extends beyond explainability: it includes informing persons that an artificial intelligence system is in use and providing information about the limitations, the overall reliability, and the intended use of the system as a whole. The binding transparency obligations discussed below are those of the EU AI Act; other jurisdictions impose related but distinct duties, e.g., the Colorado Automated Decision-Making Technology Act and the court proceedings State v. Loomis on the use of a proprietary recidivism-risk score in sentencing. The Act distributes its obligations among three roles: the provider that develops an artificial intelligence system, the deployer that uses it, and the persons who interact with the artificial intelligence system or are affected by its output (see deployer). The Act's term output denotes the predictions delivered by a learned hypothesis; the machine learning term prediction is used below. Like interpretability and explainability, which are relative to a specific user or group of users, transparency is relative to its addressee: what must be disclosed depends on the role. Concretely, Fig.~1 locates these obligations in a scatterplot of training set data points together with a learned hypothesis, for the credit-scoring example. The solid curve depicts the learned hypothesis h that the artificial intelligence system applies: it maps the income x of an applicant to a predicted credit score h(x), and a loan is approved when the predicted score exceeds an approval threshold (dotted line). Art.~13 concerns the use of this map: the deployer must be able to interpret the delivered predictions — here, to read off the prediction h(x') for an applicant with income x' (open square) and its distance from the threshold. The filled circles depict the training set D(train) of completed loans, with income as the feature x and credit score as the label y, from which h was learned, e.g., via empirical risk minimization — by minimizing the average loss of the hypothesis over D(train). Art.~11 requires the provider to document both ingredients of this training: the dataset D(train) and the design of the algorithm, including the model and the loss used. Income levels outside the range covered by D(train) (shaded region) are a limitation that the documentation must state, since no estimate of the risk computed from D(train) covers them. The right to explanation of Art.~86 concerns a single prediction: the applicant with income x', whose predicted score falls below the threshold, may ask why. One answer is a counterfactual: the smallest change of the feature that flips the decision — the income x'' (open diamond, arrow) at which h reaches the threshold. Specifically, toward the deployer, the provider must design and develop a high-risk artificial intelligence system so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable the deployers to interpret its predictions and use them appropriately. In medical diagnosis, the provider is, e.g., a company that develops an X-ray analysis tool, and a clinic that uses the tool acts as the deployer. The provider can meet the duty of Art.~13 by designing the tool to disclose to the clinician the confidence level for the predictions delivered by a learned hypothesis. This duty targets the meaning of the predictions in the context of their use; the AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology reserves the term interpretability for this contextual meaning. This usage differs from interpretability as the comprehension of the computational process of the method; Art.~13 does not require that comprehension. Toward persons who interact directly with an artificial intelligence system, such as an artificial intelligence-powered chatbot, the provider must design the artificial intelligence system so that these persons are informed of that fact. Providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must mark such content in a machine-readable format as artificially generated. This marking duty applies whether or not the artificial intelligence system is a high-risk artificial intelligence system; it is waived, e.g., where the artificial intelligence system only performs an assistive function for standard editing. For a deep fake, the deployer must, in addition, disclose visibly that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. A person can be affected by an artificial intelligence system without directly interacting with it. A patient whose diagnosis is supported by an artificial intelligence-based system deals only with the clinician. Nevertheless, the deployer must inform the patient that a high-risk artificial intelligence system is used concerning them. The EU AI Act also grants the affected person a right to explanation: the deployer must, on request, provide a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the artificial intelligence system in a decision based on its predictions. In credit scoring, for example, a loan applicant faced with an adverse automated decision may obtain from the deployer, under this right, an explanation of the contributing factors, such as income level or credit history, and use it to contest the decision (see Fig.~1). Transparency also encompasses documentation detailing the purpose and design choices underlying the artificial intelligence system. For a high-risk artificial intelligence system, the provider must provide documentation that covers the algorithm design and the datasets used for training. The provider of a general-purpose AI model must additionally publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training. Datasheets for datasets and model cards help practitioners understand the intended use cases and limitations of an artificial intelligence system. Fig.~2 summarizes these transparency obligations as information flows between the provider of an artificial intelligence system, its deployer, and the persons exposed to its predictions.

terms.name: trustworthy artificial intelligence (trustworthy AI)
terms.abstract: Trustworthy artificial intelligence (trustworthy AI) names an artificial intelligence system that meets requirements beyond accuracy: human oversight, robustness, privacy, transparency, fairness, societal well-being, and accountability. The seven key requirements of the EU Ethics Guidelines are stated for the artificial intelligence system as a whole, including the people and the organization around the machine learning method inside it. Five of them constrain the components of empirical risk minimization: the training set, the model, the loss function, the algorithm, and the learned hypothesis. Each such requirement is a measurable property of that hypothesis or of the method that learned it: a bound on the change of a prediction under a perturbation of the feature vector, the change of the prediction when only a sensitive attribute is flipped, the counterfactual that explains a rejection, or the share of borderline decisions passed to a person. The EU AI Act makes several of these requirements binding for a high-risk artificial intelligence system, and they can conflict, so trustworthiness is a set of measured properties balanced for the application rather than a single number.
terms.description: Consider a bank that uses an artificial intelligence system to decide on loan applications. The system applies a hypothesis h, learned from the records of completed loans, to the feature vector x of an applicant, which collects the income, the gender, and further attributes. The loan is approved when the predicted creditworthiness h(x) exceeds a threshold τ. The bank, its supervisor, and the applicant rely on these decisions only if the system meets requirements beyond accuracy. A small change of the income must not flip the decision, the gender alone must not flip it either, a rejected applicant must learn why, and a loan officer must be able to overrule the system. Trustworthy AI names an artificial intelligence system that meets such requirements. The Ethics Guidelines of the European Commission's High-Level Expert Group state seven key requirements (KRs): human agency and oversight (KR1), technical robustness and safety (KR2), privacy and data governance (KR3), transparency (KR4), diversity, nondiscrimination, and fairness (KR5), societal and environmental well-being (KR6), and accountability (KR7). The accompanying assessment list turns each requirement into questions that the provider and the deployer of the artificial intelligence system answer about their system. The requirements are stated for an artificial intelligence system as a whole, which includes the data pipeline, the user interface, and the organization that operates it, and not only for the machine learning method inside it. KR6 and KR7 concern the purpose and the governance of the system and have no counterpart in the machine learning method. KR1 to KR5, in contrast, constrain the components of empirical risk minimization: the training set D(train), the model H, the loss function, and an algorithm that minimizes the average loss over D(train), as well as the learned hypothesis h that results. Each of these requirements can be stated as a measurable property of h or of the method that learned it, and the design choices for the components of empirical risk minimization are the means to meet it. Fig.~1 places KR1, KR2, KR4, and KR5 in the credit-scoring example. The horizontal axis is a one-dimensional sketch of the feature vector x: the income, the gender, and the further attributes of an applicant collapsed into one coordinate. The vertical axis is the creditworthiness, the label y. The filled circles are the training set D(train) of m = 5 completed loans, the solid curve the hypothesis h learned by minimizing the average loss over D(train), and the dotted line the approval threshold τ = 3.8. The applicant with feature vector x' (open square) obtains the predicted creditworthiness h(x') = 2.94 and is rejected. KR2 asks that a small perturbation of the feature vector changes the prediction little. The perturbation of x' by δ = 0.5 (horizontal arrow) moves the predicted creditworthiness from 2.94 to 3.19 (vertical arrow). The slope of h never exceeds 1.225, so no perturbation by δ changes the prediction by more than 1.225 δ: the learned hypothesis is Lipschitz continuous with constant 1.225 (see robustness). KR2 also covers perturbations of D(train), e.g., by data poisoning, against which the stability of the machine learning method protects. KR5 asks that the decision does not depend on a sensitive attribute s such as gender. The open triangle depicts the same applicant with only the gender flipped, the feature vector x⋆. The predicted creditworthiness rises to h(x⋆) = 3.93, above τ, and the loan is approved: the decision depends on the gender, which violates the counterfactual criterion of fairness. The gap h(x⋆) - h(x') = 0.99 measures the violation. It is closed by a design choice for a component of empirical risk minimization: the model (excluding the sensitive attribute and the features correlated with it), the loss function (a penalty term for the gap), or D(train) (resampling the groups). KR4 asks for transparency: the rejected applicant is told that an artificial intelligence system was used and may obtain an explanation. The counterfactual x'' (open diamond), at which h reaches τ, is such an explanation. It is the smallest change of the income, at fixed gender, that flips the decision, and it tells the applicant the income at which the loan would be approved. The gender flip x⋆ also flips the decision, but it is not a change the applicant can make, which is what makes it a violation of KR5 rather than an explanation. KR1 asks that a person can oversee and overrule the decisions. The shaded band marks predicted creditworthiness within ε = 0.3 of τ. Applications in this band are passed to a loan officer, who decides; one of the five loans in D(train) falls into it. A wider band passes more applications to the officer and leaves fewer borderline decisions to the system (see human oversight). KR3 asks that the records of completed loans, which are personal data, are protected during training and cannot be recovered from h; differential privacy and federated learning are design choices for the algorithm and for D(train) to that end (see data governance). The requirements are increasingly codified. The EU AI Act makes KR1 to KR4 binding for a high-risk artificial intelligence system, a class that includes the credit scoring of natural persons: risk management (Art.~9), data governance (Art.~10), transparency (Art.~13), human oversight (Art.~14), and accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity (Art.~15). ISO/IEC~42001 specifies a certifiable management system for artificial intelligence, and the AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology structures trustworthiness into the functions govern, map, measure, and manage. The requirements can conflict: closing the gender gap raises the average loss on D(train), and the noise that differential privacy adds to the training makes explanations less precise. Trustworthiness is therefore a set of measured properties that are balanced for the application, not a single number.

terms.name: unsupervised learning
terms.abstract: Unsupervised learning refers to machine learning methods that do not require knowledge of the label of any data point. These methods learn a hypothesis by loss functions that are constructed from the features of data points only. Two important examples of unsupervised learning are clustering and dimensionality reduction. Clustering methods use some notion of clustering error to learn model parameters that encode a cluster structure. Dimensionality reduction methods construct a loss from the reconstruction error.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows data points representing daily weather conditions at Krems an der Donau. Each data point is characterized by two features, the daily minimum and the daily maximum temperature. Unsupervised learning methods learn a hypothesis map that predicts a label that is not known for any of these data points. For example, the label could be an index that selects one out of two clusters to which the data point belongs. Another label could be the optimal scalar representation of a data point. Formally, an unsupervised machine learning method learns a hypothesis out of a hypothesis space based on an unlabeled dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) of feature vectors x(r) ∈ X, with no label space. The model parameters are typically learned by an instance of empirical risk minimization, minimizing the average loss over the dataset, \[ \widehat{h} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},h \right) \text{.} \] What sets unsupervised methods apart from supervised methods, such as linear regression, is the choice of loss function. Two important families of unsupervised methods are obtained by specific constructions of the loss, clustering and dimensionality reduction. The clustering method k-means uses k cluster centroids as model parameters w = w(1), …, w(k). They are learned by minimizing the average clustering error, the loss \[ L\left({\mathbf x},{\mathbf w} \right) = \min_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \] Principal component analysis is a dimensionality reduction method that learns a linear feature transformation x ↦ W x together with a reconstruction map z ↦ R z that rebuilds the feature vector from it. Both are model parameters, and for a given R the loss of a data point is its reconstruction error \[ L\left({\mathbf x},\left( {\mathbf W},{\mathbf R} \right) \right) = \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf R} {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \] One R is used for the whole dataset, and empirical risk minimization learns it together with W by minimizing the average of this loss. For the learned pair the reconstruction is the orthogonal projection of the feature vector on a subspace of dimension d'.

terms.name: validation error
terms.abstract: The validation error Ev of a learned hypothesis is its average loss over a validation set. For a fixed hypothesis and data points that are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, the validation error is an unbiased estimator of the risk. If the training set is itself modelled as random, the learned hypothesis becomes a random variable too, and the validation error is unbiased conditioned on the learned hypothesis. The validation error characterizes a learned hypothesis that some machine learning method obtained from a training set. It can therefore be used to choose between different models or, more generally, between different machine learning methods. The validation error also helps to diagnose a machine learning method and to guide its revision.
terms.description: Fig.~1 shows a scatterplot of data points that represent daily weather conditions at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria), 2020 to 2024. Each day is a data point: its feature x is the morning minimum temperature, its label y the maximum temperature of the day. Three of the days, drawn in black, form the training set. The hypothesis h(2) learned from them is a degree-two polynomial through all three days, so its training error is zero. Three further days, drawn as red triangles, form a validation set. The dotted bars are the prediction errors of the polynomial on them, the differences between the recorded maximum and the value of the curve. The average of the three squared bars is the validation error of the polynomial, 42.58. The validation error is the average loss of h(2) on days that did not belong to the training set. The training error carries no information about such days: the polynomial passes through the three training days by construction. The validation error, 42.58, is close to the average squared error loss of h(2) over all days of the five years, 42.90. A hypothesis with a larger training error can be the better one: the linear hypothesis that empirical risk minimization delivers from the same three days over the linear model has a training error of 7.91 and a validation error of 6.98. The validation error Ev of a hypothesis h is its average loss over a validation set D(val), \[ E_{v} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}|} \sum_{{\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}} L\left({\mathbf z},\widehat{h} \right) \text{.} \] Because no data point of D(val) entered the training, Ev estimates the risk of h. The training error, computed over the training set whose average loss empirical risk minimization minimized, is below it on average: the same data points both selected h and assessed it. The validation error is an average of |D(val)| losses. For data points that are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, Ev is the realization of a random variable whose expectation is the risk of h, since each summand has that expectation. The validation error is therefore an unbiased estimator of that risk. Its variance is the variance of a single loss divided by |D(val)|, so its standard deviation decreases as |D(val)| grows. In practice h = A(D(train)) is the output of a training method, a map A that reads in the training set D(train), so it is itself the realization of a random variable: a different realization of D(train) would have delivered a different hypothesis. The validation error is then unbiased conditioned on the learned hypothesis. If the data points of D(val) are independent of those of D(train), and hence of h, the conditional expectation of Ev given h is the risk of that hypothesis, \[ \mathbb{E} \big\{ E_{v} \mid \widehat{h} \big\} = \bar{L} \big( \widehat{h} \big) \text{.} \] The training error has no such property: conditioned on h, the data points of D(train) are no longer independent and identically distributed realizations of the probability distribution of a data point, because h was chosen to make its average loss on them small. A guarantee for the validation error concerns one hypothesis only: for a loss with values in [0,1], Hoeffding's inequality gives |Ev - L ( h )| ≤ ln(2/δ) / (2 |D(val)|) with probability at least 1-δ, with no term for the hypothesis space H. A guarantee for the training error of the empirical risk minimization solution must hold uniformly over H, since empirical risk minimization compares all its hypotheses. A numerical experiment shows how much the validation error varies when the validation set is chosen at random. Consider the hypothesis \[ \widehat{h}(x) = 10.47 + 1.05 x \text{,} \] obtained by linear regression from forty of the data points of Fig.~1, every ninth day of 2024. The data points of 306 further days of that year, none of them used for training, are collected in the test set D(test), and each validation set below is drawn at random from D(test). Fig.~2 shows the value range of the validation error of h over repeated draws of a validation set of prescribed size from D(test). The standard deviation of the validation error decreases with increasing size of the validation set. This agrees with the behavior of the bound from Hoeffding's inequality above. However, strictly speaking, that bound does not apply here, since the squared error loss is not constrained to [0,1]. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting. Comparing the validation errors of several candidate models is model selection. A model has no validation error of its own. The phrase is short for the validation error of the hypothesis that A delivers from that model, since Ev is the average loss of a single hypothesis. The selected model is the one whose hypothesis attains the smallest of the compared validation errors, so that validation error is biased downward as an estimate of the risk, and a test set is kept apart for the final assessment.

terms.name: validation set
terms.abstract: A validation set consists of data points that have not been used for model training. For a learned hypothesis, the average loss on the validation set, the validation error, indicates how well the hypothesis predicts the labels of data points outside the training set. The validation error is used for model selection: the hypotheses learned by different machine learning methods are compared, and the one with the smallest validation error is selected. The selected hypothesis depends on the validation set, so assessing it requires a test set whose data points entered neither training nor selection. The size of the validation set determines how reliable the validation error is. When data points are scarce, k-fold cross-validation uses each fold of the dataset in turn as validation set and averages the k validation errors.
terms.description: Consider three days of weather recordings: for each day, the morning minimum temperature is the feature and the maximum daytime temperature is the label. Fig.~1 shows a training set D(train) of three such days along with two hypotheses learned from it: the linear hypothesis h(1) delivered by empirical risk minimization on the linear model, and a degree-two polynomial h(2) that passes through all three data points and therefore attains a training error of zero. Three further days, marked by open triangles, were held back from model training: they form a validation set D(val). The validation error of a hypothesis h learned from the training set is its average loss on the validation set, \[ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}|} \sum_{{\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}} L\left({\mathbf z},\widehat{h} \right) \text{.} \] Here, L(z,h ) is the loss of h on the data point z. In Fig.~1, the polynomial h(2) attains a training error of zero but a validation error of 17.3, while the linear hypothesis h(1) has a training error of 2.9 and a validation error of 3.0. The comparison of the two validation errors is an instance of model selection: the hypotheses learned by different machine learning methods are compared, and the one with the smallest validation error is selected. In Fig.~1, the hypothesis h(1) is selected, since 3.0 < 17.3. The selected hypothesis depends on D(val): its validation error is the smallest of the compared validation errors, so the validation error of the selected hypothesis is biased downward. A bound that covers the selected hypothesis must hold for all compared hypotheses at once, which requires a validation set larger than the size that Hoeffding's inequality suggests for one hypothesis. Assessing the hypothesis learned from the model that was chosen on the basis of the validation errors requires a third dataset whose data points entered neither training nor selection: the test set D(test). In Fig.~2, the three days of the test set, marked by open squares, yield a test error E(test) = 1.3 for the selected hypothesis h(1). The test error is the only one of the three numbers that was not used to choose anything, so it is not biased by selection. With only three test days, however, it is itself a noisy estimate of the risk of h(1). The size |D(val)| determines how well the validation error reflects the overall performance of a learned hypothesis: the validation error is an average of |D(val)| losses, one per validation data point, and a validation set that is too small results in an unreliable validation error. For a loss with values in [0,1] and a fixed hypothesis h, Hoeffding's inequality guarantees that, with probability at least 1 - δ for a confidence parameter δ ∈ (0, 1) chosen by the user, the risk of h lies within an uncertainty band of half-width ε around the measured validation error. The guarantee requires that \[ |\mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}| \geq \frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2 \epsilon^{2}} \text{.} \] Fig.~3 shows this lower bound as a function of the half-width ε for three values of δ; it holds for any validation error, not only those of the weather example. Narrowing the band is costly: halving ε quadruples the required size. To have the validation error within ε = 0.1 of the risk with δ = 0.1, it suffices to hold back |D(val)| ≥ 150 data points, the point of the dashed curve at ε = 0.1 in Fig.~3, regardless of the hypothesis space and of the size of D(train). The bound can be checked by simulation. Fig.~4 reports how often the validation error of a fixed hypothesis deviates from the risk by more than ε, when the validation set holds exactly the number of data points that the bound requires. The loss used there takes the values 0 and 1 with equal probability, so its variance is the largest a loss with values in [0,1] can have. Each share is measured over 200,000 validation sets. Every measured share stays below its δ, and below δ / 4, so the size the bound requires is larger than the size the measured deviations call for. A validation set eight times smaller does fail the guarantee: at ε = 0.1 and δ = 0.1, where the bound asks for 150 data points, 19 of them leave 36 of every 100 validation errors farther than ε from the risk. When data points are scarce, holding back a large validation set leaves few data points for the training set. As a remedy, k-fold cross-validation divides the dataset into k folds and, for each fold in turn, uses that fold as validation set and the other k - 1 folds as training set, so each of the k validation errors is computed on different data points and for a different learned hypothesis. Every fold yields a noisy validation error, an average of the losses over the few data points of the fold, and averaging the k per-fold validation errors produces a more reliable estimate of the risk. Taken together, a typical machine learning workflow splits the available dataset three ways: a training set to learn hypotheses, a validation set to select among them (or the folds of k-fold cross-validation in its place), and a test set, used only once, to assess the selected hypothesis.

terms.name: variance
terms.abstract: The variance of a real-valued random variable is the expectation of the squared difference between the random variable and its mean. It quantifies the spread of the probability distribution of the random variable around the mean: a small variance means that realizations concentrate near the mean. The term also refers to the sample variance of a dataset; the two usages are consistent, since the sample variance is the variance of the random variable obtained by drawing a data point uniformly from the dataset. Under the squared error loss, the variance is the smallest risk that a constant prediction of a numeric label can achieve. For a random vector, the variance is the expectation of the squared Euclidean norm of the deviation from the mean. This quantity equals the trace of the covariance matrix of the random vector, i.e., the sum of the variances of its entries.
terms.description: The Helsinki Kaisaniemi weather station recorded daily maximum temperatures of 20.1, 19.9, 22.2, 21.7, 20.3, 19.6 and 19.7 ∘C on 24--30 August 2026, and every reading lies within two degrees of their average of 20.5 ∘C. How far readings scatter around their average is what the variance measures. The variance of a real-valued random variable y is the expectation E ( y - Ey )2 of the squared difference between y and its expectation Ey, also called its mean. The term is also used to refer to the sample variance of a finite dataset D = y(1), …, y(m) ∈ R. These two usages are consistent. A dataset defines a discrete random variable y(D) = y(I) on the sample space 1, …, m. Here, the index I is chosen uniformly at random, i.e., P(I=r)=1/m for all r=1,…,m, so the probability distribution of y(D) is the empirical distribution of the dataset. The variance of y(D) is precisely the sample variance \[ \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \Big( y^{(r)} - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r'=1}^{m} y^{(r')} \Big)^{2} \text{,} \] i.e., the average squared deviation of the data points from their sample mean. Fig.~1 depicts the seven Helsinki readings of 24--30 August 2026 as realizations of such a random variable, together with their sample mean and the deviation of each measurement from it. For the seven temperatures of Fig.~1, the sample variance is the number 6.34/7 ≈ 0.91, computed from the readings alone. It estimates the variance of the random variable that generated them, which is a property of its probability distribution and is never observed exactly. The sample variance also serves as a threshold for detecting outliers: a common rule declares a data point an outlier when its squared deviation from the sample mean exceeds nine times the sample variance, i.e., three standard deviations. The reading of 22.2 ∘C deviates by 1.7 ∘C, whose square 2.89 is about three times the sample variance, so the rule keeps every reading. For a random variable with a finite second moment, i.e., E y2 < ∞, the mean is the constant b that minimizes the risk E ( y - b )2. The variance is the smallest value this risk attains, i.e., its minimum at b = Ey: \[ \mathbb{E}\big\{ \big( y - \mathbb{E}\{y\} \big)^{2} \big\} = \min_{b \in \mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E}\big\{ ( y - b )^{2} \big\} \text{.} \] This minimum-risk characterization applies directly to the simplest machine learning problem, predicting a numeric label y without using any features. The hypothesis space for this problem consists of the constant maps h(·) = b with b ∈ R. Each such hypothesis amounts to a single bias term: it delivers the same prediction b for every data point. Given a training set D(train) = y(1), …, y(m) that consists of labels y(r) ∈ R only, empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss amounts to finding the constant that best predicts the label of a data point. The solution b is the sample mean of the labels (see mean), and the training error of the learned hypothesis is the sample variance of the labels. For the temperatures of Fig.~1, the learned hypothesis is the dashed line: b = 20.5 ∘C, with training error 6.34/7 ≈ 0.91. The variance of the label is the smallest risk that a constant prediction can achieve under the squared error loss. It therefore serves as a baseline: a machine learning method that uses features is useful only if its risk falls below the variance of the label. Variance extends from a real-valued random variable to a random vector x as the expectation of the squared Euclidean norm of the deviation from the mean, E ‖ x - Ex ‖22 = tr (C(x)). This is the sum of the variances of the entries of x, written compactly as the trace of the covariance matrix C(x), whose diagonal carries those variances.

terms.name: explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)
terms.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is the subfield of artificial intelligence concerned with making the predictions of machine learning methods understandable to humans. Much of it can be posed as a function approximation problem: a learned hypothesis is explained by a simpler function that a human can comprehend. Explanations differ in what they are made of. One kind reports a score for each feature, the weights of a linear map fitted near the data point (local interpretable model-agnostic explanations) or additive contributions to the prediction (SHapley Additive exPlanations). A counterfactual instead names another feature vector, the closest one whose prediction differs. A concept activation vector states the explanation in a concept the user names, located in the activations inside the trained method. All three are post hoc and treat the learned hypothesis as fixed. The alternative is a hypothesis that needs no separate explanation, reached by restricting the hypothesis space to hypotheses a human comprehends or by regularization that favors such hypotheses. Explainable empirical risk minimization instead keeps the hypothesis space and penalizes deviations from the predictions of one specific user.
terms.description: XAI is the subfield of artificial intelligence concerned with making the predictions of machine learning methods understandable to humans. It aims to complement each prediction by an explanation of how it has been obtained. If the machine learning method uses a sufficiently simple hypothesis space, the learned hypothesis may be inherently interpretable and no separate explanation is needed; see interpretable machine learning, discussed further below. The term XAI was popularized by a program of the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency; in the context of machine learning, the synonymous term explainable machine learning is also used. The underlying property is explainability, which the international terminology standard for artificial intelligence defines for AI systems in general. XAI can be posed as a function approximation problem. A trained hypothesis h: X → Y, e.g., delivered by an opaque deep net, is typically a composition of many nonlinear layers, a function on a high-dimensional feature space X. Explaining h at a data point with feature vector x ∈ X means answering one question about that function in a form a human can comprehend. The examples of explanations below are of three kinds, distinguished by what the explanation is made of. The first is a score for each feature of the data point. The scores are the coefficients of a simpler hypothesis that agrees with h near x and comes from a user-parsable hypothesis space. Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations fits a linear map as that simpler hypothesis, and its weights are the scores. Fig.~1 draws that construction. The second is another feature vector, one whose prediction differs. The third is a concept the user names, located inside the trained method rather than among the features of the data point. All three are post hoc: they treat the learned hypothesis as fixed and construct the explanation after training. The first kind of explanation reports one score per feature, saying how much that feature contributed to the prediction. Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations obtains the scores as the weights of a linear map fitted to h near x. SHapley Additive exPlanations obtains them by decomposing the prediction into a base value and one contribution per feature, the contributions being Shapley values. The two deliver the same kind of explanation and differ in how its scores are computed. When features are properties of image pixels, the feature scores are a second image of the same size: one relevance score per pixel (see Fig.~2). The class activation map is one construction of such a per-pixel score. The second kind of explanation is a counterfactual. It reports no scores and approximates nothing. It asks instead where h takes a different value, pointing out how the features must be modified for the prediction h(x) to come out differently. A counterfactual identifies the smallest such modification, with closeness measured by a chosen metric (see Fig.~3). In a loan-approval setting, for example, local interpretable model-agnostic explanations reports which of the applicant features, such as income and credit history, its local linear approximation assigns the largest weight to in a rejection. A counterfactual instead states the smallest modification of those features that would turn the prediction into an approval. The third kind of explanation refers not to the features of the data point but to a concept the user specifies. Such a concept is defined by a dataset of examples the user supplies. A concept activation vector locates such a concept as a direction in the space of the activations of one hidden layer of an artificial neural network: the normal vector of a decision boundary that separates the supplied examples carrying the concept from those that do not. In contrast to local interpretable model-agnostic explanations and counterfactual explanations, a concept activation vector needs access to the internal computations of a machine learning system. One such internal computation is the activation z = f(x) of a hidden layer in a deep net. A deep net computes h by feeding the activations z to the final layers, which deliver a score s(z) for each label; the prediction h(x) follows from those scores (see concept activation vector). In an image classifier, for example, a user who suspects that photographs are labeled zebra through the concept stripes supplies photographs that show stripes and photographs that do not. Each of these photographs results in an activation z in the layer of interest. These activations are then used to fit a linear classifier that separates the two sets, and its normal vector is the concept activation vector for stripes. How much the concept contributed to the prediction of a zebra photograph is then measured by the directional derivative of the score s along that concept activation vector. The above XAI methods construct an explanation after training, for a learned hypothesis that is already fixed. The alternative is to arrive at one that needs no separate explanation. Interpretable machine learning does so by admitting only hypotheses a human comprehends directly. This can be achieved by manually choosing a hypothesis space that is simple enough, or by regularization that favors hypotheses with specific properties, such as sparsity or predictability. Explainable empirical risk minimization uses regularization but not to that end: it leaves the hypothesis space as it is and delivers explainability to one specific user. That user supplies their own predictions for the data points of a training set, and the penalty term measures the deviation of the predictions of the learned hypothesis from the user predictions. Three aspects of an explanation are studied: whom it serves, how much of the learned hypothesis it covers, and whether it is faithful. How much an explanation achieves depends on who receives it: explainability is measured relative to a specific user. Explanations can be local, concerning a single prediction, or global, characterizing the learned hypothesis as a whole. An explanation must be faithful, i.e., reflect the computation that the learned hypothesis carries out. When the explanation scores the features, this can be tested rather than asserted. A class activation map is faithful for a prediction if flipping the pixels it scores highest changes that prediction more often than flipping as many of the pixels it scores lowest. Perturbing the highest-scoring regions first and recording how quickly the predicted class score falls is the standard form of the test. For the image of Fig.~2 and a linear classifier fitted to images of that kind, flipping the three highest-scoring pixels changes the prediction, while flipping the pixels in the opposite order leaves it unchanged through all 36 of them. The map-guided order also changes the prediction sooner on each of 200 noisy variants of the image. Faithfulness also limits what a post hoc explanation can achieve: one that agreed with the learned hypothesis everywhere would be that hypothesis itself, so a simpler explanation deviates from it somewhere. Two legal instruments explicitly state requirements on XAI. Under the general data protection regulation, a person subjected to a decision taken by automated means is entitled to ``meaningful information about the logic involved'' in that decision. Communicating the algorithm itself is not a sufficiently concise and intelligible explanation. Counterfactual information can be appropriate: the extent to which a variation in the personal data would have led to a different result. The second instrument is the EU AI Act, which requires for a high-risk artificial intelligence system that affected persons obtain ``clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure'' (see right to explanation).
